# How Much Does a Website Cost for a Small Business in 2026?
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/how-much-does-a-website-cost-small-business/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Real price ranges for small business websites in 2026, what drives the cost up or down, and how to avoid paying for things you don't need.

Key takeaways:
- Most small business websites cost between $1,500 and $10,000 to build professionally
- Page count matters less than features like booking, payments and custom design
- Ongoing costs (domain, hosting, maintenance) usually run $10 to $150 a month
- A fixed quote and a preview before you pay removes most of the risk

"How much does a website cost?" is the first question almost every business owner asks us, and the honest answer is a range. A website is closer to a renovation than a product on a shelf: the price depends on what you're building, who builds it and how much of the thinking is done for you.

This guide gives you real numbers, explains what actually moves the price, and shows you how to budget without getting burned.

## The short answer

Here are the typical ranges we see across the market in 2026 for a small business website:

| Route | Typical upfront cost | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace) | $0 to $500, plus your time | Brand-new businesses testing an idea |
| Freelancer using a template | $500 to $2,500 | Simple brochure sites on a tight budget |
| Custom design by a small studio | $2,500 to $10,000 | Established businesses that need leads |
| Agency build with strategy and content | $10,000 to $50,000+ | Larger companies with complex needs |

Most established small businesses (a coaching practice, a salon, a solar installer, a wedding photographer) land in the third row. That's the range where you get custom design, proper SEO foundations and someone thinking about conversion, without paying for a room full of account managers.

## What actually drives the cost

Page count is the thing people fixate on, but it's rarely the biggest factor. These are.

### 1. Custom design vs a template

A template gives you someone else's layout with your logo dropped in. Custom design starts from your customers: what they need to see, in what order, to trust you and get in touch. Custom takes more hours, which is why it costs more, but it's also why it tends to convert better.

### 2. Functionality

A five-page site that only displays information is simple. The cost rises when the site has to *do* things:

- Online booking or appointment requests
- Payments, deposits or a full online store
- Calculators, quizzes or quote builders
- Member areas, courses or client portals
- Integrations with your CRM, calendar or email platform

Each of these is a mini software project. A solar savings calculator, for example, can take longer to build than the rest of the site combined.

### 3. Content

Someone has to write the words and source the images. If you supply polished copy and professional photos, the build is faster. If your designer is also writing your copy, structuring your offers and directing photography, expect to pay for that time. It's usually worth it: content is what persuades.

### 4. SEO depth

Every decent build should include the basics: fast pages, clean structure, title tags, a sitemap. Deeper work costs extra: keyword research, location pages, schema markup, and migrating an old site without losing rankings. If you rely on Google for leads, read our technical SEO checklist (/blog/technical-seo-checklist/) before you sign anything.

### 5. Who you hire

A freelancer has low overheads. An agency has project managers, strategists and an office. A small founder-led studio sits in between: senior work without the layers. Rates also vary a lot by country, which is why a studio like ours can deliver agency-level work for clients in the US, UK and Australia at a lower price than a local agency.

## The ongoing costs people forget

The build is a one-off. These are not:

- **Domain name:** $10 to $20 a year for most `.com` names.
- **Hosting:** $5 to $50 a month for a typical small business site. Builders like Wix and Squarespace bundle this into a $16 to $40 monthly plan.
- **Maintenance:** $0 to $150 a month depending on the platform. WordPress sites need regular plugin and security updates. Hand-coded static sites need very little.
- **Email:** around $6 to $12 per user per month for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
- **Tools:** booking software, email marketing and CRM subscriptions, if you use them.

A fair all-in running cost for most small businesses is $20 to $100 a month. If you're being quoted $300 a month for "hosting" on a five-page site, ask exactly what's included. We cover this in detail in our website maintenance guide (/blog/website-maintenance-guide/).

## Three sample budgets

To make this concrete, here's how three common projects typically price out.

**A one-page site for a new coach.** A single long page with an about section, services, testimonials and a booking link. Expect $800 to $2,500 depending on design polish and whether copy is included.

**A lead-generation site for a local service business.** Eight to fifteen pages: home, about, a page per service, a few location pages, reviews, contact and a quote form. Expect $3,000 to $8,000 with proper SEO setup.

**A booking or e-commerce site.** A salon with online booking and deposits, or a store with 50 products and Stripe checkout. Expect $5,000 to $15,000 depending on the catalog and integrations.

## How to avoid overpaying

1. **Get a fixed quote, in writing.** Hourly billing puts all the risk on you. A fixed price for a defined scope puts it where it belongs.
2. **Ask what you'll own.** You should get the domain, the code, the design files and admin access. If the answer is vague, walk away. More on this in do you really own your website? (/blog/website-ownership-explained/)
3. **Check live work, not mockups.** Anyone can make a pretty picture. Click through real sites they've launched and test them on your phone.
4. **Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.** Launch with what you need to win customers, then add features once the site is paying for itself.
5. **See something before you pay.** A studio confident in its work will show you a direction first. That's why we offer a free website preview (/free-website-preview/): we design your homepage on a live link before you commit to anything.

## Is a cheap website a false economy?

Sometimes. A $300 website that brings in no enquiries costs more than a $5,000 website that brings in two new clients a month. The right question isn't "what's the cheapest site I can get?" but "what will this site be worth to my business?"

If one new client is worth $2,000 to you, a site that converts even one extra visitor a month pays for itself quickly. That's the lens to use.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I build a website for free?
Yes. Builders like Wix and Google Sites have free plans, but they show ads, use a subdomain and limit features. They're fine for testing an idea, not for a business that wants to look established.

### Why do quotes for the same website vary so much?
Because the scope behind them differs. One quote may be a template with your logo; another includes strategy, copywriting, custom design and SEO. Ask each provider to list exactly what's included and compare like for like.

### Should I pay monthly or upfront?
Upfront builds usually cost less over three years and leave you owning the site. "Website as a service" monthly plans lower the barrier but often mean you're renting, and lose the site if you stop paying. Check the contract.

---

# Custom Website vs Wix vs Squarespace: Which Should You Choose?
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/custom-website-vs-wix-squarespace/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

An honest comparison of custom-built websites and DIY builders like Wix and Squarespace: cost, speed, SEO, flexibility and when each one makes sense.

Key takeaways:
- Builders are the right choice when you're starting out and budget matters more than polish
- Custom sites win on speed, flexibility, SEO control and standing out from competitors
- The real cost of DIY is your time and the leads a generic site doesn't convert
- Many businesses start on a builder and move to custom once the website becomes a sales channel

Website builders have made it possible for anyone to get online in a weekend. So why do businesses still pay for custom websites? Because "online" and "winning customers online" are different goals.

We build custom sites for a living, so you might expect a one-sided answer. You won't get one: there are situations where a builder is exactly the right call, and we'll tell you when.

## The quick comparison

| | Wix / Squarespace | Custom website |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upfront cost | $0 to $500 | $2,500 to $10,000+ |
| Monthly cost | $16 to $40 | $5 to $50 hosting |
| Time to launch | Days (of your time) | 1 to 4 weeks |
| Design | Templates, limited tweaks | Built around your brand |
| Page speed | Average | Fast when built well |
| SEO control | Good basics, limited depth | Full control |
| Custom features | Whatever the platform allows | Anything you can describe |
| Ownership | You rent the platform | You own the code |

## When a builder is the right choice

A builder makes sense if:

- **You're validating a new business.** Don't spend $5,000 on a website for an idea you haven't sold yet.
- **Your budget is under $1,000.** A good template beats a bad custom build.
- **You enjoy doing it yourself** and have the time to learn design, copy and SEO basics.
- **Your site is a simple brochure** and most of your customers come from referrals anyway.

Squarespace in particular produces clean, respectable sites, and for a lot of new businesses that's enough for year one.

## Where builders start to hurt

### Everyone looks the same

Templates are popular for a reason, which means your competitors are using them too. When a customer has three tabs open and all three sites share the same layout, the cheapest price tends to win. Distinctive design is how you avoid competing on price.

### Speed and Core Web Vitals

Builders load their entire platform on every page, whether you use the features or not. That extra weight shows up in load times, especially on mobile. A hand-coded site only ships what the page needs. Speed affects both rankings and conversion; we explain how in Core Web Vitals explained (/blog/core-web-vitals-explained/).

### The feature ceiling

Builders are great until you want something they don't offer: a savings calculator, a multi-step quote form, a custom booking flow, a page layout the template doesn't support. Then you're stacking third-party widgets, each with its own monthly fee and its own look.

### SEO depth

Modern builders handle the basics well. Where they fall short is fine control: custom schema markup, clean URL structures, precise control over what loads and when. For competitive local searches, those details add up. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/) for what you'd be missing.

### You're renting

On a builder, your site lives on their platform under their terms. If they raise prices or retire a feature, you adapt. You can't take a Wix site and host it elsewhere. A custom site is a set of files you own outright.

## The hidden cost of DIY: your time

A builder's sticker price ignores the biggest cost. Business owners typically spend 30 to 60 hours building their own site, then more hours every month fiddling with it. If your time is worth $75 an hour, that "free" website cost $3,000 before you count the leads a generic site didn't convert.

The question isn't whether you *can* build it yourself. It's whether that's the best use of your week.

## What custom actually gets you

A good custom build isn't just a prettier template. It includes:

- **Strategy.** Someone who has built dozens of sites in your industry knows what your customers need to see.
- **Conversion design.** Every page has a job and a clear next step.
- **Performance.** Lean code that loads fast on a phone with two bars of signal.
- **Flexibility.** If you can describe it, it can be built.
- **Ownership.** Your code, your content, your accounts.

Here are two custom builds where a template wouldn't have done the job:

## A middle path

It doesn't have to be all or nothing. Three options sit between DIY and fully bespoke:

1. **Start on a builder, upgrade later.** Totally valid. Just make sure you own your domain so the move is painless.
2. **Buy a ready-made custom site.** A pre-built, professionally designed site that you rebrand. We sell a small number of these on our templates page (/templates/); each sells to one owner only.
3. **Custom design, simple build.** A focused one-page custom site costs far less than a full build and still looks nothing like a template.

## How to decide

Ask yourself three questions:

1. **Is the website a sales channel or a business card?** If customers find and choose you through it, invest. If it just confirms you exist, a builder is fine.
2. **What's one new customer worth?** If the answer is more than a few hundred dollars, a better-converting site pays for itself quickly.
3. **Do you want to spend your evenings on this?** Be honest.

If you're on the fence, the lowest-risk way to decide is to see what custom would look like for your business. Our free website preview (/free-website-preview/) exists for exactly this: we design your homepage on a live link, you compare it with what you have, and you decide with real evidence.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Wix or Squarespace bad for SEO?
No. Both cover the fundamentals and plenty of builder sites rank well. They offer less control over speed and advanced technical SEO, which matters more in competitive markets.

### Can I move from Squarespace to a custom site later?
Yes. Your content can be migrated and your URLs redirected so you keep your rankings. Read how to redesign without losing SEO (/blog/seo-migration-redesign/) before you switch.

### Is WordPress a builder or custom?
Both, depending on how it's used. A WordPress site with a bought theme and 30 plugins behaves like a builder. A custom-coded WordPress theme is closer to a custom site, with more maintenance than a static build.

# How Long Does It Take to Build a Website? Realistic Timelines
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-build-a-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Realistic timelines for building a small business website, from one-page sites to e-commerce, plus the delays that derail projects and how to avoid them.

Key takeaways:
- A focused small business website takes 1 to 4 weeks with an experienced team
- Content, not code, is the most common cause of delay
- A clear brief and one decision-maker can halve the timeline
- E-commerce and custom features add weeks, not days

The honest answer: anywhere from a few days to a few months. A one-page site for a coach is a very different project from a 200-product online store. What matters more than the average is understanding which parts take time, and which of those you control.

## Typical timelines by project type

| Project | Typical timeline |
| --- | --- |
| One-page site or landing page | 3 to 7 days |
| Small business site (5 to 10 pages) | 1 to 3 weeks |
| Larger site with location and service pages (15 to 40 pages) | 3 to 6 weeks |
| Booking site with payments | 3 to 6 weeks |
| E-commerce store | 4 to 10 weeks |
| Web app or custom platform | 2 to 6 months |

These assume an experienced team and a client who responds within a day or two. Stretch either and the numbers stretch with them.

## The four phases of a website project

### 1. Discovery (1 to 3 days)

A conversation about your business, customers, competitors and goals. The output is an agreed scope: which pages, which features, what success looks like. Skipping this phase is the fastest way to make a project slow.

### 2. Design (3 to 7 days)

The homepage usually comes first because it sets the visual language for everything else. Once that direction is approved, inner pages follow quickly. At Code Bunny this is where our free website preview (/free-website-preview/) fits: we design your homepage on a live link before you've committed, so the riskiest decision is made early.

### 3. Build (1 to 3 weeks)

Design becomes working pages: responsive layouts, forms, animations, integrations, SEO setup. For a brochure site this is fast. Features like booking, payments and calculators are where build time grows.

### 4. Launch (2 to 4 days)

Testing on real devices, connecting the domain, setting up analytics and Search Console, redirecting old URLs and submitting the sitemap. It's tempting to rush this. Don't: a broken form on launch day costs real enquiries.

## What actually causes delays

In our experience across more than a hundred projects, the code is almost never what holds things up. These are the real culprits.

### Waiting for content

This is the big one. The design is done, the pages are built, and everyone waits three weeks for the about page copy. If you take one thing from this article: **start gathering your content before the project starts.** That means:

- A short description of each service
- Your story and credentials
- Testimonials and reviews
- Logo files and brand colours
- Photos of you, your team and your work
- Logins for your domain and any existing tools

If writing isn't your strength, ask your designer to draft the copy for you to edit. Reacting to a draft is far quicker than staring at a blank page.

### Too many decision-makers

Feedback from one person takes a day. Feedback from a committee takes a week and often contradicts itself. Nominate one person to collect opinions and give a single, consolidated response.

### Scope creep

"Can we also add a blog, a members area and a quiz?" Each addition is reasonable. Together they double the project. Park new ideas in a phase-two list and launch what was agreed.

### Slow feedback loops

A two-week project has room for two or three review rounds. If each one takes five days to come back, it's now a six-week project.

## How to launch faster

1. **Write a brief.** Even one page helps. Use our website brief template (/blog/website-brief-template/).
2. **Collect content first.** See the list above.
3. **Share examples.** Three sites you like and one you don't saves days of guessing.
4. **Agree the scope and freeze it.** New ideas go on the phase-two list.
5. **Give feedback in one batch, within 48 hours.**
6. **Launch, then improve.** A good site that's live beats a perfect site that isn't. You can refine copy and add pages after launch.

## Can a website really be built in a week?

Yes, when the scope is tight and the content is ready. We regularly take a business from first call to live site in under two weeks. The projects that manage it share the same traits: a clear offer, a decisive owner and content supplied up front.

What can't be rushed is the thinking. A site built quickly on a muddled message will underperform a site built quickly on a clear one. If you're not sure what your site should say, start with what pages a small business website should have (/blog/what-pages-should-a-small-business-website-have/).

## How long until the website brings in leads?

Launch day isn't the finish line. Visitors from ads and social media can arrive immediately. Search traffic takes longer: Google needs to crawl, index and trust a new site, which typically takes a few weeks for brand searches and three to six months for competitive terms. We break this down in how long does SEO take? (/blog/how-long-does-seo-take/)

## Frequently asked questions

### Why do some agencies quote three months for a simple site?
Often it's process overhead: multiple teams, scheduled review meetings and a queue of other projects. A small senior team can move faster because the person you speak to is the person doing the work.

### Does a faster build mean lower quality?
Not necessarily. Speed comes from experience, reusable components and clear decisions. Quality drops when testing is skipped or content is rushed, so make sure those aren't what's being cut.

### What do you need from me to get started?
A short description of your business and customers, any existing website or social profiles, your logo if you have one, and a few sites you like. That's enough for us to design a first preview.

# 12 Signs Your Business Needs a New Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/signs-you-need-a-new-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Twelve clear signs your website is costing you customers, from slow load times to falling enquiries, and what to do about each one.

Key takeaways:
- If enquiries have dropped or never came, the website is the first place to look
- Slow mobile load times and confusing navigation lose visitors within seconds
- You don't always need a full rebuild; some problems have quick fixes
- A redesign should protect your existing Google rankings with proper redirects

Websites rarely fail loudly. They just quietly stop pulling their weight: fewer enquiries, more "I couldn't find your prices" phone calls, an awkward pause when someone asks for your web address.

Here are twelve signs it's time for a change, roughly in order of how much they cost you.

## 1. It doesn't bring in enquiries

The clearest sign of all. If people visit and leave without calling, booking or filling in a form, the site isn't doing its job. Check your analytics: if you get 500 visitors a month and two enquiries, the problem isn't traffic.

## 2. It's slow on a phone

More than half of web traffic is mobile, and visitors won't wait. Test your site at PageSpeed Insights (https://pagespeed.web.dev/). If the mobile score is in the red or the page takes more than three seconds to become usable, you're losing people before they've read a word. See Core Web Vitals explained (/blog/core-web-vitals-explained/) for what the numbers mean.

## 3. It looks dated

Design trends move, and visitors judge credibility in a fraction of a second. Tiny text, stock photos of handshakes, a cluttered sidebar and a copyright date from years ago all say the same thing: this business isn't paying attention.

## 4. It's awkward to use on mobile

Being technically "responsive" isn't enough. Can you tap the phone number? Are the buttons big enough for a thumb? Does the menu work? Is the text readable without zooming? Borrow a friend's phone and try to book your own service.

## 5. You're embarrassed to share it

If you hesitate before giving out your URL, or apologise for the site when you do, trust that instinct. Your website should be something you're proud to put on a business card.

## 6. You can't update it yourself

If changing your opening hours means emailing a developer and waiting a week, the site will always be out of date. A modern site should let you edit everyday content yourself. When we launched Dan Reynolds Photography, it shipped with a built-in editor and blog so Dan can publish his own stories.

## 7. It doesn't show up on Google

Search your main service plus your town. If you're nowhere on the first page (and competitors with worse reviews are), the site likely has thin content, weak structure or technical problems. Our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/) explains what Google looks for.

## 8. Your business has changed

New services, new prices, a new location, a new audience. If the website describes the business you ran three years ago, it's attracting the wrong customers and under-selling the right ones.

## 9. Visitors leave immediately

A high bounce rate on your homepage usually means a mismatch: people expected one thing and found another, or couldn't tell within five seconds what you do. A clear headline, a strong image and one obvious next step fix most of it. See homepage design best practices (/blog/homepage-design-best-practices/).

## 10. It isn't secure

No padlock in the address bar (HTTPS) means browsers show a "Not secure" warning. That alone will stop people filling in your contact form. Outdated plugins are a related risk: they're the most common way small business sites get hacked.

## 11. Your competitors' sites are better

Customers compare. Open your top three competitors side by side with your own site. If theirs are clearer, faster and more convincing, that's where the enquiries are going.

## 12. It's built on something nobody supports

A discontinued builder, a theme that hasn't been updated since 2019, or code written by a developer who's disappeared. If nobody can safely change the site, it's a liability.

## Redesign, rebuild or repair?

Not every problem needs a new website.

**Repair** when the design is fine but specific things are broken: slow images, a missing call to action, outdated copy. These are often a few days' work.

**Redesign** when the structure and platform are sound but the look and messaging are tired.

**Rebuild** when the platform itself is the problem: it's slow, insecure, impossible to edit or can't support what you need.

If you ticked four or more signs on this list, a rebuild is usually cheaper in the long run than patching.

## What a good redesign protects

A new site should never cost you the traffic you already have. Before anything is switched off:

- Every old URL should redirect to its new equivalent
- Page titles and content that rank well should be kept or improved
- Analytics and Search Console should stay connected
- The new site should be tested on real phones

Our website redesign checklist (/blog/website-redesign-checklist/) walks through all 30 steps, and how to redesign without losing SEO (/blog/seo-migration-redesign/) covers the redirects in detail.

## Where to start

You don't have to commit to a full project to find out what's possible. Two low-effort options:

1. **Get a second opinion.** Send us your URL and we'll tell you honestly whether it needs a repair, a redesign or a rebuild.
2. **See the alternative.** With our free website preview (/free-website-preview/), we design a new homepage for your business on a live link. Put it next to your current site and the decision usually makes itself.

## Frequently asked questions

### How often should a business redesign its website?
Most businesses benefit from a significant refresh every three to five years, with smaller updates in between. If the site still converts well and loads fast, there's no need to change it just because time has passed.

### Will a redesign hurt my SEO?
It can if it's done carelessly. With proper redirects and preserved content, a redesign normally improves rankings because the new site is faster and better structured.

### How much does a redesign cost?
Similar to a new build of the same size, sometimes a little less if your content is in good shape. See how much a website costs (/blog/how-much-does-a-website-cost-small-business/) for ranges.

---

# The Website Redesign Checklist: 30 Steps to Relaunch Without Losing Traffic
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/website-redesign-checklist/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A 30-step website redesign checklist covering planning, content, SEO redirects, testing and launch, so your new site keeps its rankings and wins more leads.

Key takeaways:
- Benchmark your current traffic and rankings before changing anything
- Map every old URL to a new one with 301 redirects
- Test forms, speed and mobile on real devices before launch
- Watch Search Console daily for the first two weeks after relaunch

A redesign is the highest-leverage marketing project most small businesses ever run. It's also the easiest way to accidentally erase years of Google rankings in an afternoon. This checklist keeps the upside and removes the risk.

Work through it in order. Each phase builds on the one before.

## Phase 1: Before you touch anything

1. **Write down the goal.** "Look more modern" isn't a goal. "Increase enquiries from 6 to 15 a month" is.
2. **Benchmark current performance.** Record monthly visitors, enquiries, top landing pages and conversion rate from your analytics.
3. **Export your rankings.** In Google Search Console, export the queries and pages report for the last 12 months. These are the pages you must protect.
4. **Crawl the existing site.** Use a free tool like Screaming Frog (up to 500 URLs) to list every URL, title and meta description.
5. **List what works.** Pages that rank, copy that converts, photos customers mention. Keep them.
6. **List what doesn't.** Confusing navigation, dead pages, outdated services.
7. **Back everything up.** Download a full copy of the current site and database.

## Phase 2: Plan the new site

8. **Decide the sitemap.** Which pages stay, merge, split or go. See what pages a small business website should have (/blog/what-pages-should-a-small-business-website-have/).
9. **Build the redirect map.** A spreadsheet with two columns: old URL, new URL. Every old page needs a destination. This single document protects your SEO.
10. **Keep URLs where you can.** If `/services/boiler-repair/` ranks well, don't rename it for the sake of tidiness.
11. **Write a brief.** One page covering audience, goals, pages, features and examples. Use our website brief template (/blog/website-brief-template/).
12. **Choose the platform deliberately.** If the old platform was the problem, don't rebuild on it.

## Phase 3: Content and design

13. **Rewrite the homepage headline.** It should say what you do, for whom and where, in one line.
14. **Give every page one job.** One primary call to action per page.
15. **Update proof.** Fresh testimonials, current review counts, recent work.
16. **Keep ranking content.** If a page ranks, improve its copy rather than replacing it wholesale.
17. **Optimise images.** Export in WebP at the size they'll be displayed. Our image SEO guide (/blog/image-seo/) covers this.
18. **Write unique titles and meta descriptions** for every page. See title tags and meta descriptions (/blog/title-tags-meta-descriptions/).

## Phase 4: Build and test

19. **Build on a staging link** that search engines can't index.
20. **Test every form.** Submit each one and confirm the email arrives.
21. **Test on real phones.** At least one iPhone and one Android.
22. **Check speed.** Run PageSpeed Insights on the homepage and a service page. Aim for green on mobile.
23. **Add schema markup.** Organization, LocalBusiness, Service and FAQ where relevant. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/).
24. **Check accessibility basics.** Colour contrast, alt text, keyboard navigation.

## Phase 5: Launch

25. **Implement the 301 redirects** from your redirect map and test a sample of old URLs.
26. **Remove the noindex** from staging settings. Forgetting this is the classic launch-day mistake.
27. **Reconnect analytics and Search Console** and submit the new XML sitemap.
28. **Update your Google Business Profile** and social links if any URLs changed.

## Phase 6: After launch

29. **Monitor Search Console daily for two weeks.** Watch for 404 errors and coverage issues and fix them as they appear.
30. **Compare against your benchmark after 30, 60 and 90 days.** A small dip in the first two weeks is normal. A sustained drop means redirects or content need attention.

## The three mistakes that cause most redesign disasters

**No redirects.** Old URLs return 404 errors, and Google drops them. Rankings that took years vanish in weeks.

**Deleting content that ranks.** A designer trims a 900-word service page to three sentences because it "looks cleaner". The page stops ranking.

**Launching with noindex still on.** The whole site disappears from search until someone notices.

All three are avoidable with the checklist above. We go deeper in how to redesign without losing SEO (/blog/seo-migration-redesign/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does a redesign take?
Most small business redesigns take two to six weeks. See realistic website timelines (/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-build-a-website/).

### Should I redesign in stages or all at once?
For most small sites, a single well-planned launch is simpler and safer. Staged rollouts make sense for large sites with hundreds of pages.

### Can you redesign my site without changing the platform?
Often, yes. But if the platform is the reason the site is slow or hard to edit, a rebuild on something better usually costs less over time.

---

# What Pages Should a Small Business Website Have?
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/what-pages-should-a-small-business-website-have/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

The essential pages every small business website needs, what each one should contain, and which extra pages are worth adding for SEO and conversions.

Key takeaways:
- Five core pages cover most small businesses: home, about, services, proof and contact
- Give each service its own page so it can rank on Google
- Location and FAQ pages add search visibility with little effort
- Every page needs one clear next step

You can build a successful business website with five pages. You can also build a failing one with fifty. What matters is that every page has a clear purpose and leads the visitor one step closer to getting in touch.

Here's what to include, in priority order.

## The five essentials

### 1. Home

Your homepage has about five seconds to answer three questions: what do you do, who is it for, and what should I do next? It needs a clear headline, one strong image, proof you're trustworthy and a prominent call to action. Everything else is supporting detail. We break it down in homepage design best practices (/blog/homepage-design-best-practices/).

### 2. About

One of the most-visited pages on any small business site. People want to know who they'd be dealing with. Include your story, your credentials, real photos and what you believe about your work. Then end with a call to action; about pages convert when they ask.

### 3. Services (one page each)

This is where most small sites go wrong. They list eight services on a single page with a sentence each. Google can't rank one page for eight different searches, and customers can't find the detail they need.

Give each core service its own page with:

- Who it's for and the problem it solves
- What's included and how it works
- Pricing or a starting price, if you can share it
- Proof: a testimonial or example specific to that service
- Answers to common questions
- A call to action

### 4. Proof

Testimonials, reviews, case studies or a portfolio. For a photographer or designer the portfolio is the product. For a service business, a page of real reviews with names does the same job. Scatter proof across other pages too; don't hide it all in one place.

### 5. Contact

Make it effortless. A short form, a phone number that's tappable on mobile, your email, your address and hours if you have a location, and a note about how quickly you reply. See contact forms that convert (/blog/contact-form-best-practices/).

## Pages that earn their place

Once the essentials are solid, these add real value.

### Location or service-area pages

If you serve several towns, a dedicated page for each helps you appear in local searches. They must contain real, local content: thin copy-and-paste pages can hurt more than help. Our guide to local landing pages that rank (/blog/local-landing-pages/) shows how.

### FAQ

A good FAQ page answers the questions you're tired of answering by email, removes objections and gives search engines and AI assistants clear question-and-answer content to quote. Marked up with FAQ schema, it's one of the easiest SEO wins.

### Pricing

Controversial, but usually worth it. Visitors who can't find any indication of cost often assume they can't afford you, or that you're hiding something. Even "packages start from $X" filters out poor fits and builds trust.

### Blog or guides

Useful articles bring in visitors who aren't ready to buy yet and position you as the expert when they are. It only works if you publish genuinely helpful content. See does your business need a blog? (/blog/website-blog-for-business/)

### Booking

If customers book appointments, let them do it online. Fewer missed calls, fewer no-shows, and bookings while you sleep.

## Pages you legally or practically need

- **Privacy policy.** Required in most countries if you collect any personal data, including through a contact form.
- **Terms.** Needed if you sell online.
- **404 page.** A friendly "page not found" with links back to your main pages keeps lost visitors on the site.

## Recommended structures by business type

**Coach or consultant:** Home, About, Work With Me (programmes), Testimonials, Blog, Contact / Book a Call.

**Local service business:** Home, About, a page per service, Service Areas, Reviews, FAQ, Contact / Get a Quote.

**Photographer or creative:** Home, Portfolio (by category), About, Investment, Journal, Contact.

**Clinic or salon:** Home, Services / Treatments, Team, Pricing, Book Online, Reviews, Contact.

## How many pages is too many?

There's no upper limit, only a quality limit. Ten strong pages outperform forty weak ones. Add a page when you have something specific and useful to say that a customer would search for. Remove or merge pages that say nearly the same thing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a one-page website work?
Yes, for a simple offer or a new business. The trade-off is SEO: one page can only target a handful of search terms. Many businesses start with one page and expand.

### Do I need a separate page for every town I serve?
Only for towns where you want to rank and can write something specific. Five solid location pages beat fifty near-duplicates.

### Where should testimonials go?
Everywhere they're relevant: the homepage, each service page and near every call to action, plus a dedicated page for people who want to read more.

# How to Choose a Web Designer: 15 Questions to Ask Before You Hire
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/how-to-choose-a-web-designer/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Fifteen questions to ask any web designer or agency before hiring, with the answers you want to hear and the red flags to walk away from.

Key takeaways:
- Judge designers on live websites, not mockups or promises
- Make sure you'll own the domain, code and content outright
- Ask who actually does the work and how you'll communicate
- A fixed quote, clear timeline and a preview before paying are strong trust signals

Hiring a web designer is hard because you're buying something that doesn't exist yet. Portfolios all look good. Everyone says they do SEO. Prices range from a few hundred dollars to tens of thousands for what sounds like the same thing.

These fifteen questions cut through it. Ask them on the first call and listen carefully to the answers.

## About their work

### 1. Can I see live websites you've built, not just screenshots?

Click through real sites. Test them on your phone. Are they fast? Does the contact form work? Screenshots hide a lot.

### 2. Have you built sites for businesses like mine?

Industry experience means the designer already knows what your customers need to see. Someone who has built ten coaching sites or five solar sites will ask better questions than a generalist.

### 3. Can I speak to a past client?

A confident designer will happily connect you. Ask the client what communication was like and whether the project finished on time.

## About the process

### 4. Who will actually do the work?

At agencies, the person who sells is often not the person who builds. Find out whether your project will be handled by a senior designer, a junior, or outsourced.

### 5. What's your process and timeline?

You want clear phases with dates: discovery, design, build, launch. Vague answers now mean delays later. Compare what you hear with our realistic website timelines (/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-build-a-website/).

### 6. What do you need from me?

Good designers tell you up front what content, access and decisions they'll need and when. This is the biggest factor in finishing on time.

### 7. How many rounds of revisions are included?

Two or three is typical. Unlimited sounds generous but usually signals a vague process.

### 8. Will I see the design before I commit?

This is rare, and valuable. A designer who shows you a direction before taking payment is confident in their work. It's why we offer a free website preview (/free-website-preview/): your homepage, designed and live on a link, before you pay anything.

## About ownership and money

### 9. What exactly is included in the price?

Get a written scope: number of pages, features, copywriting, SEO setup, training. "A website" isn't a scope.

### 10. Is the price fixed?

A fixed price for a fixed scope protects you. If they bill hourly, ask for a cap.

### 11. Who owns the website when it's finished?

The only acceptable answer: you do. The domain should be registered in your name, and you should receive the code, design files and all logins. Read do you really own your website? (/blog/website-ownership-explained/) before signing anything.

### 12. What are the ongoing costs?

Hosting, maintenance, licences. Ask for all recurring fees in writing and what happens if you stop paying them.

## About results

### 13. How will the site be optimised for search?

Listen for specifics: page speed, title tags, schema markup, redirects from your old site, Search Console setup. "We do SEO" isn't an answer. Use our technical SEO checklist (/blog/technical-seo-checklist/) to judge what you're told.

### 14. Can I update the site myself?

You should be able to change text, photos and prices without paying a developer each time. Ask to see the editor.

### 15. What happens after launch?

Is there a support window? Who fixes bugs? What does ongoing help cost? Launch is the start of a website's life, not the end.

## Red flags

Walk away if you hear any of these:

- **"We'll register the domain for you"** in their own account. You may never get it back.
- **Guaranteed #1 rankings.** Nobody controls Google.
- **No contract or written scope.**
- **Full payment up front** with no milestones.
- **Proprietary platforms** you can't leave without rebuilding from scratch.
- **Slow replies before you've paid.** It doesn't get faster afterwards.

## Freelancer, studio or agency?

**Freelancers** are affordable and personal, but one person covers design, code, copy and SEO, and availability can be a risk.

**Agencies** bring teams and process, with prices and timelines to match.

**Small studios** sit in between: senior people doing the work directly, with enough experience to cover strategy, design, build and SEO. For most small businesses this is the best balance. It's how we work at Code Bunny: you talk to the founder, who is also the person building your site.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much should I expect to pay?
Most professional small business sites cost $2,500 to $10,000. See our full cost breakdown (/blog/how-much-does-a-website-cost-small-business/).

### Is it risky to hire a designer in another country?
Not if you check their work, get a contract and keep ownership of your domain. Many of our clients are in the US, Canada, the UK and Australia; time zones are rarely a problem with clear communication.

### Should I choose the cheapest quote?
Compare scope first. The cheapest quote often leaves out copywriting, SEO or mobile testing, and the redo costs more than doing it properly once.

# Do You Really Own Your Website? Domains, Hosting and Code Explained
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/website-ownership-explained/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Many business owners discover too late that they don't control their own website. Here's what ownership really means and how to check yours in ten minutes.

Key takeaways:
- Your website has four parts to own: the domain, the hosting, the code and the content
- The domain is the most important; it must be registered in your name
- Website builders and some agencies rent you a site rather than sell it
- A ten-minute check today can prevent a very expensive problem later

A surprising number of businesses don't own their own website. They find out when they try to switch designers, their agency closes, or an invoice dispute ends with the site going dark.

It's avoidable. Here's what "owning your website" really means and how to check where you stand.

## The four things you need to own

### 1. The domain name

Your domain (`yourbusiness.com`) is your address on the internet. Your website, your email and often your Google rankings all hang off it.

**It must be registered in an account you control**, with your name or company as the registrant and your email as the contact. If your web designer registered it in their account "to make things easier", you're depending on their goodwill and their continued existence.

**Check now:** search your domain at a WHOIS lookup such as lookup.icann.org (https://lookup.icann.org/). Then make sure you can log in to the registrar it names.

### 2. The hosting

Hosting is the server where your website's files live. You don't need to own a server, but you do need access to the hosting account, or at least the right to take a full copy of your site and move it elsewhere.

### 3. The code and design

When you pay for a custom website, your contract should say you own the finished work: the code, the design files and any custom graphics. Some agencies license it to you instead, meaning you can use it only while you keep paying them.

### 4. The content

Your copy, photos, blog posts and customer data. You should be able to export all of it.

## Who really owns it? Common setups

| Setup | Domain | Site | Can you leave freely? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Custom site, handed over | You | You | Yes |
| WordPress, self-hosted | You | You | Yes |
| Wix / Squarespace | You (if you registered it) | The platform | Content yes, design no |
| "Website as a service" monthly plan | Often the provider | The provider | Usually no |
| Agency proprietary platform | Varies | The agency | No |

Builders aren't a trap; they're just a rental. You can export text and images, but the design and functionality stay on the platform. We compare the options in custom website vs Wix vs Squarespace (/blog/custom-website-vs-wix-squarespace/).

## The ten-minute ownership check

1. **Domain:** Can you log in to the registrar? Is your name on the registration? Is auto-renew on with a valid card?
2. **Hosting:** Do you have the login, or a written right to a full backup?
3. **Website admin:** Do you have an administrator account, not just an editor role?
4. **Analytics and Search Console:** Are they in a Google account you own? Years of data live there.
5. **Google Business Profile:** Are you listed as the primary owner?
6. **Email:** Is it tied to the same domain account, and do you control it?
7. **Contract:** Does it say you own the finished site?

If any answer is "no" or "not sure", ask your provider this week. It's a simple request when relationships are good and a painful one when they aren't.

## What to ask before you sign with any designer

- Will the domain be registered in my name and my account?
- Will I get full admin access and all logins at launch?
- Do I own the code and design outright once I've paid?
- Can I move the site to another host or developer whenever I like?
- What happens to the site if I stop paying a monthly fee?

At Code Bunny the answer to all of these is yes: clients get the full source code, design files and every account. No lock-in. It's one of the 15 questions we suggest asking any designer (/blog/how-to-choose-a-web-designer/).

## What to do if you don't control your domain

1. **Ask politely for a transfer.** Most providers will move the domain to your account. It takes a few minutes and an authorisation code.
2. **Check your invoices.** If you paid for the registration, you have a strong claim.
3. **Use the registrar's dispute process** if the provider refuses or has vanished.
4. **Don't let it expire.** An expired domain can be bought by anyone, including people who'll charge thousands to give it back.

## Frequently asked questions

### My designer hosts my site. Is that a problem?
Not by itself. Many good designers offer hosting. It's only a problem if you have no access, no backups and no contractual right to leave.

### Can I move a Wix or Squarespace site to another host?
No. You can export content, but the site must be rebuilt elsewhere. Your domain can move with you.

### Who owns the website if I haven't paid the final invoice?
Usually the designer, until you do. That's normal and fair. Ownership should transfer in full on final payment, and your contract should say so.

# How to Write a Website Brief (With a Free Template)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/website-brief-template/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A simple website brief template you can copy, plus guidance on what to include so designers can quote accurately and build the right site first time.

Key takeaways:
- A one-page brief gets you more accurate quotes and a faster project
- Describe your customers and goals before you describe pages and colours
- Share three sites you like and say why
- You don't need technical language; plain answers are best

A website brief is a short document that tells a designer what you need and why. It doesn't need to be long or technical. One clear page will get you better quotes, fewer misunderstandings and a faster launch than a dozen back-and-forth emails.

Below is the template we'd love every client to send us. Copy it, answer in plain language, and you're done.

## The template

### 1. About your business

- Business name and what you do, in one or two sentences
- How long you've been running
- Where you operate (town, region, country, or online only)
- What makes you different from competitors

### 2. Your customers

- Who is your ideal customer? (Age, situation, what they're struggling with)
- How do they usually find you today?
- What questions do they ask before buying?
- What would stop them choosing you?

### 3. Goals for the website

Pick the one that matters most and be specific:

- More enquiries or quote requests
- More online bookings
- Online sales
- Looking more credible to win bigger clients
- Ranking on Google for particular searches

Add a number if you can: "We get about five enquiries a month and want fifteen."

### 4. Your current website

- URL, if you have one
- What you like about it
- What frustrates you or your customers
- Who built it and what platform it's on

### 5. Pages and features

- Pages you know you need (see what pages a small business site should have (/blog/what-pages-should-a-small-business-website-have/))
- Features: booking, payments, quote form, calculator, blog, gallery, members area
- Tools it must connect to: calendar, CRM, email marketing, payment provider

### 6. Look and feel

- Three websites you like and what you like about each
- One you dislike and why
- Existing brand assets: logo, colours, fonts, photography
- Three words you want visitors to feel (for example: calm, expert, friendly)

### 7. Content

- Who will write the copy? You, the designer, or a mix
- What photos and videos do you have?
- Do you have testimonials and reviews ready to use?

### 8. Practicalities

- Budget range
- Ideal launch date and any fixed deadlines
- Who makes the final decisions
- Who'll update the site after launch

## Tips for filling it in

### Start with customers, not colours

The most useful part of any brief is the description of your customers and what they need. Design decisions follow from that. A site for nervous first-time dental patients looks and reads differently from one for corporate buyers.

### Be honest about budget

Sharing a range isn't giving away negotiating power; it's saving everyone's time. A good designer will tell you what's achievable inside it. For typical ranges, see how much a website costs (/blog/how-much-does-a-website-cost-small-business/).

### Examples beat adjectives

"Clean and modern" means something different to everyone. A link to a site you admire, with a note saying "I like how simple the menu is", is unambiguous.

### Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves

Mark each feature as essential for launch or a possible phase two. It keeps the first version focused and the quote realistic.

## A filled-in example

> **Business:** Rowan & Co, a two-person mortgage broker in Leeds, trading 6 years. // **Customers:** first-time buyers aged 25 to 40 who feel overwhelmed and are comparing three or four brokers. // **Goal:** go from 8 to 20 enquiries a month. // **Current site:** five years old, slow on mobile, no reviews shown. // **Pages:** home, about, first-time buyers, remortgage, self-employed, reviews, contact. // **Features:** mortgage calculator, callback form, Google reviews feed. // **Look:** trustworthy and warm, not corporate. // **Content:** we need help with copy; have 180 Google reviews. // **Budget:** £3,000 to £5,000. // **Launch:** before spring.

That's under 120 words and tells a designer almost everything they need to quote and start.

## What happens after you send it

A good designer will reply with questions, a proposed scope, a fixed price and a timeline. Compare responses using our 15 questions to ask a web designer (/blog/how-to-choose-a-web-designer/).

If you'd rather skip straight to seeing ideas, send us the brief through our free website preview (/free-website-preview/) form and we'll turn it into a designed homepage on a live link.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should a website brief be?
One to two pages. Enough to be clear; short enough that people actually read it.

### What if I don't know what I want?
Fill in the sections about your business, customers and goals, and leave the rest. A good designer can recommend pages and features from there.

### Should I send the same brief to several designers?
Yes. It's the only way to compare quotes fairly, because everyone is pricing the same thing.

# How to Choose a Domain Name for Your Business
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/domain-name-tips/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Practical rules for choosing a business domain name: length, extensions, keywords, what to avoid, and how to protect it once you've bought it.

Key takeaways:
- Short, easy to spell and easy to say beats clever every time
- A .com is still the safest choice, with your country extension a strong alternative
- Register the domain yourself, in your own account
- Keywords in a domain give little SEO benefit; brand clarity matters more

Your domain name is on your van, your business card, your email address and every link anyone ever shares. It's worth ten minutes of thought before you click buy.

## The rules that matter

### Keep it short

Aim for under 15 characters if you can. Shorter names are easier to type, remember and fit on a sign.

### Make it easy to say out loud

Try the radio test: say it to a friend and ask them to type it. If they hesitate over spelling, hyphens or numbers, choose something else. Avoid:

- Hyphens (`best-plumber-leeds.com`)
- Numbers (`4` or `four`?)
- Double letters where words meet (`pressservice.com`)
- Creative spellings (`kwikfix.com`)

### Use your business name if you can

If your business is Harbour Dental, `harbourdental.com` is the obvious choice. If it's taken, add your town or a short word: `harbourdentalyork.com` or `visitharbourdental.com`.

### Choose the right extension

- **`.com`** is still the default people type and trust.
- **Country extensions** (`.co.uk`, `.ca`, `.com.au`, `.ie`, `.co.nz`, `.in`) are excellent for businesses serving one country and can help signal local relevance.
- **Newer extensions** (`.studio`, `.photography`, `.coach`) can work for creative brands, but some people still add `.com` out of habit.

If you can afford it, buy both the `.com` and your country version and point one at the other.

## Do keywords in a domain help SEO?

Much less than they used to. Google has said for years that exact-match domains get no special treatment. `cheapplumberleeds.com` won't outrank a well-built site on a brand name.

A light, natural keyword can still help *people* understand what you do: `aristafilms`, `ecohorizon`, `capturedbykatherine`. That's about clarity, not ranking tricks. For what actually moves rankings, see our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Before you buy

1. **Check trademarks** in your country to avoid a legal headache later.
2. **Check social handles.** Matching names across Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn look professional.
3. **Search the name.** Make sure it isn't associated with something you wouldn't want to be confused with.
4. **Read it as one word.** Some innocent phrases look unfortunate when run together.
5. **Check its history.** Paste it into the Wayback Machine. A domain previously used for spam can carry baggage.

## Where to register

Use a mainstream registrar: Namecheap, Cloudflare, Porkbun, GoDaddy or Google Workspace's partners. Expect to pay $10 to $20 a year for a `.com`. Watch out for low first-year prices that jump at renewal.

**Register it yourself, in your own account.** Don't let a designer or agency register it in theirs. This is the single most important point in this article; we explain why in do you really own your website? (/blog/website-ownership-explained/)

## Protect it once you own it

- Turn on **auto-renew** and keep the payment card current
- Enable **two-factor authentication** on the registrar account
- Turn on **domain lock** to prevent unauthorised transfers
- Use **WHOIS privacy** to keep your personal details off public records
- Register for several years if the business is established

## What if the name you want is taken?

- Add your location: `harbourdentalyork.com`
- Add a verb: `getharbour.com`, `visitharbour.com`, `hello` or `try`
- Add what you do: `harbourdentalcare.com`
- Use your country extension
- Check if it's for sale, but be cautious: premium domains can cost thousands and rarely justify it for a local business

## Domain and email

Once you have the domain, set up professional email on it (`you@yourbusiness.com`) through Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. An address at your own domain looks far more credible than a free Gmail or Hotmail account, and keeps your business email separate from any one website platform.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I change my domain name later?
Yes, but it takes care. Every old URL needs redirecting to the new domain so you keep your rankings. It's much easier to choose well now.

### Should I buy multiple domains?
Buying the main `.com` and your country extension is sensible. Buying dozens of variations is rarely worth it.

### How long should I register for?
At least a year with auto-renew on. Longer terms won't boost SEO but reduce the risk of forgetting.

---

# Website Maintenance: What It Is, What It Costs and What You Can Skip
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/website-maintenance-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What website maintenance actually involves, what it should cost for a small business, and which tasks you can do yourself in 30 minutes a month.

Key takeaways:
- Maintenance covers security, backups, updates, performance and content
- Costs range from almost nothing for static sites to $50 to $300 a month for complex ones
- WordPress needs the most upkeep because of plugins
- A 30-minute monthly check catches most problems early

A website isn't finished at launch. Like a shop, it needs someone to sweep the floor, change the window display and make sure the lock works. The good news: for most small business sites, that's not much work, and you shouldn't be paying a fortune for it.

## What maintenance actually covers

### Security and updates

Any site built on software (WordPress, plugins, e-commerce platforms) needs regular updates to patch security holes. Out-of-date plugins are the most common way small business websites get hacked.

### Backups

A complete copy of your site, taken automatically and stored somewhere other than the web server, so a mistake or attack can be undone in minutes.

### Uptime and performance

Checking the site is online, loads quickly and that nothing has broken after an update.

### Content

Keeping information accurate: hours, prices, team members, services, recent work. An out-of-date site quietly erodes trust.

### Technical health

Fixing broken links, renewing the domain and SSL certificate, and watching Search Console for errors.

## How much maintenance does your site need?

It depends heavily on how the site was built.

| Site type | Maintenance need | Typical monthly cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hand-coded static site | Very low | $0 to $30 |
| Wix / Squarespace | Low (platform handles it) | Included in plan |
| WordPress with plugins | Medium to high | $50 to $150 |
| E-commerce store | High | $100 to $300+ |
| Custom web app | High | Quoted individually |

This is one reason we build many client sites as fast static sites: there's no database to hack and no plugins to update, so upkeep is close to zero.

## What a care plan should include

If you pay someone monthly, you should be getting:

- Software, theme and plugin updates, tested after each one
- Daily or weekly off-site backups
- Uptime and security monitoring
- A set amount of time for small content changes
- A short monthly report
- A guaranteed response time when something breaks

If your "maintenance" fee is really just hosting with a markup, ask for the list above.

## The 30-minute monthly check you can do yourself

1. **Open the site on your phone.** Does everything look right?
2. **Submit your own contact form.** Did the email arrive?
3. **Check Search Console** for new errors. Our Search Console guide (/blog/google-search-console-guide/) shows where to look.
4. **Run PageSpeed Insights** on your homepage.
5. **Read your homepage** as if you were a customer. Is anything out of date?
6. **Confirm a recent backup exists.**
7. **Check your domain's renewal date.**

Put it in your calendar for the first Monday of each month.

## Signs your site is being neglected

- Copyright year is out of date
- "Latest news" is from three years ago
- A browser warning says "Not secure"
- The site is noticeably slower than it used to be
- Forms stopped sending emails and nobody noticed
- You find spammy links or pages you didn't create

Any of the last three needs attention today.

## Should you maintain it yourself or pay someone?

**Do it yourself** if you're on a builder or a static site and comfortable editing text and images.

**Pay someone** if you're on WordPress or run a store, if the site generates real revenue, or if you simply don't want to think about it. An hour of your time is usually worth more than the monthly fee.

## When maintenance costs more than it's worth

If you're spending hundreds a month patching an old, slow site, compare that with the cost of a rebuild on a lower-maintenance platform. It often pays for itself within a year. See 12 signs you need a new website (/blog/signs-you-need-a-new-website/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a maintenance plan for a simple site?
Not always. A static or builder-based brochure site mainly needs occasional content updates and a renewed domain.

### What happens if I don't update WordPress?
Sooner or later a known vulnerability gets exploited. Hacked sites can be flagged by Google and removed from search results until cleaned.

### How often should I update my content?
Whenever something changes, and review everything at least twice a year. Adding fresh work, reviews or articles regularly also helps SEO.

# Why You Should See a Website Preview Before You Pay
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/free-website-mockup-before-paying/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Paying a deposit for a website you've never seen is a leap of faith. Here's why a free preview is a better way to hire a designer, and how ours works.

Key takeaways:
- A preview shows you real work for your business, not a sales promise
- It reveals how a designer listens, communicates and delivers before money changes hands
- A coded preview on a live link is worth more than a static mockup
- There should be no obligation to continue

The usual way to hire a web designer goes like this: you look at a portfolio, sit through a sales call, pay a 50% deposit, and then wait to find out whether they understood you. Sometimes it works out. Sometimes you're two thousand dollars in and looking at a design that feels nothing like your business.

There's a better order of events: see the work first.

## What a website preview is

A website preview is a designed homepage for *your* business, made before you've paid or signed anything. Done properly, it isn't a generic template with your logo swapped in. It uses your real services, your tone and your brand, and it's built in code on a live link so you can open it on your phone and click around.

## Why it's better for you

### You judge real work, not promises

A portfolio shows what a designer did for someone else. A preview shows what they'd do for you. It's the difference between reading a restaurant review and tasting the food.

### You see how they listen

Did they pick up on what makes you different? Did they understand your customers? A preview tells you in thirty seconds whether you've been heard.

### You test the working relationship

How quickly did they reply? Did they ask sensible questions? Did they deliver when they said they would? You learn all of this before any money is involved.

### You can compare with what you have

Put the preview next to your current site. If the difference is obvious, the decision is easy. If it isn't, you've lost nothing.

### It removes the risk

No deposit to lose. No contract to escape. If you don't love it, you say thanks and walk away.

## Why would a designer work for free?

Fair question. For us the maths is simple: most people who see a preview they love want to build the rest. The few hours we invest are our marketing budget, spent on proving the work rather than on adverts claiming it.

It also keeps us honest. If a preview doesn't impress, we haven't earned the project.

## Mockup or coded preview?

Not all "free previews" are equal.

| | Static mockup | Coded preview |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Format | An image or PDF | A real web page on a live link |
| Mobile view | Sometimes | Yes |
| Animations and interactions | No | Yes |
| Shows real speed | No | Yes |
| Reusable in the final build | Rarely | Yes |

A mockup shows how a site might look. A coded preview shows how it actually behaves. Ours are coded and hosted on a private link like `yourbrand.codebunny.net`.

## How the Code Bunny free preview works

1. **You tell us about your business.** A 60-second form: what you do, who you serve, any sites you like.
2. **We design your homepage.** Custom, coded, mobile-ready, with your logo, colours and services.
3. **You review it on a live link.** Share it with a partner or a colleague. Ask for tweaks.
4. **You decide.** If you love it, we send a fixed quote for the full site. If not, no cost and no hard feelings.

Many of the sites in our portfolio (/work/) are live on a codebunny.net link in exactly this way:

## What to send to get a great preview

The more we know, the closer the first version lands. Useful things to include:

- Your current website or social profiles
- Your logo and any brand colours
- A sentence about your ideal customer
- Two or three websites you admire
- The one thing you most want visitors to do

If you'd like a structure, use our website brief template (/blog/website-brief-template/).

## Questions to ask about any free preview offer

- Is it custom, or a template with my name on it?
- Is it a live page or just an image?
- Is there any obligation or hidden fee?
- Who owns the design if I go ahead? (With us: you do.)
- What happens to it if I don't? (With us: we take it offline.)

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the preview really free?
Yes. No card, no deposit, no contract. You only pay if you choose to build the full site with us.

### How long does it take?
We aim to deliver previews within a few business days. We limit how many we take on each week so each gets proper attention.

### What if I only want small changes to my current site?
Tell us. We'll give you an honest view on whether a refresh or a rebuild makes more sense, and what each would cost.

# How to Build a Life Coach Website That Books Discovery Calls
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/website-for-life-coaches/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A step-by-step guide to building a life coach website that builds trust, explains your offer clearly and turns visitors into booked discovery calls.

Key takeaways:
- Your website's one job is to get the right person onto a discovery call
- Lead with the client's problem and the change you help them make, not your certifications
- Show your face, your story and real client results
- Put a booking button in the header, the hero and at the end of every page

People don't hire a life coach the way they buy a product. They hire someone they trust with the parts of their life that aren't working. Your website has to earn that trust quickly, then make the next step (a free call) feel safe and easy.

We've built coaching sites for life, executive, wellness, career and relationship coaches in five countries. This is what the ones that book calls have in common.

## Start with one goal

Almost every successful coaching site is built around a single action: **book a free discovery call.** Not "learn more", not "follow me on Instagram". One call to action, repeated consistently.

Before you design anything, decide what that call is named (First Step call, clarity call, chemistry session), how long it is, and how people book it.

## The homepage, section by section

### 1. A headline about them

Weak: "Certified Life Coach and NLP Practitioner."
Strong: "Feeling stuck? Find your footing and choose your path."

Your visitor is thinking about their own problem. Meet them there. Follow the headline with one sentence on who you help and how, and a booking button.

### 2. Your face

Coaching is personal. A warm, professional photo of you in the hero section does more for trust than any stock image of a sunrise.

### 3. The problem, in their words

Three or four lines that describe how your ideal client feels right now. When someone reads this and thinks "that's me", they keep scrolling.

### 4. The change you offer

What will be different after working with you? Be concrete: "set boundaries without guilt", "make the career move you've been postponing for two years".

### 5. How it works

Three simple steps: book a free call, choose a programme, start. Removing uncertainty about the process removes a major barrier.

### 6. Proof

Testimonials with full names and photos where clients allow it. Results are more persuasive than praise: "I left the job I'd hated for six years" beats "She's a wonderful coach." More in how to use testimonials on a coaching website (/blog/coaching-testimonials/).

### 7. About you, briefly

A short version of your story with a link to the full about page (/blog/coach-about-page/). Credentials belong here, as supporting evidence.

### 8. The call to action, again

End with a clear invitation and a booking button.

## Here's what that looks like in practice

## The other pages you need

- **About:** your story, told in a way that shows you understand the client's.
- **Work with me:** your programmes and packages. See how to write a coaching packages page (/blog/coaching-packages-page/).
- **Testimonials:** a fuller collection of client stories.
- **Book a call:** an embedded calendar, not a form that leads to email tennis.
- **Blog or resources:** optional, but powerful for SEO and trust.

## Make booking effortless

Embed a scheduler (Calendly, TidyCal, Acuity or Google Calendar's booking pages) directly on your site. Every extra step between "I'm interested" and "I'm booked" loses people. Ask only what you need: name, email and one question about what they'd like help with.

We map the whole journey in the discovery call funnel (/blog/discovery-call-booking-funnel/).

## Mistakes we see on coaching websites

- **Leading with qualifications.** Clients care about their outcome first, your training second.
- **Trying to help everyone.** "I help people live their best life" speaks to nobody. See positioning your coaching niche (/blog/coaching-niche-positioning/).
- **No prices or even a hint.** Mystery reads as expensive or evasive.
- **Walls of text.** Short paragraphs, clear headings, generous space.
- **A hidden booking link.** If it takes more than one click to find, it's hidden.
- **Slow, template-heavy pages.** They look like every other coach's site.

## Don't forget Google

Clients search for coaches: "career coach Vancouver", "life coach for women", "executive coach Auckland". A site with clear service pages, your location and helpful articles can bring in enquiries every month without ads. Start with SEO for coaches (/blog/seo-for-coaches/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a website if I get clients from Instagram?
Yes. Social platforms are rented space, and serious prospects will look you up. A website is where they decide whether to book.

### Should I put prices on my coaching website?
At least a starting price or range. It filters out poor fits and makes the discovery call more productive.

### How many pages does a coaching website need?
Five is plenty to start: home, about, work with me, testimonials and booking. Add a blog when you're ready to invest in SEO.

# 15 Must-Haves for a Coaching Website in 2026
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coaching-website-must-haves/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

The fifteen elements every coaching website needs to build trust and book clients, from a clear niche statement to embedded booking and real testimonials.

Key takeaways:
- Clarity about who you help beats clever design
- Booking should be one click from anywhere on the site
- Real photos and named testimonials build trust faster than anything else
- A fast, mobile-friendly site is non-negotiable because most visitors arrive from social on their phone

Use this as a checklist against your current site. Score yourself honestly: most coaching websites we review are missing at least five.

## 1. A clear niche statement

Within five seconds a visitor should know who you help and with what. "Career transition coaching for tech professionals" tells the right person they're in the right place.

## 2. A client-focused headline

Speak to the feeling or goal your client has today. Save your title and credentials for the about section. For formulas and examples, see coaching website copywriting (/blog/coach-website-copywriting/).

## 3. A professional photo of you

Not a selfie, not a stock image. A warm, well-lit portrait where you're looking at the camera.

## 4. One primary call to action

"Book a free call" in the header, the hero and the footer. Same wording each time.

## 5. Embedded online booking

A live calendar on your site. No "email me to arrange a time".

## 6. A signature method or framework

Naming your process (a four-step method, a framework with an acronym) makes your coaching tangible and memorable. Lasting Change Wellness, for example, builds its whole site around the S.H.I.N.E. method.

## 7. Clear programmes or packages

What's included, how long it lasts, who it's for. See how to write a coaching packages page (/blog/coaching-packages-page/).

## 8. Testimonials with names and results

Specific outcomes from real people. Video is even better.

## 9. Credentials and affiliations

ICF, EMCC, certifications, relevant career history. Shown as logos or a short list, supporting your story rather than leading it.

## 10. An about page that connects

Your story, framed around why you understand your clients. See how to write a coach about page (/blog/coach-about-page/).

## 11. A lead magnet

Most visitors aren't ready to book today. A useful free resource in exchange for an email keeps the conversation going. Ideas in 20 lead magnets for coaches (/blog/lead-magnets-for-coaches/).

## 12. Mobile-first design

Most coaching traffic comes from Instagram and LinkedIn links opened on a phone. Design for the small screen first.

## 13. Fast loading

A slow site loses people before they've read your headline. Aim for under two seconds on mobile.

## 14. SEO foundations

A page per service, your location if you coach locally, proper title tags and a few genuinely helpful articles. Start with SEO for coaches (/blog/seo-for-coaches/).

## 15. A privacy policy and clear contact details

You're collecting names and emails. A privacy policy is a legal requirement in most places, and visible contact details signal you're a real business.

## Nice-to-haves once the basics are solid

- **Media and speaking page** with logos of podcasts and publications you've appeared in
- **A quiz or self-assessment** that qualifies leads and gives instant value
- **A client portal or resource library**
- **Retreat or event pages** with their own booking flows
- **Corporate or B2B page** if you also sell to organisations

## See these in real sites

Each of these coaching sites covers the fifteen essentials in its own style:

## Frequently asked questions

### What's the most important page on a coaching website?
The homepage, because it decides whether anyone sees the rest. After that, your booking page.

### Do I need a blog?
Not on day one. It becomes valuable when you want steady traffic from Google and something to share on social.

### Can I build a coaching website myself?
Yes, with a builder like Squarespace. The trade-off is time and a template look. If you'd like to compare, we'll design a free preview (/free-website-preview/) of a custom homepage for you.
