# 11 Coaching Website Examples (and What Makes Each One Work)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coaching-website-examples/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Eleven real coaching websites across life, executive, wellness and career coaching, with a breakdown of what each one does well and what you can borrow.

Key takeaways:
- The best coaching sites lead with the client's problem, not the coach's biography
- Each example uses one clear call to action, usually a free call
- Distinct colour, typography and photography stop a site looking like a template
- You can borrow structure from any of them without copying the style

Looking at good examples is the fastest way to work out what you want from your own site. These eleven are all sites we designed and built at Code Bunny. For each, we've pulled out the one idea worth borrowing.

## 1. High Fifteen: executive coaching with attitude

High Fifteen helps senior leaders build inclusive, high-performing cultures. The site is bold and confident, with a headline that names the stakes ("Cultures that perform under pressure") and a founder photo that's impossible to ignore.

**Borrow this:** a point of view. The site says what it's against as well as what it's for.

## 2. Take Root Life Coaching: calm and grounded

Whole-person life coaching presented with natural imagery and a gentle palette. The "First Step call" is on every screen.

**Borrow this:** give your discovery call a name that fits your brand.

## 3. Co-Allies: sensitive topics handled with care

Coaching for fertility journeys, life transitions and conscious leadership. The design is soft and human, and the copy never rushes the reader.

**Borrow this:** match your tone to how your client feels when they arrive.

## 4. Live in Flow Coaching: a tight niche

Career-transition coaching for tech professionals. The headline ("Feeling stuck? Find your flow.") and every section speak to that one audience.

**Borrow this:** name your niche in the first line.

## 5. Polish: coaching meets AI leadership

Executive coaching, AI leadership programmes and keynote speaking for leaders in New Zealand and Australia. Dramatic photography and crisp type signal a premium offer.

**Borrow this:** separate pages for separate audiences (coaching, programmes, speaking).

## 6. Lasting Change Wellness: a named method

The whole site hangs on the S.H.I.N.E. method, turning an abstract service into a clear, step-by-step journey.

**Borrow this:** name your framework and build your pages around it.

## 7. Sharon Tabak: credibility through association

A certified Jay Shetty life coach specialising in trauma, identity and big transitions. The certification is shown early, and the headline promises a specific transformation.

**Borrow this:** if you have a recognisable credential, put it near the top.

## 8. Arielle Innou Coaching: warmth and clarity

Life, relationship and corporate coaching plus retreats. A friendly portrait and a three-word promise ("Clear, confident, in control") do the heavy lifting.

**Borrow this:** a short promise people can repeat.

## 9. George Dupont Leadership: authority branding

A former pro hockey captain sells a leadership system to sports franchises and C-suites. Dark, cinematic design and a trademarked method position him as the obvious expert.

**Borrow this:** let your background shape the visual language.

## 10. Insight Transformational Coaching: clear tiers

Three coaching levels for women ready to move from wishing to action, each clearly explained.

**Borrow this:** offer good, better and best so prospects choose *which*, not *whether*.

## 11. Lauren Powers: a personal brand that performs

A ten-time bodybuilding champion, TV host and author. The site is loud, bold and unmistakably hers.

**Borrow this:** don't sand off your personality to look "professional".

## What all eleven have in common

1. **A headline about the client.** Not one opens with a job title.
2. **One call to action.** A free call, on every screen.
3. **A real person, front and centre.**
4. **A distinct look.** None of them could be mistaken for a template.
5. **Speed.** Hand-coded pages that load quickly on a phone.

## How to use these examples

Pick two or three you're drawn to and note *what* you like: the layout, the tone, the way packages are shown. Include those notes in your website brief (/blog/website-brief-template/). It gives a designer a far clearer target than "something modern".

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I have a site like one of these?
Yes. Tell us which you like and we'll design a free preview (/free-website-preview/) of your own homepage in a similar spirit.

### What platform are these built on?
They're custom-coded, which is why they're fast and don't look like templates.

### How long did each take?
Most went from first conversation to live in one to three weeks.

# Executive Coach Website: How to Look Credible to the C-Suite
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/executive-coach-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What an executive coach website needs to win senior leaders and corporate buyers: positioning, proof, programme pages and a design that signals authority.

Key takeaways:
- Senior buyers look for evidence, specificity and discretion
- Speak to two audiences: the leader being coached and the HR sponsor who signs it off
- Case studies with business outcomes beat generic praise
- The design should feel premium and restrained, with fast, flawless execution

Executive coaching is sold differently from life coaching. Your buyer is busy, sceptical and often spending the company's money. They may be a leader looking for themselves or an HR director choosing for someone else. Either way, they'll judge you on your website in under a minute.

## Know your two audiences

**The leader** wants to know: do you understand my world, and have you helped people like me?

**The sponsor** (HR, L&D or a board member) wants to know: is this credible, measurable and safe to recommend?

A strong executive coaching site answers both, often with separate pages: "For leaders" and "For organisations".

## Positioning: be specific

"I help leaders reach their potential" is forgettable. Specific positioning wins:

- "Coaching for first-time CEOs in scale-ups"
- "Inclusive leadership for global teams"
- "AI leadership programmes for executive teams"

Specificity is itself a credibility signal. It tells a senior reader you've done this before. More in positioning your coaching niche (/blog/coaching-niche-positioning/).

## Proof that works at this level

### Client logos

If you've worked with recognisable organisations and have permission, show them near the top.

### Outcome-based case studies

Senior buyers want business impact: retention, engagement scores, promotion readiness, a successful transition. Structure each case as situation, approach, result. Anonymise where needed ("CFO, FTSE 250 retailer").

### Credentials

ICF PCC or MCC, EMCC, an executive education background, board or operating experience. At this level your own leadership history is often your strongest credential.

### Thought leadership

Articles, a TEDx talk, podcast appearances, a book. These show you have a point of view worth paying for.

## Pages an executive coach site needs

- **Home:** positioning, proof and a path for each audience
- **Executive coaching:** how one-to-one engagements work, duration and what's measured
- **Team and organisational programmes**
- **Speaking** with topics, a showreel and a booking enquiry
- **Case studies**
- **About** with career history
- **Insights** (articles)
- **Contact:** a short enquiry form and a calendar link

## Here are three in the wild

## Design: premium, restrained, fast

- **Typography carries the brand.** A confident serif or a clean grotesque, used consistently.
- **Photography is editorial**, not corporate stock.
- **White space signals confidence.**
- **Nothing is broken.** A typo or a slow page undermines a premium fee instantly.

## The enquiry path

Executives won't fill in a ten-field form. Offer two routes:

1. **Book a confidential conversation:** an embedded calendar for a 20 to 30 minute call.
2. **Organisation enquiry:** a short form for HR with fields for company, role and what they're looking to solve.

Mention confidentiality explicitly. It matters at this level.

## Should you show pricing?

Most executive coaches don't publish exact fees, because engagements are scoped individually. A line such as "Engagements typically run six months and start from £X" still helps qualify enquiries. For structuring your offers, see how to write a coaching packages page (/blog/coaching-packages-page/).

## SEO for executive coaches

Senior buyers do search: "executive coach London", "leadership coaching for CTOs", "CEO coach". Service pages, location signals, and articles that answer real leadership questions build visibility over time. See SEO for coaches (/blog/seo-for-coaches/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do executive coaches need a blog?
It's one of the best ways to demonstrate thinking. Even one strong article a month gives prospects something to forward to their boss.

### Should I use a personal name or a company brand?
Either works. A personal brand builds trust quickly; a company name is easier to grow beyond yourself. Many coaches use both.

### How important is LinkedIn compared with my website?
LinkedIn starts conversations. Your website closes them. Senior buyers nearly always check both.

# How to Write a Coaching Packages Page That Sells
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coaching-packages-page/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to structure, name and price coaching packages on your website so prospects understand your offer and arrive at the discovery call ready to buy.

Key takeaways:
- Offer two or three packages, not a menu of ten
- Describe outcomes first and logistics second
- Showing a price or starting price improves the quality of enquiries
- Every package should end with the same call to action

Your packages page (often called "Work with me") is where interest turns into intent. Done well, it means people arrive at the discovery call already knowing what they want. Done badly, it's a list of session counts that leaves them more confused than before.

## Sell the outcome, then the logistics

Nobody wants "six 60-minute sessions". They want to stop dreading Monday mornings, lead their team with confidence, or finally make the move.

For each package, lead with:

1. **Who it's for.** "For professionals who know they want out but don't know what's next."
2. **The outcome.** What will be true at the end.
3. **How it works.** Duration, session rhythm, support between sessions.
4. **What's included.** Sessions, assessments, worksheets, message access.
5. **The investment.**
6. **The next step.** Book a free call.

## How many packages?

Two or three. Any more and people freeze. A classic structure:

| Package | For | Typical format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starter / Clarity | Someone with one specific challenge | 4 sessions over 6 weeks |
| Signature | Your ideal client, your full method | 3 months, fortnightly sessions plus support |
| Premium / VIP | Those who want more access | 6 months, weekly sessions, priority messaging |

Make the middle option the one you'd most like to sell and mark it "most popular". Many people choose the middle.

## Naming your packages

Names should describe a result or a stage of the journey, not a metal. "Find Your Footing", "The Transition", "Lead with Confidence" tell a story that "Bronze, Silver, Gold" doesn't.

## Should you show prices?

There's no universal rule, but here's what we've seen across dozens of coaching sites:

**Show prices if** you want fewer, better-qualified enquiries, and your pricing is fixed.

**Show a "from" price if** engagements vary but you want to filter out people for whom it's far out of reach.

**Hide prices if** you sell mainly to organisations with bespoke scopes. Even then, say so explicitly.

Whatever you choose, never make visitors feel foolish for asking. "Investment is discussed on your free call, with options from $X" is clear and respectful.

## Elements that lift conversions

- **A testimonial under each package** from someone who took that programme
- **An FAQ** covering refunds, rescheduling, online vs in person, and how quickly they can start
- **A "not sure which?" line** pointing to the discovery call
- **Payment options:** pay in full or in instalments
- **A guarantee or clear cancellation policy**

## Example layout

1. Short intro: who you work with and the change you help create
2. Two or three package cards side by side
3. A "how it works" strip: call, choose, start
4. Testimonials
5. FAQ
6. Final call to action

You can see tiered offers presented clearly on sites like these:

## Common mistakes

- **Describing only the format.** Sessions and minutes, with no mention of results.
- **Too many options.** Hourly, packages, group, VIP days, retreats, all on one page.
- **No call to action** under each package.
- **Jargon.** If a client wouldn't say it, don't write it.
- **Out-of-date prices.** Review the page every quarter.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I offer single sessions?
Usually not as your main offer. Transformation takes time, and single sessions attract people who aren't committed. A paid one-off "intensive" can work as an entry point.

### How do I price coaching packages?
Start from the value of the outcome to your client and what comparable coaches in your niche charge, then test. Raising prices as demand grows is normal.

### Where should the packages page sit in my menu?
In the main navigation, labelled plainly: "Work with me", "Coaching" or "Programmes".

---

# How to Write a Coach About Page That Clients Connect With
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coach-about-page/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A simple structure for writing a coaching about page that builds trust, tells your story with purpose and leads readers to book a call.

Key takeaways:
- Your about page is really about the client and why you're the right guide for them
- Open with their situation before telling your story
- Share the turning point that led you to coaching, not your whole CV
- End with a clear invitation to book a call

Your about page is usually the second most-visited page on your site. People go there with one question: *can I trust this person with something that matters to me?* Most about pages answer a different question: *what has this person done since university?*

Here's a structure that answers the right one.

## The five-part structure

### 1. Start with them

Open with a line or two that shows you understand where your reader is.

> "You've done everything right. Good job, good salary, and a quiet feeling on Sunday evenings that this can't be it."

Now they're listening.

### 2. Introduce yourself as the guide

One or two sentences: who you are and who you help. "I'm Maria, a career transition coach. I help tech professionals move into work that feels like flow."

### 3. Tell the relevant part of your story

Not your biography; the part that explains why you do this work. Usually that's a turning point:

- A moment you were in your client's shoes
- What you tried that didn't work
- What changed
- Why you now help others through the same thing

Keep it honest and specific. A real detail ("I cried in a car park before a board meeting") is worth ten abstract sentences.

### 4. Show your credibility

Now bring in the evidence: certifications, training, years of experience, number of clients, notable organisations, media features. A short list or a row of logos works well.

### 5. Invite the next step

End with what to do now: "If this sounds familiar, let's talk. Book a free 30-minute call." Add the button.

## Voice: write like you speak

Write in first person, in the tone you'd use on a discovery call. Read it aloud. If you wouldn't say a sentence to a client's face, rewrite it.

Avoid:

- "Passionate about empowering individuals to unlock their potential"
- Long lists of every course you've taken
- Third-person bios ("Jane is a certified...") unless it's a separate speaker bio

## Photos

Include at least two: a professional portrait and something more relaxed that shows your personality. Clients are choosing a person; let them see one.

## Add a few human details

A short "outside of coaching" section makes you relatable: where you live, what you love, a quirk or two. Three lines is enough.

## A fill-in-the-blanks template

> **[Line that names your client's situation.]** // I'm [name], a [type] coach. I help [who] to [outcome]. // [Two or three short paragraphs: your turning point and what you learned.] // Today I've worked with [number/type of clients] and trained with [credentials]. // [One line on your approach or method.] // Away from work you'll find me [human detail]. // **Ready to talk? [Book a free call.]**

## Examples that do it well

These coaching sites handle the "about" story with warmth and purpose:

## Common mistakes

- **Starting with "I".** Start with "you".
- **The full CV.** Nobody needs your 2009 job title.
- **No photo.**
- **No call to action.** An about page with no next step is a dead end.
- **Hiding it.** Link to it from your homepage and main menu.

## A separate speaker bio

If you speak or get quoted in the press, add a short third-person bio at the bottom of the page (50 and 150-word versions) with a downloadable headshot. Event organisers will thank you.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should a coaching about page be?
Roughly 300 to 600 words. Long enough to tell a real story, short enough to read on a phone.

### Should I share personal struggles?
Share what's relevant and what you're comfortable having public. The aim is to show you understand, not to overshare.

### Do I need professional photos?
They're one of the best investments you can make for a coaching site. A two-hour shoot gives you images for the whole website and a year of social posts.

# The Discovery Call Funnel: From Website Visitor to Booked Call
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/discovery-call-booking-funnel/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to design the journey from first visit to booked discovery call on a coaching website, including booking tools, forms, reminders and follow-up.

Key takeaways:
- Reduce the path from interest to booked call to two clicks
- Embed your calendar on the site instead of asking people to email you
- Ask two or three qualifying questions, no more
- Automated confirmations and reminders cut no-shows sharply

Every coaching website is, underneath, a funnel with one output: a booked call with a good-fit prospect. Each unnecessary step between "this person gets me" and "I'm in your calendar" loses a share of people. Here's how to build the path so fewer drop out.

## The five stages

1. **Arrive.** From Instagram, LinkedIn, Google or a referral.
2. **Recognise.** "This is for someone like me."
3. **Trust.** Proof that you're credible and get results.
4. **Decide.** A clear, low-risk invitation.
5. **Book.** A time in the diary within a minute.

Your website's job is to move people through each stage without friction.

## Stage 1 and 2: the first screen

The top of your homepage needs a client-focused headline, one supporting sentence and a booking button. If visitors have to scroll to find out what you do, many won't. See coaching website copywriting (/blog/coach-website-copywriting/).

## Stage 3: trust

Place proof before you ask for the booking: testimonials, credentials, a short version of your story. Then ask again.

## Stage 4: frame the call

People hesitate because they fear a sales pitch. Remove the fear by saying exactly what happens:

- **Name it.** "First Step call", "Clarity call".
- **Say how long.** 20 or 30 minutes.
- **Say what they'll get.** "We'll talk through where you are, where you'd like to be, and whether coaching is the right fit."
- **Say what it isn't.** "No pressure, no obligation."

## Stage 5: the booking page

### Embed the calendar

Use Calendly, TidyCal, Acuity, Cal.com or Google Calendar appointment schedules, embedded on your own page. Sending people to "email me your availability" can lose half of them.

### Ask the right questions

Two or three is the sweet spot:

1. What would you most like help with?
2. What have you tried so far?
3. How did you hear about me?

These prepare you for the call and screen out poor fits without feeling like an application.

### Keep the page clean

Remove the main navigation distractions. Show a short reminder of what the call is, a testimonial, and the calendar.

## After they book

This is where many coaches lose the sale they just earned.

- **Instant confirmation** with a calendar invite and video link
- **A welcome email** with a short note from you and, ideally, one thing to think about before the call
- **Reminders** 24 hours and 1 hour before, by email and SMS if your tool supports it
- **An easy reschedule link**

Automated reminders are the single biggest lever for reducing no-shows.

## For visitors who aren't ready

Most people won't book on the first visit. Give them a smaller step:

- A lead magnet (/blog/lead-magnets-for-coaches/) in exchange for an email
- A short email series that shares your thinking
- A gentle invitation to book at the end of each email

## Measure it

Track three numbers each month:

| Metric | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Visitors to booking page | Is the site sending people there? |
| Bookings ÷ booking page visitors | Is the booking page convincing? |
| Clients ÷ calls held | Is the call converting? |

If lots of people reach the booking page but few book, simplify the page. If few reach it, your homepage and calls to action need work.

## See it in action

## Frequently asked questions

### Should the discovery call be free?
For most coaches, yes. It lowers the barrier and lets both sides check fit. Some established coaches charge a small fee to filter for commitment.

### How long should it be?
Twenty to thirty minutes is enough to understand the situation and explain how you work.

### Which booking tool is best?
Any of the mainstream ones work. Choose the one that syncs with your calendar, sends reminders and embeds cleanly on your site.

---

# 20 Lead Magnet Ideas for Coaches (That People Actually Want)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/lead-magnets-for-coaches/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Twenty lead magnet ideas for life, career, executive and wellness coaches, plus how to choose one, where to put it and what to send afterwards.

Key takeaways:
- A lead magnet should solve one small, specific problem quickly
- Quizzes and checklists usually outperform long ebooks
- Promote it in your hero, mid-page and footer
- Follow up with a short email series that leads to a discovery call

Most people who visit your coaching website aren't ready to book a call today. A lead magnet gives them a useful first step and gives you permission to keep in touch until they are.

The best ones share three traits: they're specific, they're quick to consume, and they give a real result.

## Quick-win formats

1. **Checklist.** "The 10-point Sunday reset for a calmer week."
2. **One-page worksheet.** "Find your top five values in ten minutes."
3. **Script or template.** "Three ways to say no without feeling guilty."
4. **Cheat sheet.** "20 questions to ask yourself before changing careers."
5. **Journal prompts.** "Seven prompts for the week after a breakup."

## Interactive formats

6. **Quiz.** "What's your leadership style?" Quizzes convert well because people love learning about themselves.
7. **Self-assessment scorecard.** "Rate your work-life balance across eight areas."
8. **Wheel of life.** A classic coaching tool, made interactive or printable.
9. **Calculator.** "What is your burnout costing you?"

## Deeper formats

10. **Short email course.** Five days, one small action a day.
11. **Mini video training.** 15 minutes on one problem.
12. **Guided audio.** A meditation, visualisation or pep talk.
13. **Workbook.** A longer guided exercise around your method.
14. **Webinar or masterclass replay.**
15. **First chapter of your book.**

## Niche-specific ideas

16. **Career coaches:** a CV or LinkedIn headline template, or a "should I stay or go?" decision guide.
17. **Executive coaches:** a 90-day plan for new leaders, or a one-to-one meeting template.
18. **Wellness coaches:** a seven-day energy tracker or simple meal planner.
19. **Relationship coaches:** conversation starters for couples.
20. **Business coaches:** a pricing calculator or weekly planning template.

## How to choose

Ask: what's the first small problem my ideal client wants solved, the one that sits just before the bigger problem I'm paid to solve? Your lead magnet should fix that small thing and reveal the bigger one.

A career coach's checklist on "signs it's time to leave your job" naturally leads to a call about what to do next.

## Where to put it on your website

- **In the hero** as a secondary button under "Book a call"
- **A dedicated section** halfway down the homepage
- **At the end of every blog post**
- **In the footer**
- **A dedicated landing page** you can link to from social

Keep the form to first name and email. Every extra field lowers sign-ups.

## What happens after they sign up

The download is the start, not the goal. Set up a short welcome sequence:

1. **Immediately:** deliver the resource and say who you are.
2. **Day 2:** a quick tip that builds on it.
3. **Day 4:** a client story.
4. **Day 6:** common mistakes people make with this problem.
5. **Day 8:** an invitation to book a discovery call.

Then add them to your regular newsletter. For the full journey, see the discovery call funnel (/blog/discovery-call-booking-funnel/).

## Make it look good

A scruffy PDF undermines a premium service. Use your brand fonts and colours, keep layouts clean and add your photo and booking link on the last page.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Too long.** A 40-page ebook rarely gets read.
- **Too broad.** "A guide to a better life."
- **No follow-up.**
- **Asking for a phone number** on the form.
- **Hiding it** on one page.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do lead magnets still work?
Yes, when they're genuinely useful. People are more selective about giving their email, so quality matters more than ever.

### What tool do I need?
An email platform such as MailerLite, Kit (ConvertKit), Flodesk or Mailchimp. They provide the form, delivery and automated emails.

### How many lead magnets should I have?
Start with one strong one. Add more later for different audiences or blog topics.

---

# SEO for Coaches: How to Get Coaching Clients from Google
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/seo-for-coaches/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A practical SEO guide for coaches: the keywords clients actually search, the pages you need, local SEO, blogging and how to appear in AI search results.

Key takeaways:
- Clients search by niche and location, like "career coach Toronto", so build a page for each service
- A Google Business Profile helps even if you coach online
- Helpful articles answering client questions bring steady traffic
- Clear, well-structured pages also help you appear in ChatGPT and Google AI answers

Most coaches rely on referrals and social media. Both are valuable, and both stop when you do. Search is different: a page that ranks keeps bringing in prospects month after month while you're busy coaching.

You don't need to become an SEO expert. You need to do a handful of things well.

## How people search for coaches

Searches fall into three groups:

- **Service + location:** "life coach Denver", "executive coach London"
- **Service + niche:** "career coach for tech workers", "coach for women in leadership", "divorce coach online"
- **Problem-based:** "how to change careers at 40", "feeling stuck in life what to do"

The first two are people ready to hire. The third are people earlier in the journey who may hire later.

## Step 1: one page per service

If you offer life coaching, career coaching and corporate workshops, each needs its own page. One page can't rank for three different things.

On each page include:

- The service and audience in the page title and main heading
- Who it's for and the problems it solves
- How it works
- Testimonials specific to that service
- FAQs
- A booking call to action

Read title tags and meta descriptions (/blog/title-tags-meta-descriptions/) to get the basics right.

## Step 2: claim your location

Even if you work on Zoom, many clients prefer someone "local". Mention your city and region on your homepage, contact page and footer, and set up a Google Business Profile. You can hide your home address and list a service area. Our Google Business Profile checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/) walks through it.

Then ask happy clients for Google reviews. They influence both rankings and trust.

## Step 3: write what your clients are Googling

List the ten questions you hear most on discovery calls. Each is an article:

- "How do I know if I need a career coach?"
- "What happens in a life coaching session?"
- "How much does executive coaching cost?"
- "Life coach vs therapist: what's the difference?"

Answer each clearly in 800 to 1,500 words, with a call to action at the end. One good article a month is enough. See how to write a blog post that ranks (/blog/how-to-write-a-blog-post-that-ranks/).

## Step 4: get the technical basics right

- **Speed:** fast on mobile
- **Mobile-friendly:** obviously
- **HTTPS:** the padlock
- **Clear structure:** one H1 per page, logical headings
- **Schema markup:** tells Google you're a professional service with reviews and FAQs

Our technical SEO checklist (/blog/technical-seo-checklist/) covers these in plain English.

## Step 5: earn a few good links

Links from other sites tell Google you're trusted. Good sources for coaches:

- Your certifying body's directory (ICF, EMCC)
- Podcast guest appearances
- Guest articles for industry publications
- Local business associations
- Collaborations with therapists, HR consultants and other coaches

## Getting found in AI search

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews for recommendations: "who's a good career coach for engineers in Vancouver?" These tools pull from clear, specific, well-structured web pages.

To be included: state plainly who you help, where and how; use question-style headings with direct answers; keep your details consistent across your site, LinkedIn and directories. We cover this in depth in how to get mentioned in AI search (/blog/ai-search-optimization/).

## How long will it take?

Expect brand searches (your name) to work within weeks, niche and local terms within three to six months, and competitive terms longer. SEO compounds: the work you do this quarter keeps paying next year. More in how long does SEO take? (/blog/how-long-does-seo-take/)

## A simple 90-day plan

| Month | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Service pages, titles, Google Business Profile, Search Console |
| 2 | Three helpful articles, ask five clients for reviews |
| 3 | Two more articles, one guest appearance, review Search Console data |

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I rank if I only coach online?
Yes. Target niche terms ("online career coach for nurses") and still claim your home city for local searches.

### Is SEO worth it for a solo coach?
If one new client is worth $1,500 or more, even one extra enquiry a month from Google is a strong return.

### Do I need to blog every week?
No. One genuinely helpful article a month beats four thin ones.

---

# How to Use Testimonials on a Coaching Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coaching-testimonials/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to collect, write up and display coaching testimonials that build trust and persuade, including what to ask clients and where to place them.

Key takeaways:
- The best testimonials describe a before, an after and what changed
- Ask clients specific questions instead of "can you write me a testimonial?"
- Place proof next to every call to action, not only on one page
- Always get written permission and respect confidentiality

Coaching is invisible. There's no product photo, no before-and-after picture. Testimonials are how prospects see the result before they buy, which makes them the most persuasive content on your site.

## What makes a testimonial persuasive

Compare:

> "Sarah is an amazing coach. I highly recommend her!"

> "I'd been in the same role for nine years and couldn't see a way out. Within three months of working with Sarah I'd landed a director role at a company I love, and I negotiated a 25% raise."

The second has the three ingredients that matter:

1. **Before:** the situation and how it felt
2. **After:** the specific result
3. **Bridge:** what the coaching did

## How to ask

Don't ask for "a testimonial". Ask questions that produce the story:

1. What was going on for you before we started working together?
2. What made you hesitate about coaching?
3. What changed as a result of our work?
4. What specifically was most helpful?
5. Who would you recommend this to?

Send them by email, or ask on your final session and offer to write it up for the client to approve. Most people are happy to help and relieved not to face a blank page.

**When to ask:** right after a win, at the end of a programme, or when a client says something lovely unprompted ("Would you mind if I quoted that?").

## Permission and confidentiality

Coaching is private. Always:

- Get written permission before publishing
- Offer options: full name and photo, first name and role, or anonymous ("Marketing Director, tech company")
- Let clients approve the final wording
- Remove a testimonial promptly if asked

Named testimonials with photos are most powerful, but an honest anonymous one beats none.

## Formats

- **Short quotes** for scattering across pages
- **Mini case studies** (150 to 300 words) for programme pages
- **Video testimonials:** highly convincing and reusable on social
- **Screenshots** of messages, with permission
- **Google reviews** for extra credibility and SEO

Real messages can be especially convincing because nobody wrote them for marketing. One of our own favourite pieces of feedback is a WhatsApp from a client that simply says: "I got a lot of compliments on it."

## Where to put them

Not all on one page that few people visit.

- **Homepage:** two or three of your best, near the top
- **Each programme page:** testimonials from people who took that programme
- **Next to every booking button**
- **About page:** one that speaks to what you're like to work with
- **Booking page:** to reassure at the moment of decision
- **A dedicated page** for those who want more

## Match testimonials to objections

List the reasons people hesitate: "it's expensive", "I've tried coaching before", "I don't have time". Find a testimonial that answers each and place it where that doubt arises, such as a "worth every penny" quote next to your pricing.

## Add specifics

Wherever possible include name, role, location, programme and a photo. Details make a testimonial believable.

## Keep them fresh

Add new testimonials every quarter. Dates aren't essential, but a wall of quotes that hasn't changed in four years looks stale.

## Mark them up for Google

Review schema can help search engines understand your testimonials. Use it honestly and only for genuine reviews. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/).

## Frequently asked questions

### What if I'm a new coach with no testimonials?
Offer a few pro bono or discounted sessions in exchange for honest feedback. Character references from colleagues can also help while you build.

### Can I edit a testimonial?
You can tidy grammar and shorten it, but never change the meaning, and always get the client's approval of the final version.

### How many should I show?
Three to five strong ones on the homepage is plenty. Quality over quantity.

---

# Wellness Coach Website Guide: Design, Pages and Booking
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wellness-coach-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build a wellness or health coach website that feels calm and credible, explains your method and turns visitors into clients.

Key takeaways:
- Wellness clients need to feel safe and understood before they'll book
- A named method and clear programme structure make an intangible service concrete
- Be careful with health claims; promise support, not cures
- Calm design still needs a strong, visible call to action

Wellness coaching covers a lot of ground: health, nutrition, stress, sleep, hormones, burnout, habits. What unites the clients is that they've often tried things before and feel discouraged. Your website's job is to make them feel understood, show them a believable path and make starting easy.

## Set the tone

Wellness sites work best when they feel like a deep breath:

- **Colour:** soft, natural palettes with one confident accent
- **Photography:** real, warm, natural light; you, not stock models with salads
- **Space:** generous margins and short paragraphs
- **Language:** kind, clear and free of guilt

Calm doesn't mean vague. The booking button should still be the most obvious thing on the page.

## Say who you help

"I help people feel better" won't land. Specific does:

- "Coaching for women navigating perimenopause"
- "Burnout recovery for healthcare professionals"
- "Helping impact-driven women quiet self-doubt"

The narrower the statement, the more the right person feels seen. See positioning your coaching niche (/blog/coaching-niche-positioning/).

## Make your method visible

Clients want to know there's a plan. Name your approach and show the steps. Lasting Change Wellness does this with the S.H.I.N.E. method: a simple acronym that turns an abstract service into a journey people can picture.

## Pages to include

- **Home:** who you help, the change you offer, proof and a call to action
- **About:** your own wellness story and credentials
- **Programmes:** clear options with what's included
- **Success stories**
- **Resources or blog:** recipes, guides, articles
- **Book a call**

Optional: a quiz ("What's your stress type?"), a free challenge, an online course area.

## Be careful with claims

Health is regulated, and trust is fragile. Protect both:

- Don't promise to diagnose, treat or cure
- Use phrases like "support", "guide" and "work towards"
- Add a short disclaimer that coaching isn't a substitute for medical care
- Be clear about your qualifications and scope
- Only use testimonials that reflect typical, honest experiences

## Credentials that matter

Display relevant ones: NBHWC board certification, health coaching diplomas, nutrition qualifications, a clinical background if you have one. A former psychologist turned wellness coach, for example, should say so prominently.

## Lead magnets that fit wellness

- A seven-day reset plan
- An energy or symptom tracker
- A simple meal-planning template
- A guided breathing audio
- A self-assessment quiz

More ideas in 20 lead magnets for coaches (/blog/lead-magnets-for-coaches/).

## Booking and intake

Offer a free introductory call with an embedded calendar. For wellness, a short intake question helps: "What would you most like to feel different three months from now?" Keep anything medical for a secure form after they've become a client.

## Selling programmes online

If you sell a group programme or course, your site can take payment directly through Stripe or connect to a course platform. Make the path short: programme page, pay, welcome email with next steps.

## SEO for wellness coaches

People search for help with specific struggles: "burnout coach", "health coach for PCOS", "stress management coaching". Build a page for each area you specialise in and write articles answering the questions clients ask. See SEO for coaches (/blog/seo-for-coaches/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I show prices on a wellness coaching site?
A starting price helps set expectations. Many wellness coaches share full pricing for programmes and discuss bespoke options on a call.

### Can I sell supplements or products on my site?
Yes, with an online shop, but be careful about claims and check local regulations.

### Do I need a blog?
It helps with SEO and gives you content for social. Recipes, practical guides and myth-busting articles tend to do well.

---

# Career Coach Website Guide: Win Clients Who Are Ready for a Change
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/career-coach-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What a career coach website needs to attract and convert professionals: niche positioning, proof of outcomes, packages and a simple booking path.

Key takeaways:
- Career clients want tangible outcomes, so lead with results
- Niche by industry, career stage or transition type
- LinkedIn drives most traffic, so your site must match your profile
- Show a clear process from first call to new role

Career coaching clients are usually motivated and measurable. They want a new role, a promotion, a pivot or the confidence to ask for more. That makes your website easier to write than most coaching sites, as long as you're specific.

## Lead with outcomes

Career coaching has something most coaching doesn't: clear results. Use them.

- "Clients typically land a new role within four months"
- "From senior engineer to engineering manager in one promotion cycle"
- Logos of companies clients have moved to (with permission)

Only publish numbers you can back up.

## Pick a niche

Career coaching is crowded. Niches cut through:

| Niche by | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Industry | Tech, healthcare, law, finance |
| Stage | Graduates, mid-career, executives |
| Transition | Career change, return to work, redundancy |
| Identity | Women in leadership, international professionals |

Live in Flow Coaching, for example, focuses on career transitions for tech professionals, and every line of the site speaks to that audience.

## What to put on the homepage

1. **Headline:** the feeling and the outcome. "Feeling stuck? Find your flow."
2. **Who you help:** in one line.
3. **How it works:** three steps.
4. **Results:** testimonials with role changes.
5. **Your credentials:** ICF level, recruiting or HR background, industries you know.
6. **Call to action:** a free 20 to 30 minute call.

## Services to consider listing

- One-to-one career coaching programmes
- CV and LinkedIn review
- Interview preparation
- Salary negotiation coaching
- Career change discovery
- Corporate outplacement

Give each its own section or page. Smaller, fixed-price services (like a CV review) are good entry points to longer programmes.

## Match your LinkedIn

Most career coaching clients find you on LinkedIn and click through. Your headline, photo and message should be consistent across both. Link your site's booking page in your LinkedIn featured section.

## Content that attracts career clients

Write the articles your clients are searching for:

- "How to change careers at 40"
- "Signs you've outgrown your job"
- "How to answer 'tell me about yourself'"
- "How to negotiate salary without losing the offer"

Each ranks on Google, shares well on LinkedIn and ends with an invitation to book. See how to write a blog post that ranks (/blog/how-to-write-a-blog-post-that-ranks/).

## Lead magnets that work

- CV or LinkedIn headline templates
- A "stay or go" decision worksheet
- Interview question bank
- Salary negotiation scripts
- A career values quiz

## The booking path

Embed a calendar, ask two questions (current role and what they want to change), and send automatic reminders. The full approach is in the discovery call funnel (/blog/discovery-call-booking-funnel/).

## B2B: outplacement and corporate programmes

If you work with employers, add a separate page for organisations with case studies, the outcomes you measure and an enquiry form for HR. Corporate buyers need different proof from individual clients.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should career coaches guarantee results?
No. You can share typical outcomes and client stories, but a job offer depends on factors outside your control.

### Do I need separate pages for each service?
Yes, if you want each to rank on Google and to give prospects enough detail to choose.

### How do career coaches get clients online?
A mix of LinkedIn content, search-optimised articles, referrals and a website that converts visitors into discovery calls.

---

# How to Position Your Coaching Niche on Your Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coaching-niche-positioning/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to choose and communicate a coaching niche on your website so the right clients recognise themselves instantly and feel confident booking.

Key takeaways:
- A clear niche makes marketing easier and fees higher
- Define it with three parts: who, problem and outcome
- Put your positioning statement in the first line of your homepage
- You can niche your marketing without turning away other good clients

"I help people live their best life" is true of every coach and persuasive to no one. A niche isn't a cage; it's a signpost. It tells the right person, in a second, "this is for you".

## Why niching works

- **Recognition.** People respond to messages that describe their exact situation.
- **Referrals.** "She's the coach for new managers in tech" is easy to remember and pass on.
- **Search.** "Career coach for nurses" is far easier to rank for than "life coach".
- **Pricing.** Specialists charge more than generalists.
- **Content.** You always know what to write about.

## The three-part positioning formula

**I help [who] to [outcome] without/despite [problem].**

- "I help first-time founders lead growing teams without burning out."
- "I help women navigating fertility treatment feel supported and in control."
- "I help tech professionals move into work that feels like flow."

Write ten versions. Read each aloud. The right one feels slightly scary because it's specific.

## Four ways to niche

| Dimension | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Who | Lawyers, new mothers, expats, creatives |
| Problem | Burnout, imposter feelings, divorce, redundancy |
| Outcome | Promotion, career change, confidence, boundaries |
| Method | Somatic work, strengths-based, a named framework |

The strongest niches combine two: a who and a problem.

## Put it on your website

### The hero

Your positioning belongs in your headline or the line directly beneath it. Don't make visitors hunt for it.

### The "is this you?" section

Three or four bullet points describing your ideal client's situation in their own words.

### Your programmes

Name and describe them in terms of the niche outcome.

### Your testimonials

Choose stories from clients who fit the niche. People look for someone like themselves.

### Your content

Articles, lead magnets and social posts all speak to the same person.

## Examples of clear positioning

Each of these sites tells you who it's for within seconds:

George Dupont Leadership targets sports franchises and C-suite teams with a trademarked system. Co-Allies speaks to women on the path to motherhood and leaders in transition. Different audiences, same clarity.

## "But I don't want to turn clients away"

You won't. Niching is about marketing focus, not a rule about who you can work with. People outside your niche will still find you through referrals and often say "I know I'm not exactly your usual client, but...". What changes is that your ideal clients finally recognise you.

## How to find your niche

1. **Look at your best clients.** Who did you love working with and get great results for? What did they have in common?
2. **Look at your own story.** Many coaches serve a past version of themselves.
3. **Check demand.** Are people searching for it and paying for it?
4. **Test.** Change your headline and LinkedIn bio for 90 days and see who shows up.

## Signs your positioning is working

- Discovery calls start with "I read your site and it felt like you were describing me"
- Referrals arrive pre-sold
- You stop competing on price
- Writing content gets easier

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I have more than one niche?
You can serve two closely related audiences, each with its own page. More than that and the homepage message blurs.

### What if I pick the wrong niche?
You adjust. Updating a headline and a few pages is quick. Staying vague costs more than choosing imperfectly.

### Do I need to niche from day one?
No. Many coaches discover their niche after their first 20 clients. Start reasonably specific and narrow as patterns emerge.

---

# Coaching Website Copywriting: Headlines and Words That Convert
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/coach-website-copywriting/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to write coaching website copy that connects: headline formulas, section-by-section guidance, words to avoid and examples from real coaching sites.

Key takeaways:
- Write to one person in the words they'd use themselves
- Your headline should name their problem or their goal
- Cut jargon like "empower" and "unlock your potential"
- Every section should end by pointing to the next step

Design gets attention. Words get the booking. Most coaching websites lose people in the first sentence by talking about the coach when the visitor is thinking about themselves.

Here's how to write copy that sounds like you and speaks to them.

## Rule one: write to one person

Picture a real client, ideally your favourite one. Write as if you're sending them a message. Use "you" twice as often as "I".

## Rule two: use their words

Go through discovery call notes, emails and testimonials. Collect the exact phrases clients use: "I feel like I'm treading water", "I know I'm capable of more". Those phrases are your copy. They'll outperform anything you invent.

## Headline formulas that work

**Problem then promise**
"Feeling stuck? Find your flow."

**The outcome**
"Clear, confident and in control again."

**The transformation**
"Transform life's hardest moments into your greatest comeback."

**The enemy**
"Cultures that perform under pressure. Without burnout, blame or busy nonsense."

**The identity**
"For women who are done wishing and ready to act."

Notice what none of them say: "Welcome to my website" or "Certified Professional Coach".

## Section by section

### Subheadline

One sentence: who you help and how. "One-to-one coaching for tech professionals ready for a career that fits."

### The problem section

Describe their situation so accurately they feel understood. Three short lines beat one long paragraph.

### The solution section

Introduce your coaching as the bridge. Focus on what changes for them.

### How it works

Three steps. Short verbs: Book. Plan. Grow.

### About snippet

Two or three sentences on why you, with a link to your about page (/blog/coach-about-page/).

### Call to action

Specific and low-pressure: "Book your free 30-minute call". Add a reassurance: "No pressure. Just a conversation."

## Words to cut

| Instead of | Try |
| --- | --- |
| Empower you to unlock your potential | Help you [specific outcome] |
| Holistic, transformative journey | A three-month programme |
| I am passionate about | (just say what you do) |
| Solutions | (name the actual thing) |
| Leverage, synergy, optimise | Use, together, improve |

If a phrase could appear on any coach's site, it isn't doing any work on yours.

## Make it scannable

Most visitors skim first and read second.

- Short paragraphs (one to three lines)
- A heading every few paragraphs
- Bullet points for lists
- Bold for the key phrase in a section, sparingly

## Calls to action that get clicked

- Use the same wording everywhere so it becomes familiar
- Start with a verb: Book, Start, Get
- Say what happens: "Book a free 30-minute call"
- Place one after every major section

For more examples, see call-to-action examples that convert (/blog/call-to-action-examples/).

## The read-aloud test

Read every page out loud. Anywhere you stumble, sound stiff or wouldn't say it to a client's face, rewrite. This catches most problems.

## Should you use AI to write your copy?

AI tools are useful for outlining and tidying, but they default to the same generic phrases every other coach's site uses. Use them to speed up a draft built from your own client language, then edit until it sounds like you.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should my homepage be?
Long enough to answer the visitor's main questions and build trust; usually 500 to 900 words broken into clear sections.

### Should I write in first person?
Yes, for a solo coach. "I" and "you" feel personal. Use "we" only if you're genuinely a team.

### Can you write my copy for me?
Yes. Copy support is part of our builds, and our free website preview (/free-website-preview/) includes a drafted homepage headline and structure for your business.

---

# How to Build a Wedding Photographer Website That Books Couples
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photographer-website-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A complete guide to building a wedding photography website that shows your best work, loads fast, ranks locally and turns browsing couples into enquiries.

Key takeaways:
- Couples decide in seconds, so your first screen must show your best image and where you work
- Curate hard: 30 exceptional images beat 300 good ones
- Speed matters as much as beauty because most couples browse on phones
- An availability check or simple enquiry form on every page turns swooning into bookings

A wedding photographer's website has one of the hardest jobs on the internet. It has to be beautiful enough to make a couple fall for your work, fast enough that they don't leave while it loads, and clear enough that they know how to hire you. Most manage one of the three.

We've built sites for wedding photographers and filmmakers in Chicago, Hawaii, Brisbane, Denver, Ottawa and Christchurch. Here's what consistently works.

## The first screen

When a couple lands on your homepage, they should see, without scrolling:

1. **One stunning image or short film clip.** Your single best frame, not a slideshow of twelve.
2. **Who you are and where you work.** "Chicago & Peoria wedding photographer."
3. **A line that captures your style.** "Moments you'll see again."
4. **A way to enquire.** "Check your date" or "Inquire".

That's it. Everything else comes after the scroll.

## The pages you need

### Portfolio

Organise by what couples want to see: weddings, engagements, and perhaps by style or season. Show full galleries from a few real weddings as well as highlights; couples want to know what a whole day looks like, not only the hero shots. See how many photos should be in your portfolio (/blog/photographer-portfolio-curation/).

### About

Couples will spend their whole wedding day with you. They want to like you. Show your face, share your approach and let your personality come through. More in writing an about page couples connect with (/blog/wedding-photographer-about-page/).

### Investment

Whether to show prices is the eternal debate. Our view: show at least a starting price. We explain why in should you show prices on your wedding photography website? (/blog/wedding-photography-pricing-page/)

### Real weddings / journal

Individual blog posts for weddings you've shot. They show range, help couples picture their own day and are the backbone of your SEO, especially when you name the venue.

### Contact

A form that asks the right questions without feeling like homework. See the perfect wedding inquiry form (/blog/wedding-inquiry-form/).

## Speed: the invisible dealbreaker

Photography sites are image-heavy by nature, and that's where most go wrong. A homepage with 40 full-resolution JPEGs can take ten seconds to load on mobile data. Couples won't wait.

The fix isn't fewer images; it's smarter delivery: modern formats (WebP or AVIF), images sized for the screen they're shown on, and lazy loading so pictures only download as they scroll into view. Done properly, a gallery-rich page can still load in under two seconds. Details in how to make your photography website load fast (/blog/photography-website-speed/).

## Get found locally

Couples search for "[city] wedding photographer" and "[venue name] wedding photos". To appear:

- Put your location in your homepage title and headline
- Create a page for each area you serve
- Blog real weddings with the venue name in the title
- Set up and maintain a Google Business Profile
- Collect Google reviews

Our full guide: SEO for wedding photographers (/blog/wedding-photographer-seo/).

## Proof

- **Reviews** from Google, The Knot or WeddingWire, shown on the site
- **Awards and features** ("ranked in the top 10 in Illinois")
- **Numbers** that reassure: years in business, weddings photographed
- **Kind words** next to matching images from that couple's day

## Make enquiring easy

Put an enquiry button in the header on every page. On mobile, make it sticky. An availability checker ("Check your date in seconds") is a lovely touch: it gives the couple instant gratification and starts the conversation.

## Design principles for photography sites

- **Let the work breathe.** Neutral backgrounds, generous spacing.
- **Type with character.** An elegant serif or refined sans sets the mood without competing.
- **Consistent editing** across images shown together.
- **Subtle motion.** Gentle fades and reveals; nothing that fights the photos.
- **Mobile first.** The majority of couples will see your site on a phone, often from an Instagram link.

## Template or custom?

Squarespace, Showit and Pixieset make attractive sites and are fine when you're starting. Custom becomes worth it when you want to stand apart from the hundreds of photographers on the same templates, load faster, and rank better. We compare them in Squarespace vs custom websites for photographers (/blog/squarespace-vs-custom-for-photographers/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many images should be on my homepage?
Fewer than you think: one hero image and 10 to 20 carefully chosen frames further down is plenty.

### Should I include video on my homepage?
A short, silent, well-compressed clip can be powerful, especially if you also offer films. Make sure it doesn't slow the page.

### How often should I update my portfolio?
At least once a season. Replace older work with your latest best so the site reflects how you shoot today.

# SEO for Wedding Photographers: The Complete Guide
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photographer-seo/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How wedding photographers can rank on Google: local keywords, venue pages, blogging real weddings, image SEO, Google Business Profile and reviews.

Key takeaways:
- Target "city + wedding photographer" on your homepage and venue names in blog posts
- Each real-wedding post is a landing page for a venue search
- Image file names, alt text and compression all matter
- A complete Google Business Profile with reviews puts you in the map results

Instagram shows your work to people who already follow you. Google shows it to couples who are actively looking to book. For many wedding photographers, search is the single biggest source of enquiries, and it's work that keeps paying for years.

## How couples search

- **"[City] wedding photographer"** — high intent, high competition
- **"[Venue] wedding photographer"** or **"[venue] wedding photos"** — high intent, low competition
- **"[Style] wedding photographer [region]"** — documentary, elopement, Catholic, destination
- **Planning questions** — "best time for wedding photos", "how many hours of photography do I need"

A good SEO plan covers all four.

## Step 1: optimise your homepage for your main location

- **Title tag:** "Chicago & Peoria Wedding Photographer | Dan Reynolds Photography"
- **H1 heading:** include location and "wedding photographer" naturally
- **First paragraph:** say where you're based and where you travel
- **Footer:** location and contact details

See title tags and meta descriptions (/blog/title-tags-meta-descriptions/) for how to write them.

## Step 2: location pages

If you serve several areas, give each a page: "Milwaukee Wedding Photographer", "Wisconsin Wedding Photographer". Each needs unique content: weddings you've shot there, favourite venues, local tips. No copy-and-paste. Our guide to local landing pages (/blog/local-landing-pages/) shows how.

## Step 3: venue pages and real-wedding posts

This is the most underused strategy in wedding photography. When a couple books a venue, they immediately search for photos taken there. If your blog post or venue guide appears, you're talking to a couple with a confirmed date and location.

For each wedding you blog:

- Title: "[Venue Name] Wedding | [Couple's names]"
- 300+ words telling the story of the day and mentioning the venue, town and vendors
- 30 to 60 well-optimised images
- Links to the venue and other vendors
- A call to action for couples marrying there

We go deeper in venue pages for wedding photographers (/blog/venue-pages-for-photographers/).

## Step 4: image SEO

Your images are your content, so make them readable to Google:

- **File names:** `kualoa-ranch-wedding-ceremony.webp`, not `IMG_4821.jpg`
- **Alt text:** a plain description: "Bride and groom walking through the gardens at Kualoa Ranch"
- **Compression:** WebP or AVIF, sized appropriately
- **Lazy loading** for everything below the first screen

More in our image SEO guide (/blog/image-seo/).

## Step 5: Google Business Profile

Your profile decides whether you appear in the map results. Fill in every field, choose "Wedding photographer" as the primary category, add your service areas, upload fresh photos monthly and reply to every review. Full walkthrough: Google Business Profile for wedding photographers (/blog/google-business-profile-photographers/).

## Step 6: reviews

Ask every couple for a Google review when you deliver their gallery; that's when they're happiest. Make it easy with a direct link. Reviews influence both rankings and bookings. See how wedding vendors can get more reviews (/blog/reviews-for-wedding-vendors/).

## Step 7: links from the wedding world

- Venue "preferred vendor" lists
- Features on wedding blogs and magazines
- Vendor friends linking to your blog posts about shared weddings
- Local directories and associations

When you publish a wedding, send the link to every vendor involved. Many will share and link to it.

## Step 8: technical health

A beautiful site that's slow or broken on mobile won't rank. Check:

- Mobile PageSpeed score
- HTTPS
- One H1 per page
- An XML sitemap submitted in Search Console
- No broken links

Our technical SEO checklist (/blog/technical-seo-checklist/) lists everything.

## Helpful content couples search for

- "How many hours of wedding photography do I need?"
- "Wedding day timeline for the best photos"
- "Best wedding venues in [region]"
- "What to wear for engagement photos"

More in 40 blog post ideas for wedding photographers (/blog/wedding-photographer-blog-ideas/).

## How long does it take?

Venue posts can rank in weeks because competition is low. City-level terms usually take six to twelve months of consistent work. Start now; the photographers ranking today began years ago.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Instagram help my Google ranking?
Not directly. It builds awareness, which leads to people searching your name, which helps.

### Should I blog every wedding?
Blog the ones at venues you'd love to shoot again and the ones that best show your style.

### Is Squarespace or Showit bad for SEO?
They cover the basics. Custom sites offer more control over speed and structure, which matters in competitive cities.

# Wedding Videographer Website: Showcasing Films Without Slowing Down
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-videographer-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build a wedding videography website that puts your films front and centre, loads quickly, and converts couples into enquiries.

Key takeaways:
- Lead with a short, silent, looping clip and let couples choose to press play
- Host films on Vimeo or YouTube and load players only when clicked
- Each film deserves a page with the story, the venue and stills
- Explain your packages and deliverables clearly because couples don't know film jargon

Film is the most emotional medium a wedding vendor has, and the hardest to present online. Video files are heavy, autoplay is unreliable and a single badly embedded player can add seconds to your load time. Get it right, though, and nothing sells better.

## The hero: motion without the wait

The strongest opening for a filmmaker's site is a short, silent background loop: 8 to 15 seconds of your best moments, compressed hard, with a still poster image that shows instantly while it loads.

Rules:

- **Keep it under 3 to 5 MB.** 720p is plenty for a background.
- **Muted and looping.** Browsers block autoplay with sound.
- **Poster image first** so the page never looks empty.
- **A fallback image on slow connections.**

Then give couples a clear "Watch the film" button for the full piece.

## Embedding films the fast way

A page with six embedded Vimeo players loads six players' worth of scripts, even if nobody presses play. Instead:

1. Show a thumbnail with a play button.
2. Load the actual player only when clicked.

This "facade" technique can cut seconds off load time and is one of the biggest wins on film sites. See website animations and performance (/blog/website-animations-performance/) for more on keeping rich sites fast.

**Where to host:** Vimeo gives clean, ad-free playback and privacy controls. YouTube adds discoverability. Many filmmakers use Vimeo on the site and YouTube for reach.

## Give each film a home

Don't just list embeds on one page. Give your best films their own pages with:

- The film
- A few paragraphs on the couple and the day
- The venue, location and vendors
- A handful of stills (frame grabs work beautifully)
- A call to action

These pages rank for venue searches the same way photographers' blog posts do. See venue pages (/blog/venue-pages-for-photographers/).

## Explain what couples are buying

Couples know what a photo album is. They often don't know the difference between a highlight film, a feature film, a teaser and documentary edits. Spell it out:

| Deliverable | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Teaser | 60 to 90 seconds for social, delivered quickly |
| Highlight film | 4 to 8 minutes, the story of the day |
| Feature film | 15 to 30 minutes with full speeches and vows |
| Documentary edit | Ceremony and speeches in full |

Mention anything distinctive: 4K, drone, Super 8, same-day edits, licensed music.

## Pricing

Film packages confuse couples more than photography. A clear investment page with starting prices and what's included will save you hours of email. Alpha Visuals, for instance, states that highlight films start from a set price, which immediately qualifies enquiries.

## Stills matter too

Not everyone will press play, especially at work or on mobile data. Sprinkle high-quality frame grabs throughout so the site still sells with the sound off.

## Sound and music

Never autoplay audio. Let couples choose. On film pages, mention that the film is best watched with sound on; it's a small nudge that changes how they experience it.

## SEO for filmmakers

- Homepage targeting "[city] wedding videographer"
- Film pages with venue names
- Text on every page: Google can't watch your film
- Video schema markup so films can appear in video results
- A Google Business Profile with reviews

The principles in SEO for wedding photographers (/blog/wedding-photographer-seo/) apply almost exactly.

## Photo and film together

If you offer both, or partner with a photographer, say so prominently. Couples love booking one team. Dan Reynolds Photography presents photo and film side by side for exactly this reason.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should my film autoplay on the homepage?
A muted background loop, yes. A full film with sound, no; let visitors choose.

### How many films should I show?
Five to eight of your best, covering different venues and styles.

### Can a video-heavy site still be fast?
Yes, with compressed loops, poster images and click-to-load players. Our film sites load quickly on mobile for this reason.

---

# Should You Show Prices on Your Wedding Photography Website?
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photography-pricing-page/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

The case for and against showing wedding photography prices online, what to include on an investment page, and wording that filters without scaring couples off.

Key takeaways:
- Showing a starting price saves time for you and the couple
- You don't have to publish full packages; "collections begin at" works well
- Present price alongside what's included and why it's worth it
- Follow pricing with proof and an easy way to enquire

Few questions divide wedding photographers like this one. One camp says publishing prices scares couples away before they've fallen for your work. The other says hiding them wastes everyone's time. After building sites for photographers and filmmakers across six countries, here's where we land.

## The case for showing prices

- **Couples expect it.** Most are comparing several photographers and will skip those who make them ask.
- **It filters enquiries.** You stop spending evenings replying to couples whose budget is a third of your rate.
- **It builds trust.** Openness reads as confidence.
- **It anchors value.** Seeing a number next to what's included frames the conversation.

## The case against

- **Bespoke quoting.** If every wedding is priced individually, a single number may mislead.
- **Competitors can see it.** True, though they can find out anyway.
- **Sticker shock without context.** A price with no explanation of value can put people off.

## The middle path most photographers should take

Show a **starting price** and explain what shapes the final figure.

> "Wedding collections begin at $3,800. Most couples invest between $4,500 and $6,000 for full-day coverage with a second photographer."

This filters effectively without boxing you in, and invites the enquiry rather than replacing it.

## What to include on an investment page

1. **A short intro** about your approach and what the experience includes
2. **Starting price** or two to three collections
3. **What's included:** hours, second shooter, engagement session, gallery, albums, turnaround time
4. **Add-ons:** extra hours, albums, film, rehearsal dinner
5. **How booking works:** retainer, contract, payment schedule
6. **Travel:** where you're based and how travel fees work
7. **Testimonials** from couples who felt it was worth every penny
8. **FAQs**
9. **A call to action:** "Check your date"

## Presenting collections

If you list full packages, three is the magic number. Name them, lead with the experience and put the most popular in the middle.

| | Essential | Signature | Complete |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coverage | 6 hours | 8 hours | 10 hours |
| Second photographer | — | Included | Included |
| Engagement session | — | Included | Included |
| Album | — | — | Included |

## Wording that reassures

- Call it "Investment" or "Pricing"; both are fine. Couples search for "pricing".
- Explain the why: "You're not only booking a day of photography. You're booking 14 months of planning support, 40 hours of editing and images your grandchildren will see."
- Offer payment plans if you have them.
- Invite conversation: "Every wedding is different. Tell me about yours and I'll put together a custom quote."

## If you truly can't show prices

Say so and give a reason, plus a response time: "Because every celebration is unique, I create a custom proposal for each couple. Send me your date and I'll reply within 24 hours." Silence is the real conversion killer.

## A pricing guide PDF

Some photographers offer a detailed guide in exchange for an email address. It works if the site still shows a starting price. If the guide is the only way to see any number, many couples won't bother.

## See how others handle it

## Frequently asked questions

### Will I get fewer enquiries if I show prices?
Possibly fewer, but better. Photographers usually find the quality and booking rate improve.

### Should I show prices on Instagram too?
A "starting at" line in your highlights or link page is helpful and saves repetitive DMs.

### How often should I raise my prices?
Review them at least once a year, or whenever you're booking more than about 70% of enquiries.

---

# Venue Pages: The Most Underrated SEO Strategy for Wedding Photographers
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/venue-pages-for-photographers/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How wedding photographers and videographers can use venue pages and real-wedding posts to rank on Google and reach couples who have already booked a venue.

Key takeaways:
- Couples search "[venue] wedding photos" the moment they book
- Venue pages face far less competition than city keywords
- Combine practical venue advice with your best images from that location
- Share each page with the venue and vendors to earn links and referrals

A couple books their venue. That night, they type "Kualoa Ranch wedding photos" into Google to see what their day might look like. Whoever appears is talking to a couple with a date, a location and a budget, who haven't yet chosen a photographer.

That's why venue pages are the best-kept secret in wedding SEO.

## Why they work

- **High intent.** These couples are booking vendors now.
- **Low competition.** Hundreds of photographers fight for "Chicago wedding photographer". A handful compete for each venue.
- **Relevance.** Seeing their actual venue through your lens is the most persuasive portfolio possible.
- **Relationships.** Venues love and share good content about themselves.

## Two formats

### 1. Real-wedding blog posts

One wedding at one venue. Tell the story of the day with 30 to 60 images.

**Title:** "A Summer Wedding at Lanikuhonua | Maya & Chris"

### 2. Venue guides

An evergreen page about the venue itself, drawing on several weddings you've shot there.

**Title:** "Four Seasons Oahu Wedding Photography: A Photographer's Guide"

Guides take more effort and rank for longer. Aim for a guide for each of your top five to ten venues, and real-wedding posts for everything else.

## What to include in a venue guide

1. **An introduction** to the venue and why you love shooting there
2. **Your best images** from that location, across seasons and lighting
3. **Best photo spots** on the property
4. **Timing advice:** when the light is best, sunset times, where to do portraits
5. **Rain plan:** indoor options that still look great
6. **Practical details:** capacity, ceremony locations, getting-ready rooms
7. **Recommended vendors** you've worked with there
8. **Links** to full galleries from weddings at the venue
9. **A call to action:** "Getting married here? Check your date."

Aim for 600 to 1,200 words of genuinely useful advice. This is what separates a page that ranks from a gallery that doesn't.

## On-page SEO checklist

- Venue name and "wedding" in the page title and H1
- Venue name and town in the first paragraph
- Descriptive image file names and alt text (image SEO guide (/blog/image-seo/))
- A link to the venue's own website
- Internal links to and from related posts
- Fast loading despite many images (photography website speed (/blog/photography-website-speed/))

## Getting links and referrals from the page

When you publish:

1. **Email the venue coordinator** with the link and a few images they can use, credited.
2. **Tag and message every vendor** involved.
3. **Ask to be considered for the preferred vendor list.**
4. **Share on Pinterest** with the venue name in the pin title.

Venues regularly link to good guides, and those links lift your whole site.

## Which venues to prioritise

- Venues you've shot at and want to return to
- Popular venues with high search volume
- New venues with little content yet
- Venues that suit your style and price point

Check demand by typing the venue name plus "wedding" into Google and seeing what autocomplete suggests.

## What if you haven't shot there yet?

Be honest. You can still write a useful guide based on a site visit or styled shoot and say so. Never imply you've photographed weddings there if you haven't.

## Examples from real sites

These sites build their SEO around real weddings and locations:

## Keep them updated

Each time you shoot at the venue again, add a few new images and a link to the new gallery. Fresh content keeps the page ranking.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many venue pages do I need?
Start with your top five. Each one is a long-term asset.

### Can videographers use this strategy?
Absolutely. Embed the film, add stills and write about filming at the venue.

### Do I need the venue's permission?
You don't need permission to write about a venue, but building the relationship first makes them far more likely to share and link.
