# 40 Blog Post Ideas for Wedding Photographers (That Bring in Enquiries)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photographer-blog-ideas/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Forty blog post ideas for wedding photographers and videographers, grouped by what they achieve: ranking for venues, answering couples' questions and showing your style.

Key takeaways:
- Blog for couples, not for other photographers
- Real weddings and venue guides bring in the most ready-to-book traffic
- Planning advice builds trust months before a couple enquires
- One strong post a month is enough if every post has a job

Most photographers' blogs go quiet after three posts because "blogging" feels like a chore with no clear payoff. The fix is to treat every post as a small landing page aimed at a specific search or a specific doubt in a couple's mind.

Here are forty ideas, grouped by what they do for you.

## Real weddings (your SEO engine)

1. A full wedding at a venue you'd love to shoot again
2. A rainy-day wedding that still looked incredible
3. A small or micro wedding
4. An elopement
5. A winter wedding
6. A multi-day or cultural celebration
7. A wedding with an unusual timeline (brunch, sunset ceremony)
8. Your favourite wedding of the year, and why

Put the venue in the title every time. Each of these is a page that can rank for "[venue] wedding photos". See venue pages (/blog/venue-pages-for-photographers/).

## Venue and location guides

9. A photographer's guide to your most-shot venue
10. The best wedding venues in your region
11. Best engagement photo locations in your city
12. Hidden-gem ceremony spots
13. Best venues for a small wedding
14. Where to take portraits at a specific venue
15. Best sunset spots for couple portraits
16. Indoor photo locations for bad weather

## Planning advice (trust builders)

17. A wedding day timeline that leaves room for great photos
18. How many hours of photography do you need?
19. First look or no first look?
20. How to plan family photos without chaos
21. What to do if it rains
22. Getting-ready tips for better photos
23. How to choose a ceremony time for the best light
24. Unplugged ceremonies: pros and cons
25. Do you need a second photographer?
26. Should you hire a videographer too?

Couples search for these early in their planning. If your advice helps, you're the photographer they already trust when they're ready to book.

## Engagement sessions

27. What to wear for engagement photos
28. How to feel relaxed in front of the camera
29. Engagement session ideas for couples who hate posing
30. Should you bring your dog?

## About you and your process

31. What it's like to work with you, from enquiry to gallery
32. Your editing style explained with before and afters
33. What's in your camera bag (keep it short; couples skim this)
34. Why you became a wedding photographer
35. How you choose which images to deliver
36. Behind the scenes of a wedding day

## Products and after the wedding

37. Why print your photos: albums explained
38. How to choose images for your album
39. What to do with your wedding photos after the day

## Vendor spotlights

40. Your favourite planners, florists or venues, interviewed

These earn links and referrals from the vendors you feature.

## How to write each post

- **Title:** include the venue or the question, the way couples would type it
- **Intro:** two or three sentences that set the scene
- **Body:** 300 to 800 words. Google can't read photos; it needs text.
- **Images:** well compressed, descriptive file names and alt text (image SEO (/blog/image-seo/))
- **Links:** to the venue, vendors and your related posts
- **Call to action:** "Planning a wedding at [venue]? Check your date."

More on structure in how to write a blog post that ranks (/blog/how-to-write-a-blog-post-that-ranks/).

## A realistic schedule

| Month type | Post |
| --- | --- |
| Busy season | One real wedding |
| Quiet season | One venue guide and one planning article |

Twelve to eighteen good posts a year will outperform fifty rushed ones.

## Repurpose everything

Each post becomes a Pinterest board, three Instagram carousels, a reel and an email to past enquiries. Write once, use five times.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should a wedding blog post be?
At least 300 words alongside the images. Venue guides and planning articles do better at 800 to 1,200.

### Should I blog every wedding?
No. Blog the ones that show your style and target venues or locations you want more of.

### Do blogs still work when couples use Instagram?
Yes. Instagram is for discovery; Google is where couples research venues and vendors with intent to book.

# How to Make Your Photography Website Load Fast (Without Losing Quality)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/photography-website-speed/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Practical steps to speed up an image-heavy photography website: formats, sizing, lazy loading, galleries and video, with no visible loss in quality.

Key takeaways:
- Export at the size the image is displayed, not full resolution
- WebP or AVIF cut file sizes dramatically with no visible difference
- Lazy-load everything below the first screen
- Load video players only when someone clicks play

Photographers face a real tension: the work has to look incredible, and incredible images are heavy. A slow site loses couples before they've seen a single frame, and Google ranks slow pages lower. The good news is that you can have both speed and quality. It comes down to how images are prepared and delivered.

## Why speed matters more for photographers

- Most couples arrive on a phone, often on mobile data
- Portfolio pages carry dozens of images
- Visitors compare several photographers in one sitting; the slow tab gets closed
- Google's Core Web Vitals reward fast-loading pages (explained here (/blog/core-web-vitals-explained/))

## Step 1: export at display size

A camera file might be 8,000 pixels wide. Your website shows it at 1,600 at most. Uploading the original forces every visitor to download four or five times more than they can see.

**Guidelines:**

| Use | Width to export |
| --- | --- |
| Full-width hero | 2,000 to 2,400 px |
| Gallery image | 1,400 to 1,800 px |
| Grid thumbnail | 600 to 800 px |

## Step 2: use modern formats

**WebP** is supported by every modern browser and is typically 25 to 35% smaller than JPEG at the same visual quality. **AVIF** is smaller still. Export JPEGs from Lightroom at around 80 quality, then convert to WebP at 75 to 82 with a tool like Squoosh, ShortPixel or your site's built-in optimiser.

At normal viewing sizes, nobody can tell the difference. You'll see it in your load times.

## Step 3: serve the right size to each device

A phone doesn't need the desktop version. Responsive images (`srcset`) let the browser choose the smallest file that still looks sharp on that screen. A good custom build or a quality platform handles this automatically; if yours doesn't, it's worth fixing.

## Step 4: lazy-load below the fold

Only the first image or two should load immediately. Everything else should load as the visitor scrolls towards it. This single change can turn a ten-second page into a two-second one.

## Step 5: reserve space for images

If images pop in and shove the text around, the page feels janky and Google counts it against you (it's called layout shift). Setting width and height on every image reserves the space before it loads.

## Step 6: tame your galleries

- **Paginate or "load more"** for galleries beyond 40 to 60 images
- **Avoid heavy slider plugins** that load every slide up front
- **Use a lightbox** that loads the large version only on click

## Step 7: handle video carefully

- Compress background loops hard and keep them short
- Always set a poster image
- For Vimeo and YouTube, show a thumbnail and load the player on click

More in wedding videographer websites (/blog/wedding-videographer-website/).

## Step 8: trim everything else

- **Fonts:** two families at most, self-hosted or preloaded
- **Plugins and widgets:** each one adds weight; remove those you don't need
- **Third-party scripts:** chat widgets, pixels and Instagram feeds are common culprits
- **Hosting:** a good host with a CDN delivers images from a server near the visitor

## How to test

1. Open PageSpeed Insights (https://pagespeed.web.dev/) and test your homepage and a gallery page on mobile.
2. Look at **Largest Contentful Paint**; aim for under 2.5 seconds.
3. Check the "properly size images" and "next-gen formats" suggestions.
4. Test on a real phone on mobile data, not only on office Wi-Fi.

## What we do on photography builds

On sites like the ones below, every image is exported in multiple sizes as WebP, lazy-loaded with reserved space, and the hero is prioritised so it appears first. That's how a gallery-rich homepage still loads quickly.

## Frequently asked questions

### Will compressing images make them look worse?
Not at sensible settings. At WebP quality 75 to 82 and display size, the difference is invisible to visitors.

### What file size should I aim for?
Under 300 KB for large images and under 100 KB for thumbnails is a good target.

### Is my platform the problem?
Sometimes. If you've optimised images and the site is still slow, the template or plugins may be the bottleneck. We're happy to take a look.

# The Perfect Wedding Inquiry Form: Questions That Qualify Couples
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-inquiry-form/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What to ask on a wedding photography or videography inquiry form to get more, better enquiries, with a ready-to-use field list and follow-up tips.

Key takeaways:
- Ask for the date and venue first; they tell you most of what you need
- Keep required fields to six or fewer
- One open question lets couples show their personality
- Reply within a few hours; speed wins bookings

Your inquiry form is the bridge between a couple loving your work and you getting the chance to book them. Ask too little and you're emailing back and forth for days. Ask too much and they abandon it halfway.

Here's the balance that works.

## The essential fields

1. **Names** (both partners)
2. **Email**
3. **Wedding date** (with a "we don't have one yet" option)
4. **Venue or location**
5. **What they're looking for** (photo, film or both)
6. **Tell me about your day** (open text)

That's enough to check availability, understand the scale and start a real conversation.

## Useful optional fields

- **Phone number.** Optional; some couples prefer a text.
- **Estimated guest count.** Helps you judge coverage.
- **How did you find me?** Tells you which marketing works.
- **Budget range.** Divisive. If you show starting prices on your site, you may not need it. If you don't, a range dropdown filters effectively.
- **Instagram handle.** A nice way to get to know them.

## Questions that start a conversation

Swap the dull "Message" box for a prompt:

- "Tell me about the two of you and what you're planning."
- "What matters most to you about your wedding photos?"
- "What's the part of the day you're most excited about?"

Couples who answer thoughtfully tend to be the ones who value photography. And you get something personal to respond to.

## Design details that lift completions

- **One column,** thumb-friendly on mobile
- **A date picker** rather than free text
- **Clear labels** above each field
- **A friendly button:** "Send my enquiry" or "Check my date" beats "Submit"
- **A note about response time:** "I reply within 24 hours"
- **A confirmation message** that tells them what happens next

More in contact forms that convert (/blog/contact-form-best-practices/).

## Add an availability check

A simple "Check your date" field near the top of your site is a lovely hook. The couple gets an instant answer and you get the start of an enquiry. Captured by Katherine uses this to great effect.

## Where the form should live

- A dedicated contact page
- A short version at the bottom of every portfolio and investment page
- A button in the header on every page

Don't make couples hunt for it after they've fallen for a gallery.

## What happens after they submit

### Instantly

An automatic email confirming you received it, with a link to your pricing guide or a favourite gallery while they wait.

### Within a few hours

A personal reply. Mention something specific they wrote. Confirm availability. Suggest a call. Speed matters: couples often book the first photographer who replies warmly and promptly.

### If they go quiet

Follow up after three days and again after a week. Most photographers never follow up at all; those who do book more weddings.

## Tools

Your form can feed a studio management tool (HoneyBook, Dubsado, Studio Ninja, Sprout Studio) so enquiries, replies, contracts and invoices sit in one place. A good website integrates with whichever you use.

## Protect against spam

Use a hidden "honeypot" field or an invisible challenge. Avoid old-style puzzles that make humans prove themselves.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I ask for budget on the form?
If your site shows starting prices, it's optional. If it doesn't, a budget range saves time for you both.

### How long should my form be?
Six required fields at most. Everything else can be optional or asked later.

### Is it better to use a form or just list my email?
Offer both. Forms capture structured information; some couples simply prefer to email.

# Wedding Photographer Website Examples (and What Makes Them Work)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photographer-website-examples/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Six wedding photography and videography websites we built, from Chicago to Christchurch, with a breakdown of what each one does well.

Key takeaways:
- The best photography sites open with one unforgettable image and a clear location
- Each has its own visual identity that matches the photographer's style
- All make it effortless to enquire from any page
- Fast loading is designed in, not bolted on

Templates have made wedding photography sites look increasingly alike. These six, all built by Code Bunny, show how much room there is to be distinctive while staying fast and easy to book.

## 1. Dan Reynolds Photography — Chicago & Peoria, Illinois

A husband-and-wife photo and film team ranked among the top photographers in Illinois. The homepage opens with a golden-hour frame and the line "Moments you'll see again", then moves through portfolio, films and investment.

**What works:** photo and film presented as one experience; a built-in editor and blog so the team can publish their own stories; location in the first line for local SEO.

After launch, Dan told us: "I think the site looks great. I got a lot of compliments on it."

## 2. Mark Arista Films — Oahu, Hawaii

A wedding videographer whose site feels like the opening titles of a film: a dark palette, film-strip details and a single centred title.

**What works:** the design language *is* the medium. You know it's a filmmaker's site before you read a word.

## 3. Captured by Katherine — Brisbane, Australia

Candid wedding, family and formal photography since 2009. Warm, romantic and relaxed, with an availability check couples can use in seconds.

**What works:** the "Check your date" hook turns browsing into an enquiry.

## 4. Jack Albert Weddings — Ottawa Valley, Canada

Warm, cinematic wedding films across Renfrew County, Ottawa and Kingston. The headline "The day, heard again" sells what film offers that photos can't: sound.

**What works:** a headline that makes the case for video in four words.

## 5. The Things That I See — Denver, Colorado

Catholic and Christian wedding photography and film. The site leads with reverence and a clear statement of who it's for.

**What works:** a tight niche. Couples who want a photographer who understands a Catholic ceremony know instantly they've found one.

## 6. Alpha Visuals — Christchurch, New Zealand

Candid, cinematic wedding films shot in 4K with real Super 8mm available. Pricing is stated up front.

**What works:** confident pricing and a distinctive offer (Super 8) that sets it apart.

## What they have in common

1. **One hero image or clip.** No twelve-slide carousels.
2. **Location in the first line.**
3. **A personality.** Colour, type and voice match the work.
4. **An enquiry button on every screen.**
5. **Speed.** Hand-coded, optimised images, lazy loading.
6. **Text for Google.** Beautiful galleries supported by real copy.

## How to use these as inspiration

Note what draws you to each: the mood, the layout, how pricing is handled, the enquiry flow. Share those notes with your designer. Borrow structure and ideas; keep the style your own.

For the principles behind them, read how to build a wedding photographer website that books couples (/blog/wedding-photographer-website-guide/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Are these built on Squarespace or Showit?
No, they're custom-coded, which is why they look distinct and load quickly.

### Can you build something like this for me?
Yes. Tell us which you like and we'll design a free preview (/free-website-preview/) of your homepage.

### How long does a photography site take to build?
Usually one to three weeks once we have your images and copy.

# How Many Photos Should Be in Your Portfolio? A Curation Guide
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/photographer-portfolio-curation/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How wedding photographers should curate an online portfolio: how many images to show, how to choose and order them, and what to leave out.

Key takeaways:
- Twenty to forty exceptional images beat hundreds of good ones
- Show the work you want to be hired for
- Include full wedding galleries so couples can see consistency
- Open and close with your strongest frames

The hardest part of building a photography website isn't design. It's deciding what to leave out. Every image you love has a memory attached; couples only see whether it's great. A tight portfolio signals confidence. A sprawling one hides your best work among your average.

## How many images?

| Section | Recommended number |
| --- | --- |
| Homepage | 1 hero plus 10 to 20 highlights |
| Main portfolio | 30 to 50 |
| Each category (weddings, engagements) | 20 to 30 |
| Full real-wedding gallery | 40 to 80 |

If you're unsure about an image, the answer is no.

## Show what you want to shoot

Your portfolio is a filter. If you want elopements in the mountains, show those. If you fill it with ballroom receptions because that's what you've shot most, you'll book more ballrooms.

## A five-step curation process

1. **Gather** your 200 favourite images from the last two years.
2. **First cut:** remove anything technically weak or stylistically inconsistent. Aim for 100.
3. **Second cut:** remove duplicates of the same moment or pose. Aim for 60.
4. **Third cut:** ask "would I be thrilled to deliver this as the hero image?" Aim for 40.
5. **Get an outside eye.** Ask a photographer friend or a past client which ten they'd drop.

## Variety without chaos

A strong portfolio covers the range of a wedding day:

- Getting ready and details
- Emotional moments (the look, the tears, the laughter)
- Portraits of the couple
- Family and friends
- Ceremony and reception atmosphere
- The party

It should also show different light (bright sun, golden hour, indoor, night) and reflect the diversity of the couples you serve.

## Consistency

Editing style should be coherent across images shown together. If your look has changed, retire the old work, however much you love it.

## Order matters

- **Open with your best.** The first image decides whether anyone sees the second.
- **End strong.** People remember the last frame.
- **Alternate rhythm:** wide then close, quiet then energetic, colour then black and white.
- **Pair images** that complement each other side by side.

## Full galleries build trust

Highlights show your peak. Couples also want to know what an entire day looks like in your hands. Publish three to five full weddings (as blog posts or gallery pages) so they can see consistency from the first frame to the last. These posts double as SEO assets; see venue pages (/blog/venue-pages-for-photographers/).

## What to leave out

- Styled shoots presented as real weddings (label them honestly)
- Work that's more than three or four years old, unless it's iconic
- Images where the couple's faces are hidden in every frame
- Anything you're including only because the venue was impressive

## Keep it fast

Even the best curation fails if the page takes ten seconds to load. Export at display size, use WebP and lazy-load. See photography website speed (/blog/photography-website-speed/).

## Refresh regularly

Review your portfolio at the end of each season. Swap in new favourites and remove the weakest five. A portfolio is never finished.

## Examples of tight curation

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I have separate portfolios for weddings and engagements?
Yes, if you want to book both. Keep each one tight.

### Should I include black and white images?
If it's part of your style, yes. Mix them with intention rather than at random.

### How do I choose a hero image?
Pick the frame that best represents your style and makes people stop. Test two options and see which gets more enquiries.

# Google Business Profile for Wedding Photographers: Setup and Optimisation
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/google-business-profile-photographers/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How wedding photographers and videographers can set up and optimise a Google Business Profile to appear in map results and win more local enquiries.

Key takeaways:
- Your profile is what appears in Google's map results; your website alone won't get you there
- Choose "Wedding photographer" as the primary category
- Add fresh photos monthly and reply to every review
- You can hide your home address and list a service area

Search "wedding photographer near me" and the first thing you see is a map with three businesses. Those results come from Google Business Profiles, not websites. If you haven't set yours up, or set it up once and forgot it, you're invisible in the most valuable spot on the page.

It's free and takes about an hour to do properly.

## Step 1: create or claim your profile

Go to google.com/business (https://www.google.com/business/). Search for your business name first; a listing may already exist. Create or claim it, then verify (usually by video or postcard).

## Step 2: get the basics exactly right

- **Business name:** your real trading name. Don't stuff keywords in; Google can suspend profiles for that.
- **Primary category:** "Wedding photographer". Add secondary categories such as "Photographer", "Portrait studio" or "Video production service" if they apply.
- **Service area:** if you work from home, hide your address and add the cities and regions you cover.
- **Phone and website:** match exactly what's on your site.
- **Hours:** when you answer enquiries.

Consistency of name, address and phone across the web matters for local rankings. More in our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Step 3: write a strong description

You have 750 characters. Lead with what you do and where:

> "Dan Reynolds Photography is a Chicago and Central Illinois wedding photography and film team. We document weddings across Illinois and Wisconsin in a warm, documentary style..."

Mention your style, areas, and what makes you different. Write for couples, not for an algorithm.

## Step 4: add services

List each service with a short description: wedding photography, wedding videography, engagement sessions, elopements. Add starting prices if you're comfortable.

## Step 5: photos, lots of them

Profiles with more photos get more clicks. Upload:

- 20 to 30 of your best wedding images to start
- A logo and a cover image
- A photo of you
- Short video clips

Then add a few new images every month. Fresh activity signals a live business.

## Step 6: reviews

Reviews are the biggest factor you control.

- Ask every couple when you deliver their gallery
- Send your direct review link (find it under "Ask for reviews")
- Reply to every review, warmly and specifically
- Never offer incentives; it's against Google's rules

Tactics in how wedding vendors can get more reviews (/blog/reviews-for-wedding-vendors/).

## Step 7: posts and updates

Google lets you publish short posts. Share a recent wedding, a blog post or an available date once or twice a month. They take five minutes and show activity.

## Step 8: questions and messages

Seed the Q&A with common questions ("Do you travel?", "How far in advance should we book?") and answer them. Turn on messaging only if you'll reply promptly.

## Step 9: link it to a strong website

Your profile and website reinforce each other. Make sure your site:

- States your location in the title and headline
- Has matching contact details in the footer
- Includes local business schema (schema guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))
- Has pages for the areas you serve

## What moves you up the map

Google says local ranking depends on relevance, distance and prominence. In practice:

| Factor | What you can do |
| --- | --- |
| Relevance | Right categories, complete services, good description |
| Distance | Accurate service areas |
| Prominence | Reviews, photos, website quality, links |

## Common mistakes

- Keyword-stuffed business names
- A profile with five photos from 2021
- Ignoring reviews
- Different phone numbers on the profile and website
- Duplicate listings

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a physical studio?
No. Service-area businesses are fully supported. Hide your address and list where you work.

### How many reviews do I need?
More than your nearest competitors, with a steady flow of new ones. Recency matters as much as total count.

### Can I have profiles in several cities?
Only where you have a genuine, staffed location. Use service areas and location pages on your site for the rest.

---

# Writing a Wedding Photographer About Page Couples Connect With
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/wedding-photographer-about-page/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to write an about page for a wedding photography or videography business that shows your personality, builds trust and leads couples to enquire.

Key takeaways:
- Couples are choosing a person to spend their wedding day with, so show them one
- Lead with how you work and what it feels like, then your story
- Use real photos of you, ideally at work
- End with an invitation to get in touch

A couple can find a hundred photographers whose work they like. They book the one they'd be happy to have beside them for twelve hours on the most emotional day of their lives. Your about page is where that choice gets made.

## What couples want to know

- What are you like to be around?
- How do you work on the day: directing or blending in?
- Do you understand what matters to us?
- Can we trust you to handle it?

Notice what isn't on the list: your first camera, your gear, or the year you "fell in love with capturing moments".

## A structure that works

### 1. Open with them

> "You're planning a day full of people you love, and you'd rather be with them than posing for hours."

### 2. How you work

Describe your approach in plain terms. "I'll give gentle direction for portraits, then step back and let the day unfold. Most couples tell me they forgot I was there."

### 3. Who you are

Now a little about you: where you're from, how long you've been doing this, why weddings. Keep it warm and brief. If you're a duo, introduce both of you and how you work together.

### 4. Proof you're good at this

Years of experience, number of weddings, awards or features, and a short quote from a couple about what you were like on the day.

### 5. A few human details

Coffee order, favourite film, your dog's name. Three or four lines that give couples something to connect over.

### 6. Invite them in

"I'd love to hear what you're planning. Tell me about your day." Then the button.

## Photos of you

This is non-negotiable. Include at least one clear, friendly portrait and one of you working at a wedding. Couples who can picture you in the room are far more likely to enquire.

## Voice

Write the way you'd talk to a couple over coffee. First person, relaxed, specific. Skip the phrases every photographer uses:

- "I'm passionate about capturing authentic moments"
- "More than just a photographer"
- "Telling your unique love story"

Say something only you could say.

## For duos and teams

Husband-and-wife teams and studios should explain who does what and who'll be there on the day. Couples worry about booking a brand and getting a stranger. Dan Reynolds Photography, for example, presents photo and film as the work of one close team.

## Add a short "what to expect"

Three steps from enquiry to gallery remove uncertainty:

1. **Say hello.** Tell me your date and plans.
2. **Let's chat.** A relaxed call to see if we're a fit.
3. **Book and relax.** I'll help with timelines and be there from prep to the last dance.

## Common mistakes

- No photo of yourself
- A life story in chronological order
- Gear lists
- Third-person bios for a one-person business
- No call to action

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should a photographer's about page be?
Around 250 to 500 words. Enough to feel like you, short enough to read on a phone.

### Should I mention my family or faith?
If it's part of how you connect with your ideal couples, yes. Share what feels natural.

### Should I include a video?
A 60-second hello filmed in good light can be more persuasive than any amount of text.

# Squarespace vs Custom Websites for Photographers
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/squarespace-vs-custom-for-photographers/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

An honest comparison of Squarespace, Showit, Pixieset and custom-built websites for wedding photographers: cost, speed, SEO, design freedom and when to switch.

Key takeaways:
- Templates are a sensible start when you're new and budget is tight
- Custom wins on speed, uniqueness and SEO control, which matter most in competitive cities
- The biggest cost of a template is looking like everyone else
- Switching platforms is safe if redirects are handled properly

Most wedding photographers start on Squarespace, Showit, Pixieset or a similar builder, and for good reason: they're affordable, attractive and quick to set up. The question isn't whether they're good. It's whether they're still the right tool once your business depends on standing out.

## The quick comparison

| | Template platform | Custom website |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upfront cost | $0 to $500 (plus template) | $2,500 to $8,000 |
| Monthly cost | $16 to $40 | $5 to $30 hosting |
| Look | Shared with thousands of others | Unique to you |
| Speed | Average, depends on template | Fast when built well |
| SEO control | Basics covered | Full control |
| Editing | Easy drag and drop | Easy if an editor is built in |
| Ownership | Rented | Yours |

## Where templates shine

- **Speed to launch.** You can be live in a weekend.
- **Low cost.** Ideal in year one.
- **Easy editing.** Swap images whenever you like.
- **Integrations.** Galleries, booking and email tools plug in.

If you're in your first couple of seasons, use a template and spend your money on education and gear.

## Where they hold you back

### Sameness

Popular photography templates are used by thousands of studios. When a couple has five tabs open and three share a layout, your work has to do all the differentiating.

### Speed

Builders load a lot of platform code on every page. Add 40 images and the mobile experience suffers. Custom sites ship only what the page needs. See photography website speed (/blog/photography-website-speed/).

### SEO depth

You can rank on a template; many do. In a competitive city, the extra control of a custom build (clean code, precise schema, fast load times, flexible venue pages) is an edge. See SEO for wedding photographers (/blog/wedding-photographer-seo/).

### Design limits

Want a film-strip hero, an availability checker, or a layout the template doesn't support? You're fighting the tool.

## What custom gives you

- A design built around *your* style, not adapted from someone else's
- Performance engineered for image-heavy pages
- Features made for how you work
- Full ownership of code and content

These are all custom builds, and none could be mistaken for a template:

## "But I need to update it myself"

A fair concern, and a solvable one. A custom site can include a simple editor and blog. Dan Reynolds Photography launched with exactly that: the team adds their own posts and updates content without touching code.

## When to make the switch

Consider going custom when:

- You're booking consistently and want to raise prices
- You're in a crowded market and look like your competitors
- Your site is slow and you've already optimised images
- You want to invest seriously in SEO
- You're embarrassed by how "template" it feels

## Switching without losing rankings

Moving platforms is safe when done properly:

1. List every existing URL
2. Redirect each to its new equivalent
3. Keep page titles and content that already rank
4. Resubmit your sitemap in Search Console

Full process in how to redesign without losing SEO (/blog/seo-migration-redesign/).

## A middle option

A focused custom homepage and core pages, connected to your existing gallery delivery tool (Pixieset, Pic-Time) for client galleries. You get a distinctive front door without rebuilding everything.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Showit better than Squarespace for photographers?
Showit offers more design freedom; Squarespace is simpler. Both are solid template platforms with similar limitations.

### Will a custom site get me more bookings?
A site that's faster, more distinctive and better optimised usually converts more visitors. The work still has to be good.

### Can I see what custom would look like before deciding?
Yes. We'll design a free preview (/free-website-preview/) of your homepage to compare with your current site.

# How Wedding Vendors Can Get More Reviews (Without Feeling Awkward)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/reviews-for-wedding-vendors/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A simple system for wedding photographers, videographers and vendors to collect more Google and platform reviews, with timing tips and message templates.

Key takeaways:
- Ask at the moment of peak happiness, usually gallery or film delivery
- Make it one click with a direct review link
- A short personal message outperforms an automated request
- Reply to every review and reuse the best ones on your website

Couples read reviews before they read anything else. A photographer with 80 recent five-star reviews will out-book an equally talented one with six, almost every time. Yet most vendors collect reviews by hoping.

Here's a system that takes ten minutes to set up and runs every time you deliver.

## Why reviews matter so much

- **Trust.** Couples can't try before they buy.
- **Local rankings.** Review count, rating and recency influence Google's map results.
- **Conversion.** Reviews on your website lift enquiries.
- **Words to reuse.** Couples describe your value better than you can.

## Where to collect them

1. **Google** first. It affects search visibility most.
2. **The Knot / WeddingWire / Hitched / Easy Weddings**, whichever couples use in your country.
3. **Facebook**, if your audience is active there.

Focus on Google until you have a healthy base, then spread out.

## When to ask

Timing is everything. Ask when the couple is happiest:

- The day you deliver the gallery or film
- When they message you saying they've cried over it
- After an album arrives

Not six months later when the glow has faded.

## How to ask

### 1. Get your direct link

In your Google Business Profile, choose "Ask for reviews" and copy the short link. It opens the review box directly.

### 2. Send a personal message

> "Hi Maya and Chris! I'm so glad you love the photos. It would mean a lot if you could share a few words about your experience on Google. It only takes a minute and really helps other couples find me: [link]. Thank you both, it was a joy to be part of your day."

### 3. Make it easy to write

Some couples freeze at a blank box. Offer prompts:

- What was it like working with me on the day?
- How did you feel when you saw your photos?
- Would you recommend me to a friend?

### 4. Follow up once

A gentle reminder a week or two later doubles response rates. Then let it go.

## Build it into your workflow

Add "request review" to your delivery checklist or automate it in your studio management tool, triggered a few days after delivery. The best system is the one you don't have to remember.

## Reply to every review

A thoughtful reply shows future couples you care, and signals to Google that the profile is active. Mention something specific from their day.

## Handling a negative review

It happens to everyone eventually.

1. Take a breath; don't reply angry.
2. Respond publicly, briefly and professionally.
3. Offer to resolve it privately.
4. Let your many positive reviews speak for themselves.

A calm reply to a critical review often builds more trust than a perfect record.

## Put reviews to work

- Feature the best on your homepage and investment page
- Pair each with an image from that couple's wedding
- Screenshot heartfelt messages (with permission)
- Share on Instagram stories

Sometimes the most convincing review is a casual one. After we launched Dan Reynolds Photography's site, his WhatsApp said simply: "I got a lot of compliments on it." We put it on our homepage.

## What not to do

- **Don't pay or incentivise** reviews. It breaches Google's policies.
- **Don't write your own.**
- **Don't ask only your happiest clients** in a way that screens others out; platforms prohibit "review gating".
- **Don't copy a review** from one platform to another under the couple's name without permission.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many reviews should I aim for?
More than the competitors who appear next to you in the map results, with new ones arriving regularly.

### Can I ask past couples from years ago?
Yes. A friendly anniversary message is a natural moment to ask.

### Should reviews go on my website?
Definitely. Embed or quote them near your calls to action, and consider review schema so search engines understand them.

# How to Build a Solar Company Website That Generates Leads
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-company-website-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A complete guide to solar company website design: the pages, calculators, trust signals and quote forms that turn researching homeowners into booked consultations.

Key takeaways:
- Solar buyers research for weeks, so your site must educate as well as sell
- A savings calculator and a short quote form are the two highest-converting features
- Certifications, warranties and local reviews do the trust-building
- Separate pages for homes, businesses and farms let each audience find its own answers

Solar is one of the biggest purchases a homeowner makes after the house itself. They don't decide in an afternoon. They research, compare installers, read reviews and run numbers, often over several weeks. The installer whose website answers their questions best is usually the one who gets the call.

We've built solar websites for installers in Ireland, Canada, the United States and New Zealand. This is the structure that works.

## What a solar website has to do

1. **Explain** what's possible and what it costs, in plain language
2. **Prove** you're certified, experienced and local
3. **Personalise** the numbers to the visitor's home
4. **Capture** the lead when they're ready

Miss any one and visitors move on to a competitor's site that covers it.

## The homepage

### Above the fold

- A headline about the benefit: "Go solar. Save big." or "Powering Ireland's solar future."
- A line on who you serve and where
- A primary button: "Get my free quote"
- A trust strip: years in business, installs completed, review rating, key certifications

### Further down

- Services at a glance: solar PV, batteries, EV charging
- How it works in three or four steps
- A savings calculator or estimator
- Incentives and grants available
- Recent installations
- Reviews
- FAQ
- A final quote form

## Pages every solar site needs

- **Residential solar**
- **Commercial solar**
- **Agricultural solar**, if you serve farms
- **Battery storage** and **EV charging** (how to sell them (/blog/battery-ev-charger-pages/))
- **Incentives / grants** (how to explain them (/blog/solar-incentives-content/))
- **How it works / process**
- **Projects or case studies**
- **About:** team, certifications, story
- **Service areas** (without thin content (/blog/solar-service-area-pages/))
- **FAQ** (25 questions to answer (/blog/solar-faq-content/))
- **Get a quote**

## The two features that convert

### A savings calculator

Homeowners want to know one thing: what will *I* save? A simple calculator that takes a postcode or ZIP and a monthly bill, then estimates system size, savings and payback, turns a generic pitch into a personal one. It also captures a lead at the perfect moment. More in should your solar website have a savings calculator? (/blog/solar-savings-calculator/)

### A short quote form

Three to five fields to start, more on a second step. Long forms kill conversions. See designing a solar quote form that converts (/blog/solar-quote-form/).

## Trust signals

Solar has a reputation problem in some markets: pushy sales, vanished installers, broken promises. Counter it visibly:

- Accreditation logos (SEAI, NABCEP, CEC, MCS or your local body)
- Manufacturer partnerships and warranty terms
- Years trading and number of installs
- Real photos of your team and vans
- Google reviews with a live count
- Local address and phone number

Full list in trust signals every solar website needs (/blog/solar-website-trust-signals/).

## Design for clarity

- **Clean and bright,** or premium and dark; either works if text is readable
- **Real project photos** over stock
- **Simple diagrams** for how systems work
- **Numbers shown clearly:** savings, payback, warranty years
- **Mobile first:** many visitors arrive from social ads on their phones

## Get found locally

Solar is a local business. People search "solar installers [town]" and "solar panels [county]". You need:

- Location in titles and headings
- Genuine service area pages
- A complete Google Business Profile with reviews
- Local schema markup

Our guide to SEO for solar companies (/blog/solar-seo/) covers this in depth.

## Follow up fast

A website lead is worth most in the first hour. Send an instant confirmation, route the enquiry to your CRM, and call or text the same day. The best website in the world can't rescue a lead that waits three days.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does a solar company website cost?
A lead-generation site with a calculator and quote flow typically costs $4,000 to $10,000, depending on pages and integrations.

### Do I need a calculator?
It isn't essential, but it's one of the strongest lead-capture tools available to solar installers.

### How long does it take to build?
Usually three to five weeks, including the calculator and CRM integration.

# Solar Lead Generation: 15 Ways to Get More Quote Requests
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-lead-generation/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Fifteen proven ways for solar installers to generate more qualified leads from their website, Google, reviews, referrals and content, without buying shared leads.

Key takeaways:
- Leads you generate yourself convert far better than bought, shared leads
- Your website, Google Business Profile and reviews form the foundation
- Calculators and incentive guides capture people still researching
- Speed of follow-up often matters more than lead volume

Buying leads from aggregators feels easy until you notice the same homeowner was sold to four other installers. Exclusive leads from your own marketing cost less over time and close at much higher rates, because the customer chose *you*.

Here are fifteen ways to generate them.

## Foundations

### 1. A website built to convert

Clear benefit, clear proof, clear next step. If your site doesn't have a quote button on every screen, start there. See how to build a solar company website (/blog/solar-company-website-guide/).

### 2. A savings calculator

Give visitors a personalised estimate and ask for contact details to send the full breakdown. More on calculators (/blog/solar-savings-calculator/).

### 3. A short, friendly quote form

Three to five fields. How to design it (/blog/solar-quote-form/).

### 4. Google Business Profile

Fill in everything, add project photos weekly and gather reviews. This is what puts you in the map results. See our optimisation checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/).

### 5. Reviews, constantly

Ask every customer on commissioning day. A steady flow of recent reviews lifts rankings and trust.

## Search

### 6. Local SEO

Service area pages, local keywords and schema markup. SEO for solar companies (/blog/solar-seo/) explains the plan.

### 7. Incentive and grant content

People search "solar grants [country]" and "is solar worth it in [region]" long before they request quotes. A clear, current guide captures them early. How to write it (/blog/solar-incentives-content/).

### 8. FAQ content

Answer the questions homeowners type into Google. 25 to start with (/blog/solar-faq-content/).

### 9. Google Ads on high-intent keywords

"Solar installers near me" and "solar panel quote [town]" are expensive but valuable. Send clicks to a focused landing page, not your homepage. Compare the trade-offs in SEO vs Google Ads (/blog/seo-vs-google-ads/).

## Proof and referrals

### 10. Case studies

Short write-ups with photos, system size, cost and savings. "A 6 kW system in Barrie saving $1,900 a year" is more convincing than any claim.

### 11. A referral programme

Happy customers have neighbours with identical roofs. Offer a thank-you for referrals and make it easy to share.

### 12. Yard signs and neighbour letters

Old-fashioned and effective. Add a QR code to a landing page for that street or town.

## Content and social

### 13. Project photos and video

Time-lapse installs, drone shots and customer interviews perform well on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube and reassure people that you do real work locally.

### 14. Email nurture

Most leads aren't ready immediately. A short series (how solar works, incentives, a case study, financing) keeps you front of mind.

### 15. Partnerships

Builders, roofers, electricians, EV dealers and estate agents all meet homeowners at decision points. Offer a simple referral arrangement.

## Don't waste the leads you get

Lead generation is only half the job.

- **Respond within minutes** during business hours
- **Call, then text, then email**
- **Follow up at least five times** over two weeks
- **Track every lead** in a CRM with its source

Installers who respond in five minutes win far more often than those who respond the next day.

## Measure what matters

| Metric | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Leads by source | Shows where to invest |
| Cost per lead | Keeps spending honest |
| Lead-to-survey rate | Reveals lead quality |
| Survey-to-sale rate | Reveals sales effectiveness |

## See it in practice

## Frequently asked questions

### Are bought solar leads worth it?
They can fill gaps, but shared leads are contacted by several installers and close at low rates. Building your own pipeline pays back better.

### How many leads does a website generate?
It depends on traffic and conversion rate. A well-built site typically converts 3 to 8% of visitors into enquiries.

### What's the fastest way to get more leads?
Fix your website's quote path and response time, then turn on tightly targeted Google Ads while SEO builds.

# SEO for Solar Companies: Rank in Every Town You Serve
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-seo/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A practical SEO guide for solar installers: local keywords, service area pages, Google Business Profile, content, schema and links that bring in quote requests.

Key takeaways:
- Solar searches are local, so build a strong page for each area you serve
- Service pages for residential, commercial, battery and EV each target different searches
- Incentive guides and FAQs capture homeowners early in their research
- Reviews and a complete Google Business Profile drive map visibility

When a homeowner searches "solar installers near me", three companies appear in the map and a handful below it. Those spots generate a steady stream of exclusive, high-intent leads for free. Getting there is a matter of doing a few things consistently.

## What solar customers search

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Installer + location | "solar installers Dublin", "solar company Barrie" |
| Product + location | "solar panels Auckland", "home battery San Bernardino" |
| Cost and value | "solar panel cost 2026", "is solar worth it in Ontario" |
| Incentives | "SEAI solar grant", "solar rebates [state]" |
| Comparison | "best solar panels", "Tesla Powerwall alternatives" |

Your site needs pages that match each type.

## 1. Service pages

Build a dedicated page for each service:

- Residential solar
- Commercial solar
- Agricultural solar
- Battery storage
- EV charger installation
- Maintenance and repairs

Each should cover who it's for, how it works, typical costs and savings, incentives, FAQs and a quote form.

## 2. Service area pages

Create a page for each town, city or county you serve, with unique, useful content: local projects, grid or council details, typical savings, reviews from that area. Avoid copy-and-paste. We explain how in service area pages for solar installers (/blog/solar-service-area-pages/).

## 3. On-page basics

- **Title tags:** "Solar Panel Installers in Cork | Eco Horizon"
- **One H1** with the service and location
- **Clear headings** and short paragraphs
- **Internal links** between services and areas

See title tags and meta descriptions (/blog/title-tags-meta-descriptions/).

## 4. Google Business Profile

- Primary category: "Solar energy company" or "Solar energy equipment supplier"
- Service areas listed
- Services with descriptions
- Weekly project photos
- Every review answered

Full checklist here (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/).

## 5. Reviews

Ask on commissioning day, when the customer has just seen the meter run backwards. Send a direct link by text.

## 6. Content that ranks

### Incentive guides

Keep one page per programme, updated whenever rules change. How to write them (/blog/solar-incentives-content/).

### Cost guides

"How much do solar panels cost in [region]?" with honest ranges and worked examples.

### FAQs

Each question is a potential search. Start with these 25 (/blog/solar-faq-content/).

### Case studies

Real installs with numbers and photos, tagged by location.

## 7. Schema markup

Add LocalBusiness, Service, FAQ and Review schema so Google and AI assistants understand exactly what you do and where. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/).

## 8. Speed and mobile

Many solar sites are weighed down by chat widgets, tracking scripts and uncompressed drone footage. Trim them. Aim for green Core Web Vitals on mobile. See Core Web Vitals explained (/blog/core-web-vitals-explained/).

## 9. Links

- Manufacturer "find an installer" directories
- Accreditation bodies
- Local chambers of commerce and business groups
- Local news stories about community or commercial projects
- Supplier and partner websites

## 10. Be visible in AI answers

Homeowners now ask ChatGPT and Google's AI Overviews "who are the best solar installers in [area]?" Clear facts on your site (areas served, certifications, years trading, review counts), consistent listings and FAQ content help you get mentioned. See how to get mentioned in AI search (/blog/ai-search-optimization/).

## A 90-day plan

| Weeks | Work |
| --- | --- |
| 1 to 2 | Technical audit, titles, Search Console, GBP clean-up |
| 3 to 6 | Service pages and top five area pages |
| 7 to 10 | Incentive guide, cost guide, FAQ page, schema |
| 11 to 13 | Case studies, review drive, link outreach |

## Frequently asked questions

### How long until SEO brings leads?
Map visibility and long-tail terms can improve in a few weeks; competitive city terms usually take four to nine months.

### Should I target "solar panels" nationally?
No. Local terms convert better and are far easier to win.

### Do I need a blog?
You need useful content. Guides, FAQs and case studies matter more than a traditional blog.

# Should Your Solar Website Have a Savings Calculator?
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-savings-calculator/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Why a solar savings calculator is one of the best lead-generation tools for installers, what it should include, and how to make its estimates trustworthy.

Key takeaways:
- A calculator turns a generic pitch into a personal number
- Ask for as little as possible: location and monthly bill are enough
- Show a useful estimate first, then offer a detailed quote in exchange for contact details
- Be transparent about assumptions so the numbers build trust

Every solar visitor arrives with the same question: *what would I save?* Most websites answer with "book a free consultation to find out". A calculator answers on the spot, and that changes the whole conversation.

## Why calculators work

- **Personal.** A number for their home beats a national average.
- **Instant.** No waiting for a callback.
- **Engaging.** Interacting with a tool keeps people on the page.
- **Qualifying.** You learn their bill, location and rough system size before you call.
- **Lead capture.** "Email me my full savings report" is an easy yes.

## What to ask

Keep the inputs minimal:

1. **Postcode or ZIP** (for sunlight hours and electricity rates)
2. **Average monthly electricity bill**

Optional refinements:

3. Roof direction or type
4. Whether they have or want an EV
5. Interest in a battery

Two inputs get the most completions. Offer the rest as "refine my estimate".

## What to show

- **Recommended system size** (kW and approximate panel count)
- **Estimated annual savings**
- **Estimated payback period**
- **Lifetime savings** over 25 years
- **CO₂ avoided,** translated into something relatable such as trees or car miles
- **Available incentives**

Show ranges rather than single figures. "$1,400 to $1,900 a year" is more believable than "$1,652".

## The lead capture moment

There are two approaches:

**Gate the result:** ask for contact details before showing anything. Captures more data but frustrates visitors.

**Show first, then offer more:** display the estimate, then offer a detailed report, a roof assessment or a firm quote in exchange for details. This builds goodwill and still converts strongly.

We recommend the second.

## Make the numbers trustworthy

- State assumptions: electricity price, export rate, panel output, degradation
- Link to your data sources
- Label results as estimates
- Don't inflate savings; a sales call that disappoints kills the deal
- Update rates and incentives regularly

## How it works under the hood

A basic calculator needs:

- Average solar irradiance by region
- Typical electricity tariffs
- System cost per kW
- Current incentive amounts

These can sit in a simple data table that your team updates. More advanced versions pull live data from mapping and solar APIs to assess the actual roof.

## Design tips

- Put it high on the homepage and on its own page
- Use sliders and large tap targets
- Animate the result so it feels rewarding
- Keep it fast; no heavy third-party widgets
- Follow the result with one clear button: "Get my exact quote"

## An example

Our Heliora solar template includes a ZIP-code savings and emissions estimator built into the hero, with a no-obligation quote flow straight after:

## Is it worth the build cost?

A custom calculator typically adds $1,000 to $3,000 to a website project. If it generates even a few extra qualified leads a month, it pays for itself with the first installation.

## Alternatives if you're not ready

- A simple "savings by bill size" table
- Worked examples for three typical homes
- A short quiz that ends in a quote request

## Frequently asked questions

### How accurate do the estimates need to be?
Accurate enough to be honest and consistent with what your surveyor will say. Ranges and clear assumptions protect you.

### Can the calculator feed my CRM?
Yes. Submissions can go straight to HubSpot, GoHighLevel, Pipedrive, a spreadsheet or your inbox.

### Should I use a third-party calculator widget?
They're quick to add but often slow, generic and branded by someone else. A custom calculator matches your site and keeps the lead data yours.

# Designing a Solar Quote Form That Converts
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-quote-form/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to design a solar quote request form that homeowners actually finish: which fields to ask, multi-step layouts, trust cues and what to do after submission.

Key takeaways:
- Start with three to five easy fields and ask the rest on step two
- Multi-step forms with a progress bar outperform one long page
- Reassure at the point of submission: no obligation, no spam, fast response
- Route every lead to your CRM and reply within minutes

A homeowner has read your page, likes what they see and clicks "Get a quote". Then they meet a 14-field form asking for their roof pitch and annual kilowatt-hours. Half of them leave.

Your quote form is the narrowest point of your funnel. Small improvements here are worth more than almost any other change on the site.

## The principle: easy first, detail later

Ask for the minimum needed to start a conversation, then gather detail once they've committed.

### Step 1: about the property

- Postcode or ZIP
- Property type: home, business, farm
- Average monthly electricity bill (a dropdown of ranges is easier than typing)

### Step 2: about what they want

- Interested in: solar, battery, EV charger (tick boxes)
- Roof type or a note that they're not sure
- Timeline: as soon as possible, within 3 months, just researching

### Step 3: contact details

- Name
- Phone
- Email
- Best time to call

By step three they've invested effort and are far more likely to finish.

## Why multi-step works

- Each screen looks short and achievable
- A progress bar creates momentum
- Easy questions first build commitment
- You can capture partial data from those who drop off

## What not to ask up front

- Annual usage in kWh (most people don't know)
- Roof pitch, orientation and dimensions (your survey will find out)
- A bill upload as a required field (offer it as optional)
- Full address before they trust you

## Trust cues beside the form

- "Free, no-obligation quote"
- "We'll never share your details"
- "Response within one business day"
- Accreditation logos
- A short review
- A photo of a real team member who'll call

## Button wording

"Submit" is a dead word. Use what the visitor gets:

- "Get my free quote"
- "See my savings"
- "Check my eligibility"

## Mobile matters most

Many solar enquiries start on a phone, often from a Facebook ad.

- Large tap targets and tick boxes
- Number keyboards for phone and postcode fields
- Autofill enabled
- No tiny dropdowns

## After they submit

1. **Thank-you page** confirming what happens next and when
2. **Instant email or SMS** with the same message and a link to a case study
3. **CRM entry** created automatically with source tracking
4. **A call within minutes** if in business hours

Offer a way to book a call slot directly on the thank-you page; it saves phone tag.

## Offer alternatives

Not everyone likes forms. Next to it, offer:

- Click-to-call
- WhatsApp or SMS
- A callback request with a single phone field

## Test and improve

Track how many people start the form versus finish it. If lots drop at a particular step, simplify that step. Small changes, such as removing one field or rewording a button, can lift completions noticeably.

General principles are in contact forms that convert (/blog/contact-form-best-practices/).

## Examples

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I ask for a phone number?
Yes for solar, because a conversation is needed. Make it clear why: "so we can confirm a few details about your roof".

### Should the form be on every page?
A button to it should be. Put the full form on a dedicated quote page and at the bottom of key pages.

### Can the form integrate with our CRM?
Yes. Most CRMs accept web form data directly or through tools like Zapier.

# Service Area Pages for Solar Installers (Without Thin Content)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-service-area-pages/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How solar companies can build location pages that rank in every town they serve, with a content template that avoids duplicate, thin pages.

Key takeaways:
- One strong page per priority area beats dozens of near-duplicates
- Each page needs genuinely local content: projects, reviews, conditions and incentives
- Link area pages to service pages and case studies
- Start with the five to ten areas that matter most

If you install solar across twenty towns but your website only mentions your head office, you're competing for one town's searches. Service area pages fix that, when they're done properly. Done lazily (the same paragraph with the town name swapped) they can drag your whole site down.

## Why they work

Google tries to show local results for searches like "solar installers Galway". A page that's clearly about solar in Galway, with evidence you actually work there, is a strong match.

## What makes a page "thin"

- Identical text across pages with only the place name changed
- No local detail
- No unique images
- No reason for a human to read it

Google's guidelines call these doorway pages. Avoid them.

## The template for a strong area page

### 1. Headline and intro

"Solar Panel Installation in [Town]" plus two or three sentences on your experience there.

### 2. Local proof

- Number of systems installed in the area
- Two or three local projects with photos, system size and savings
- Reviews from customers in that town

### 3. Local conditions

- Typical sunlight hours and expected generation
- Common roof types and housing stock
- Local electricity provider and export arrangements
- Planning or permit notes specific to the council or county

### 4. Incentives

National schemes plus anything regional. Link to your full incentives guide (/blog/solar-incentives-content/).

### 5. Services available

Short summaries linking to residential, commercial, battery and EV pages.

### 6. FAQs

Three or four questions specific to the area.

### 7. Call to action

A quote form with the town pre-filled.

Aim for 500 to 900 words that couldn't be pasted onto another town's page.

## How many pages?

Start with five to ten: your base and the largest towns or counties you serve. Add more as you complete projects there and have something real to say. Quality first.

## URL and linking structure

- `/areas/` index page listing every location
- `/areas/galway/` for each
- Link from each service page to the relevant area pages and back
- Link case studies to their area page

Clear structure helps both visitors and search engines. More in our internal linking guide (/blog/internal-linking-guide/).

## Titles and meta

- **Title:** "Solar Panel Installers in Galway | [Company]"
- **Meta description:** mention the area, a proof point and the quote offer

See title tags and meta descriptions (/blog/title-tags-meta-descriptions/).

## Schema

Add LocalBusiness schema with `areaServed` listing your locations, plus FAQ schema on each area page. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/).

## Keep them alive

Every time you complete an install in an area, add the photo and a line to that page. Fresh, real content keeps pages ranking and makes them more persuasive.

## Area pages and your Google Business Profile

Your profile's service areas should match the areas on your site. Consistency reinforces relevance. See the Google Business Profile checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/).

## Examples of regional positioning

These solar sites make their service region unmistakable:

For the broader approach, see how to create local landing pages that rank (/blog/local-landing-pages/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I create pages for towns where I haven't installed yet?
Yes, if you genuinely serve them and can write useful local content. Be honest about experience.

### Will many similar pages hurt my site?
Near-duplicates can. Unique, useful pages won't.

### Do I need a physical office in each area?
No. Service area pages are designed for businesses that travel to customers.
