# Trust Signals Every Solar Website Needs
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-website-trust-signals/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

The trust signals that reassure solar buyers, from accreditations and warranties to reviews and real project photos, and where to place them on your website.

Key takeaways:
- Solar is a high-cost, long-term purchase, so buyers look hard for reasons to trust you
- Accreditations, warranties and years in business belong near the top of the page
- Real photos and local reviews beat stock imagery and generic claims
- Transparency about price, process and aftercare is itself a trust signal

A solar system costs thousands and lasts 25 years. Buyers have heard stories about cowboy installers and companies that vanished before the warranty did. Before they'll hand over their details, they need evidence you're not one of them.

Here are the signals that matter, in rough order of impact.

## 1. Accreditations and certifications

Display the logos of the bodies that matter in your market: SEAI registration in Ireland, NABCEP in the US, CEC or SEANZ in Australasia, MCS in the UK, plus electrical licences. Link each to your listing where possible so visitors can verify.

## 2. Reviews, with numbers

"Rated 5/5 from 67 reviews" near the top of the page is powerful. Show the platform (Google, Trustpilot), the count and a few full reviews with names and locations.

## 3. Years in business and installs completed

"Solar PV specialists since 2015" and "1,200+ systems installed" answer the question "will you still be here?"

## 4. Warranties, spelled out

- Panel product and performance warranty
- Inverter warranty
- Battery warranty
- Your own workmanship warranty

Put the years in a simple table. Vague "industry-leading warranties" reassures nobody.

## 5. Manufacturer partnerships

Certified installer status with recognised brands shows you're trained and supported.

## 6. Real photos

Your team, your vans, your installs. Drone shots of finished roofs in recognisable local settings are ideal. Stock photos of smiling families signal the opposite of what you intend.

## 7. Case studies with real numbers

System size, cost, annual savings, payback, and a quote from the customer. Include commercial and farm projects if you do them.

## 8. A visible, local presence

Full address, local phone number, service area map, company registration number. A site with only a contact form looks like a lead broker.

## 9. A clear process

Show the steps from enquiry to switch-on with typical timings. Uncertainty feels like risk.

## 10. Transparent pricing guidance

You may not publish exact prices, but typical ranges for common system sizes show you have nothing to hide.

## 11. Aftercare and monitoring

Explain what happens after installation: monitoring apps, servicing, who to call. It shows you plan to stick around.

## 12. Finance and grant support

"We handle the grant application for you" removes a major worry and positions you as the expert.

## 13. Insurance and safety

Public liability cover and safety certifications matter especially to commercial clients.

## 14. Awards and press

Industry awards or local news coverage add third-party validation.

## 15. A professional website

The site itself is a trust signal. Fast, modern, error-free and secure (HTTPS) says "this company pays attention". Slow and dated says the opposite. More general principles in 20 website trust signals (/blog/website-trust-signals/).

## Where to place them

| Location | Signals |
| --- | --- |
| Hero / top strip | Review rating, years, installs, key accreditation |
| Mid-page | Warranties, process, case studies |
| Near forms | "No obligation", privacy note, a review |
| Footer | Full address, registrations, all logos |

Repeat the strongest ones. Nobody reads every section.

## Examples

Eco Horizon puts its founding year, grant handling and review rating up front. SunFlow leads with being 100% Canadian and its incentive expertise.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do badges really make a difference?
Yes, when they're recognised and verifiable. A row of obscure logos helps less than one that buyers know.

### What if we're a new company?
Lean on your team's individual experience, manufacturer training, strong warranties and your first customer reviews.

### Should we show prices?
Typical ranges build trust and filter enquiries. Exact quotes follow a survey.

---

# How to Explain Solar Incentives and Grants on Your Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-incentives-content/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How solar installers should present grants, rebates and tax credits on their website: structure, wording, accuracy and how to keep the page up to date.

Key takeaways:
- Incentives are one of the most searched solar topics, so a clear guide attracts early-stage buyers
- Explain each scheme with who qualifies, how much and how to claim
- Show a worked example so the saving feels real
- Date the page and review it every quarter because rules change

"Are there grants for solar?" is often the first thing a homeowner searches. Incentives can cut the cost of a system dramatically, and they're confusing: different schemes, eligibility rules and deadlines. The installer who explains them clearly earns trust and the enquiry.

## Why you need a dedicated page

- It ranks for high-volume searches like "[country] solar grant"
- It answers the biggest objection (cost) with good news
- It positions you as the helpful expert
- It gives sales teams a link to send

## Structure of a strong incentives page

### 1. A plain-English summary

Start with the headline: "Homeowners in [region] can currently claim up to [amount] towards solar panels." One or two sentences, updated whenever it changes.

### 2. A table of current schemes

| Scheme | Who it's for | Value | How it's paid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| National grant | Homeowners | Up to X | After installation |
| Farm scheme | Farmers | X% of cost | Grant aid |
| Business allowance | Companies | Tax relief | Through accounts |

### 3. A section for each scheme

- What it is
- Who qualifies
- How much you can get
- How and when to apply
- Deadlines or planned changes
- A link to the official source

### 4. A worked example

> A typical 4 kW system costs €8,000. With the grant of €1,800, the homeowner pays €6,200. With annual savings of around €1,000, payback is roughly six years.

Use your own realistic local figures. Worked examples make abstract percentages concrete.

### 5. How you help

"We complete the application for you and include the grant in your quote." This is a genuine selling point.

### 6. FAQs

- Can I combine schemes?
- Do I need to apply before installation?
- What happens if the scheme changes after I sign?
- Are batteries covered?

### 7. Call to action

"Find out what you qualify for" with a short form.

## Accuracy is everything

Incentives change, sometimes sharply. Out-of-date information damages trust and can create legal problems.

- **Link to official sources** for every scheme
- **Show a "last updated" date**
- **Review the page quarterly** and after every budget or policy announcement
- **Avoid guarantees.** Say "currently" and "subject to eligibility"
- **Don't give tax advice.** Suggest customers confirm with an adviser

## Segment by audience

Homeowners, businesses and farmers often have different schemes. Give each its own section or page so nobody wades through irrelevant detail. Eco Horizon, for instance, addresses homes, businesses and farms separately with the relevant grants for each.

## Use incentives across the site

- A banner or strip on the homepage: "Grants of up to X available"
- A line in the calculator results
- A mention on each service page
- In area pages, where regional schemes apply

## Urgency, honestly

If a scheme is reducing or ending on a known date, say so. Real deadlines motivate action. Never invent urgency; customers check.

## SEO tips

- Target "[scheme name]" and "[region] solar grant" in the title and headings
- Add FAQ schema (guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))
- Keep the same URL year after year and update the content, so the page builds authority
- Link to it from related articles and service pages

## Frequently asked questions

### How often do solar incentives change?
It varies by country, but reviewing your page every quarter is a sensible minimum.

### Should I include incentives in my quotes?
Show the price before and after incentives so customers see both the full cost and their net cost.

### What if incentives end?
Update the page immediately and shift the message to long-term savings and energy independence.

---

# Selling Batteries and EV Chargers on Your Solar Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/battery-ev-charger-pages/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How solar installers can present battery storage and EV charger installation on their website to increase average order value and win standalone enquiries.

Key takeaways:
- Batteries and EV chargers deserve their own pages, not a bullet point on the solar page
- Explain benefits in everyday terms: backup power, using your own energy at night, charging from the sun
- Address cost and payback honestly
- Past solar customers are your warmest audience for both

For many installers, batteries and EV chargers have moved from optional extras to a major share of revenue. Yet on most solar websites they're a line in a list. Giving each a proper page captures searches you're currently missing and lifts the value of every solar quote.

## Why separate pages

- People search for them directly: "home battery installation [town]", "EV charger installer near me"
- Each has its own questions and objections
- Existing solar owners want to add them later
- EV owners may not have solar yet and are a new audience

## The battery storage page

### Lead with the benefit

- "Use your solar power after dark"
- "Keep the lights on in a power cut"
- "Cut your reliance on the grid"

### Explain how it works, simply

A short diagram: panels charge the battery by day; the battery powers the home in the evening; the grid tops up only when needed.

### Who it's for

- Homes out during the day
- Areas with frequent outages
- Customers on time-of-use tariffs
- Anyone wanting more energy independence

### Options and sizing

Brands you install, typical capacities and what each can run. A simple table helps.

### Cost and payback

Be honest. Batteries often have a longer payback than panels. Give typical ranges and explain non-financial benefits such as backup power.

### Retrofit

Make it clear you can add a battery to an existing system, including ones you didn't install.

### FAQs

Lifespan, warranty, safety, where it's installed, whether it works in a power cut.

## The EV charger page

### Lead with convenience and savings

- "Charge at home for a fraction of public charging costs"
- "Charge your car from your roof"

### Cover the basics

- Charger types and speeds
- Smart charging and solar-aware charging
- Tethered vs untethered
- Typical install time and what's involved

### Grants and requirements

Any available home or workplace charger grants, and electrical requirements such as fuse board upgrades.

### Who you serve

Homes, workplaces, apartment blocks, fleets. Commercial charging can be its own page.

### FAQs

Do I need planning permission? Can I install without solar? Which cars are compatible?

## Bundle them

Offer clear packages: solar only, solar plus battery, solar plus battery plus EV charger. Show the combined benefit. Customers often choose the fuller package when it's presented as a complete system.

## Cross-link everywhere

- From the solar page: "Add a battery" and "Add an EV charger"
- From the calculator results: "With a battery you'd use X% more of your own power"
- From case studies featuring combined systems

Good internal linking helps SEO too; see our internal linking guide (/blog/internal-linking-guide/).

## Market to your past customers

Your existing solar customers already trust you. Email them when:

- Battery prices fall or new grants appear
- You start installing a new battery brand
- They've had their system long enough to see how much they export

A dedicated landing page for "add a battery to your existing solar" gives those emails somewhere to send people.

## SEO essentials

- Titles like "Home Battery Storage Installation in [Region]" and "EV Charger Installers [Town]"
- FAQ and Service schema
- Area mentions and links to your service area pages (/blog/solar-service-area-pages/)
- Real installation photos with descriptive alt text

## See it done

Lithium Solar Energy and Eco Horizon both present solar, battery and EV charging as distinct services within one coherent offer.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should batteries be mentioned in every solar quote?
Yes, as an option with its own price and benefit, so the customer can choose.

### Is there enough search demand for separate pages?
Yes. Battery and EV charger searches have grown quickly and competition is often lower than for solar itself.

### What if we only install one brand?
Explain why you chose it. A confident recommendation is more reassuring than a long list.

---

# Commercial and Agricultural Solar: Website Content That Wins B2B Deals
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/commercial-solar-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to present commercial and agricultural solar on your website: what business and farm buyers look for, the content they need and how to capture enquiries.

Key takeaways:
- Business buyers care about ROI, payback, tax treatment and disruption
- Case studies with real figures are the most persuasive content
- Farms have distinct needs and often distinct grants
- Offer a feasibility assessment rather than a generic quote

Selling solar to a business or a farm is a different sale from selling to a homeowner. There are more decision-makers, bigger numbers and a longer timeline. The website content that wins residential leads (lifestyle images, monthly bill savings) won't convince a finance director or a dairy farmer.

## What commercial buyers want to know

1. **What's the return?** Payback period, IRR, lifetime savings
2. **How is it financed?** Capital purchase, lease, power purchase agreement
3. **What's the tax position?** Allowances and depreciation
4. **Will it disrupt operations?**
5. **Who else have you done this for?**
6. **What happens after installation?** Monitoring, maintenance, performance guarantees

Your commercial page should answer all six.

## Structure of a commercial solar page

### Headline

Lead with the business outcome: "Cut your energy costs by up to 40% and fix your price for 25 years."

### Proof strip

Total kW or MW installed, number of commercial clients, sectors served, accreditations.

### Who it's for

Manufacturing, warehousing, retail, hospitality, offices, schools. Short sections or tabs for each, with relevant examples.

### The financial case

- Typical system sizes and costs per kW
- Example payback calculations
- Financing options explained
- Tax allowances and grants (with advice to confirm with their accountant)

### Process

Feasibility study, design, grid application, installation, commissioning, monitoring, with realistic timelines.

### Case studies

The centrepiece. For each:

- Client and sector
- Challenge
- System size
- Annual generation and savings
- Payback
- A quote from the decision-maker
- Photos

### Call to action

"Request a free feasibility assessment". Business buyers respond to a tangible deliverable more than "get a quote".

## Agricultural solar

Farms combine high daytime energy use, large roofs and, in many regions, dedicated grants. Give agriculture its own page.

### Speak the language

Milking parlours, grain drying, cold storage, poultry sheds. Show you understand how farms use energy.

### Cover the grant in detail

Where farm-specific schemes exist (such as TAMS in Ireland), explain eligibility, rates and the application process, and offer to handle it.

### Show farm projects

Photos of panels on sheds, with herd size or operation type, system size and savings.

### Address practical concerns

Roof condition, asbestos sheeting, livestock safety, three-phase supply, export limits.

## Lead capture for B2B

Ask slightly different questions from the residential form:

- Company name and sector
- Site location
- Approximate annual electricity spend
- Roof or land availability
- Decision timeline
- Contact name and role

Offer to review energy bills confidentially. Make it easy to upload them.

## Content that supports the sale

- **A downloadable guide:** "The business case for commercial solar"
- **An ROI calculator** for commercial systems
- **Sector pages** for your strongest industries
- **Articles** on financing, tax treatment and grid connection

Business buyers forward links to colleagues. Give them something worth forwarding.

## Utility-scale and land

If you develop solar farms or work with landowners, that's a third audience with its own page: land requirements, lease terms, the development process. Watthaus Strategy, for example, speaks separately to homeowners and to utility-scale and land projects.

## SEO for commercial solar

Target "commercial solar installers [region]", "solar for farms [country]" and sector terms like "solar for warehouses". Volume is lower than residential, but each lead is worth far more. See SEO for solar companies (/blog/solar-seo/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Should commercial and residential be on the same website?
Usually yes, with clearly separate sections so each audience sees relevant content.

### How long is the commercial sales cycle?
Often three to twelve months. Nurture with case studies and follow-up, not pressure.

### Do case studies need exact figures?
Real numbers are far more persuasive. If a client prefers privacy, use ranges and anonymise the name.

# Solar Website Examples from Four Countries (and What They Do Well)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-website-examples/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

Five solar company websites from Ireland, Canada, the USA and New Zealand, with a breakdown of the design and lead-generation ideas worth borrowing.

Key takeaways:
- Strong solar sites lead with a clear benefit and an immediate quote path
- Local identity and grant expertise are powerful differentiators
- Calculators and incentive messaging do much of the selling
- Each example adapts the same principles to its own market

Solar websites often look interchangeable: a blue sky, a roof, "Go solar today". These five, all designed and built by Code Bunny, show how a clear message and a distinct identity make an installer memorable. For each, we've highlighted the idea most worth borrowing.

## 1. Eco Horizon — Ireland

Solar PV, batteries and EV charging for Irish homes, businesses and farms. The headline, "Powering Ireland's solar future", is confident and national. Grants (SEAI and TAMS 3) are woven through the site, and a 5/5 rating from dozens of reviews sits near the top.

**Borrow this:** make grant handling part of your core promise.

## 2. SunFlow Solar & Exteriors — Barrie, Ontario

Solar, roofing and luxury exteriors under one brand. "Power from the roof up" ties the services together, and "100% Canadian" is a clear trust signal.

**Borrow this:** if you offer related services, unite them under one idea.

## 3. Lithium Solar Energy — Southern California

Solar, battery backup, panel upgrades and EV charging from a Yucaipa team with 17+ years in power. The "Go solar. Save big." hero is direct, and the end-to-end promise (designed, permitted, installed, monitored) reassures.

**Borrow this:** spell out that one team handles everything.

## 4. Watthaus Strategy — Auckland, New Zealand

Bridging real estate and renewable energy: rooftop solar for homes and land-to-construction for utility-scale farms. Two audiences, each given its own clear path.

**Borrow this:** split your homepage by audience when you serve very different buyers.

## 5. Heliora — a ready-made solar template

A premium lead-generation design with a ZIP-code savings and emissions calculator built into the hero and a no-obligation quote flow. It's one of the ready-made sites we sell (/templates/).

**Borrow this:** put the calculator at the top, where curiosity is highest.

## What they share

1. **A benefit-led headline** in a handful of words
2. **A quote button** visible at all times
3. **Proof up top:** years, reviews, accreditations
4. **Incentives explained**
5. **Separate paths** for homes, businesses and farms
6. **Real photography** and local identity
7. **Fast mobile performance**

## How to use these examples

Decide which approach fits your market. Is your edge local roots, grant expertise, premium products or breadth of services? Lead with that. Then make sure the essentials from how to build a solar company website (/blog/solar-company-website-guide/) are covered.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I buy the Heliora template?
Yes. Each ready-made site sells to one buyer only. See the templates page (/templates/).

### Can you build a custom solar site for my company?
Yes. Start with a free preview (/free-website-preview/) of your homepage.

### What makes a solar site convert?
A clear benefit, strong proof, a personal savings estimate and a short quote form, followed by a fast response.

# 25 Solar FAQs Your Website Should Answer
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/solar-faq-content/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

The 25 questions homeowners ask before buying solar, grouped by topic, with guidance on answering them to build trust, rank on Google and appear in AI answers.

Key takeaways:
- Every FAQ is a search query and an objection you can remove
- Answer in two to four plain sentences, then link to detail
- Group questions by topic so visitors find theirs quickly
- FAQ schema helps answers appear in search results and AI summaries

Before they request a quote, homeowners have questions, usually the same ones. If your website answers them clearly, you build trust, shorten sales calls and pick up search traffic for each question. If it doesn't, they'll find the answers on a competitor's site.

Here are the 25 to cover, grouped by theme.

## Cost and savings

1. **How much do solar panels cost?** Give typical ranges for common system sizes in your area.
2. **How much will I save?** Explain what affects savings and link to your calculator.
3. **How long is the payback period?** A typical range with a worked example.
4. **Are there grants or incentives?** Summarise and link to your incentives page (/blog/solar-incentives-content/).
5. **Is finance available?** Outline the options.
6. **Will solar increase my home's value?** Share what's known honestly.

## Suitability

7. **Is my roof suitable?** Orientation, pitch, shading and condition.
8. **Does solar work in cloudy weather or winter?** Yes, at reduced output; explain.
9. **How many panels do I need?** Based on usage and roof space.
10. **Do I need planning permission?** State local rules and exceptions.
11. **Can I install solar on a flat roof or the ground?** Explain options.

## How it works

12. **How do solar panels work?** Two or three sentences and a diagram.
13. **What happens to electricity I don't use?** Export payments or net metering in your region.
14. **Will solar power my home in a power cut?** Only with a battery and the right inverter; be clear.
15. **Do I need a battery?** Pros, cons and who benefits most.
16. **Can I charge an electric car with solar?** Yes; link to your EV charger page (/blog/battery-ev-charger-pages/).

## Installation

17. **How long does installation take?** Typical days on site and overall timeline.
18. **What's involved in the process?** Survey, design, install, commissioning.
19. **Will there be disruption?** Scaffolding, brief power-down, access needed.
20. **Who handles the paperwork?** Grid applications, grants, certificates.

## After installation

21. **How long do panels last?** Typical lifespan and degradation.
22. **What warranties do I get?** Product, performance and workmanship.
23. **Do panels need maintenance or cleaning?** Minimal; explain.
24. **How do I monitor my system?** App and what it shows.
25. **What if something goes wrong?** Your aftercare and response times.

## How to write good answers

- **Answer first.** Put the direct answer in the first sentence.
- **Keep it short.** Two to four sentences, then link to a detailed page.
- **Use local specifics.** Your region's rules, rates and schemes.
- **Be honest.** Admit limitations; it builds credibility.
- **Update regularly.** Especially costs and incentives.

## Where FAQs should live

- A dedicated FAQ page, grouped by topic
- The most relevant three to five on each service page
- A few on the homepage
- In area pages, for local questions

## Mark them up with schema

FAQ schema tells search engines exactly which text is the question and which is the answer. That helps your content appear in rich results and makes it easier for AI assistants to quote you. See our schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/) and how to get mentioned in AI search (/blog/ai-search-optimization/).

## Turn the big ones into articles

Questions like "how much do solar panels cost in [region]?" and "is solar worth it?" deserve full guides of their own. Link to them from the short FAQ answer. This is the backbone of SEO for solar companies (/blog/solar-seo/).

## Use them in sales

Send links to relevant answers after a call. It reinforces what you said and shows you're thorough.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many FAQs should a solar site have?
Start with these 25. Add more as your sales team hears new questions.

### Should answers include prices?
Typical ranges, yes. They're among the most searched questions and avoiding them pushes visitors elsewhere.

### Do FAQs help with SEO?
Yes. Each is a chance to match a specific search, and structured answers are favoured by both search engines and AI tools.

# Local SEO for Small Businesses: The Complete 2026 Guide
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/local-seo-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A complete local SEO guide for small businesses: Google Business Profile, reviews, on-page signals, citations, local content and how to appear in map results.

Key takeaways:
- Local rankings depend on relevance, distance and prominence
- Your Google Business Profile and reviews drive the map results
- Your website needs clear service and location pages with consistent contact details
- Steady, small actions every month beat one big push

When someone nearby searches for what you do, Google shows a map with three businesses, then a list of websites. Local SEO is the work of getting into both. For most small businesses it's the highest-return marketing there is: the people searching are close, ready and looking for exactly what you sell.

## How Google decides local rankings

Google has said local results depend mainly on three things:

- **Relevance:** how well your business matches the search
- **Distance:** how close you are to the searcher or the place named
- **Prominence:** how well known and trusted you are, online and off

You can't move your premises, but you can improve relevance and prominence a great deal.

## 1. Google Business Profile

This is the foundation. A complete, active profile is the biggest single factor for map visibility.

- Claim and verify it
- Choose the most specific primary category
- Fill in every field: hours, services, description, attributes
- Add photos every week or two
- Post updates monthly
- Answer questions

Step-by-step in our Google Business Profile optimisation checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/).

## 2. Reviews

Reviews influence rankings and whether people choose you once they see you.

- Ask every happy customer, at the moment they're happiest
- Send a direct link by text or email
- Reply to every review within a few days
- Aim for a steady flow; recency matters

## 3. Your website

Google reads your site to understand what you do and where.

### Essentials

- **Name, address and phone (NAP)** in the footer of every page, identical to your profile
- **Location in title tags and headings:** "Emergency Plumber in Leeds"
- **A page for each service**
- **A page for each key area you serve** (how to build them (/blog/local-landing-pages/))
- **An embedded map** on the contact page
- **Local business schema** (schema guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))
- **Fast, mobile-friendly pages** (Core Web Vitals (/blog/core-web-vitals-explained/))

### Content

Write for local customers: local projects, area guides, answers to questions people in your town ask.

## 4. Citations

Citations are listings of your business details on other sites: Yelp, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Facebook, industry directories, local chambers. They matter less than they once did, but consistency still counts.

- Make sure your NAP is identical everywhere
- Claim the major platforms
- Fix old addresses or phone numbers

## 5. Local links

Links from other local websites are a strong prominence signal.

- Sponsor a local team or event
- Join the chamber of commerce
- Partner with complementary businesses
- Get featured in local news
- Supply a testimonial to a local supplier

## 6. Behaviour signals

Google notices when people click your listing, ask for directions and call. Good photos, a strong rating and accurate hours all increase those actions.

## 7. Apple, Bing and AI

Local search isn't only Google.

- **Apple Business Connect** powers Apple Maps and Siri
- **Bing Places** powers Bing and Copilot, and feeds some AI assistants
- **AI search** (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews) draws on your website, listings and reviews

Clear facts and consistent details across all of them help. See how to get mentioned in AI search (/blog/ai-search-optimization/).

## A monthly local SEO routine (about an hour)

| Task | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Add 3 to 5 new photos to your profile | 10 min |
| Publish one Google post | 10 min |
| Reply to all new reviews | 10 min |
| Ask recent customers for reviews | 10 min |
| Check Search Console for issues | 10 min |
| Update one page or add one piece of local content | 10+ min |

## Common mistakes

- Keyword stuffing your business name
- Different phone numbers on different sites
- One generic "services" page
- Ignoring negative reviews
- Dozens of thin, duplicate location pages
- A slow, outdated website

## How long does it take?

Profile improvements can show within weeks. Building a lead over established competitors usually takes three to six months of consistent effort. See how long does SEO take? (/blog/how-long-does-seo-take/)

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a physical address to rank locally?
No. Service-area businesses can hide their address and list the areas they cover.

### How many reviews do I need?
Enough to beat the competitors shown beside you, with new ones arriving regularly.

### Is local SEO different from regular SEO?
It's a branch of it. The same fundamentals apply, with extra weight on your business profile, reviews and location signals.

---

# Google Business Profile Optimization Checklist (2026)
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

A step-by-step checklist to optimise your Google Business Profile: categories, description, services, photos, reviews, posts and the mistakes to avoid.

Key takeaways:
- Complete every field; incomplete profiles are outranked by complete ones
- The primary category is the most important single choice
- Fresh photos, posts and review replies signal an active business
- Never stuff keywords into your business name

Your Google Business Profile is often the first thing a customer sees: before your website, before your shopfront. It's free, it takes an hour to do well, and most of your competitors have done it badly. Work through this checklist and you'll be ahead of most of them.

## Setup

- [ ] **Claim or create** your profile at google.com/business
- [ ] **Verify** it (video, phone or postcard)
- [ ] **Add a second owner** so you're never locked out

## Core information

- [ ] **Business name:** exactly as on your signage. No added keywords or locations.
- [ ] **Primary category:** the most specific match ("Hair salon", not "Beauty")
- [ ] **Secondary categories:** up to nine, only if they truly apply
- [ ] **Address or service area:** hide your address if customers don't visit
- [ ] **Phone number:** a local number that's answered
- [ ] **Website:** your homepage, or the most relevant page for that location
- [ ] **Hours:** including holidays and special hours
- [ ] **Appointment or booking link**

## Description

- [ ] 750 characters; put the essentials in the first 250
- [ ] What you do, who for and where
- [ ] What makes you different
- [ ] Natural language; no keyword lists

## Services and products

- [ ] Every service listed with a short description
- [ ] Prices or "from" prices where possible
- [ ] Products with photos if you sell them
- [ ] Menu link for restaurants

## Attributes

- [ ] Accessibility, payment options, ownership attributes, amenities
- [ ] Anything customers filter by: "wheelchair accessible", "online appointments"

## Photos and video

- [ ] Logo and cover photo
- [ ] Exterior shots so people can find you
- [ ] Interior shots
- [ ] Team photos
- [ ] Work examples: before and afters, finished jobs, dishes
- [ ] Short videos
- [ ] **New photos added at least monthly**

Businesses with plenty of recent, real photos get more clicks, calls and direction requests.

## Reviews

- [ ] Create your short review link
- [ ] Ask every satisfied customer
- [ ] Reply to every review, good or bad
- [ ] Never offer rewards for reviews
- [ ] Report fake reviews through the profile

## Posts

- [ ] One post every week or two: offers, news, events, new work
- [ ] A photo and a call-to-action button on each

## Questions and answers

- [ ] Add your own common questions and answer them
- [ ] Monitor for new questions

## Messaging

- [ ] Turn on only if you can reply quickly
- [ ] Set a welcome message

## Connect it to your website

- [ ] Name, address and phone on your site match the profile exactly
- [ ] Local business schema on your site (how (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))
- [ ] Embed the Google map on your contact page
- [ ] Link to your profile from your site and ask for reviews there

## Track performance

- [ ] Check the Performance tab monthly: searches, views, calls, direction requests
- [ ] Add tracking parameters to your website link so visits show in analytics

## What to avoid

| Mistake | Why it hurts |
| --- | --- |
| Keywords in business name | Risk of suspension |
| Virtual office addresses | Against guidelines |
| Duplicate profiles | Splits reviews and confuses Google |
| Ignoring bad reviews | Looks careless to customers |
| Wrong hours | Frustrated customers, poor reviews |

## Keep it alive

A profile isn't a set-and-forget job. Ten minutes a week keeps it fresh. For the wider picture, see our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to see results?
Changes can show within days, but meaningful ranking gains usually take a few weeks of consistent activity.

### Can I list more than one location?
Yes, one profile per genuine, staffed location.

### What should I do if my profile is suspended?
Review Google's guidelines, fix any violations (often the business name or address) and submit a reinstatement request with evidence.

---

# How to Create Local Landing Pages That Rank
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/local-landing-pages/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build location and service-area landing pages that rank on Google without duplicate content, with a template and examples for small businesses.

Key takeaways:
- Each page must offer something unique and useful about that location
- Combine service and location in the title, heading and opening paragraph
- Local proof, such as projects, reviews and photos, is what separates ranking pages from doorway pages
- Start small with your most valuable areas

If you serve more than one town, a single homepage can't rank everywhere. Local landing pages give each area its own page to match searches like "roof repair Peoria" or "life coach Vancouver". The catch: Google has seen millions of lazy versions and filters them out. Yours need to be genuinely useful.

## When you need them

- You serve multiple towns, cities or neighbourhoods
- You have more than one location
- You want to rank beyond your immediate address

## The anatomy of a page that ranks

### Title tag and H1

"[Service] in [Location]" plus your brand.

- Title: "Mortgage Broker in Basingstoke | MDJ Mortgages"
- H1: "Mortgage advice Basingstoke trusts"

### Opening paragraph

Confirm the service and the place in the first two sentences, naturally.

### Local proof

This is what makes the page unique:

- Projects or clients in that area
- Reviews from local customers
- Photos taken there
- How long you've served the area

### Local detail

- Neighbourhoods or postcodes covered
- Landmarks and travel information
- Regulations, conditions or needs specific to the area
- Local pricing notes, if they vary

### Services available there

Summaries with links to full service pages.

### FAQs

Questions real customers in that area ask.

### Contact and map

Address or service area, phone, hours, an embedded map and a form.

### A clear call to action

"Book a free consultation in Basingstoke."

## How long should they be?

Typically 500 to 1,000 words. Length isn't the goal; uniqueness is. If you can swap the town name and the page still makes sense, it isn't local enough.

## Avoiding duplicate content

- Write each page from scratch around its local proof
- Use different photos, reviews and examples
- Vary structure where it makes sense
- Don't publish a page until you have something specific to say

## Site structure

- An index page: `/areas/` or `/locations/`
- One page per place: `/areas/basingstoke/`
- Links from the homepage footer and relevant service pages
- Links between nearby areas

See our internal linking guide (/blog/internal-linking-guide/).

## Schema

Use LocalBusiness schema with the correct address or `areaServed`, and FAQ schema for the questions. Details in the schema markup guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/).

## Service + location combinations

Larger businesses sometimes build pages for every service in every location. That multiplies quickly (10 services × 20 towns = 200 pages) and is hard to keep unique. Start with:

1. A page for each service
2. A page for each priority area
3. Combination pages only for your most valuable pairs

## Multi-location businesses

If you have several physical branches, each needs:

- Its own page with unique content, team and photos
- Its own Google Business Profile linking to that page
- Its own reviews

## Measure

In Search Console, filter by page to see which searches each landing page appears for. Improve pages that rank on page two; they're closest to paying off. See our Search Console guide (/blog/google-search-console-guide/).

## Examples of clear local positioning

## Frequently asked questions

### How many location pages should I create?
Start with five to ten for the areas that matter most. Add more as you gather local proof.

### Can I rank in a town where I have no office?
Yes, with a strong page and real evidence you serve it. Map results are harder without a nearby address; organic results are achievable.

### Should each page have its own phone number?
Only if calls are genuinely answered locally. Otherwise use your main number consistently.

# Salon & Spa Website Guide: Booking, Pricing and Local SEO
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/salon-website-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build a salon or spa website that fills your appointment book: online booking, service menus, galleries, team pages and local search visibility.

Key takeaways:
- Online booking is the most important feature; put it one tap away
- A clear service menu with prices reduces calls and no-shows
- Photos of real work and your space sell better than stock images
- A Google Business Profile with reviews brings in new local clients

For a salon or spa, a website has a simple job: get people booked. Clients decide fast, usually on their phone, often late in the evening when you're closed. If booking takes more than a couple of taps, they'll book somewhere else.

## Online booking first

- **A "Book now" button** in the header on every page, sticky on mobile
- **Real-time availability** through your booking system (Fresha, Booksy, Vagaro, Square, Timely, GlossGenius)
- **Embedded or seamlessly linked**, so it feels part of your site
- **Deposits or card capture** to reduce no-shows
- **Automatic reminders** by SMS and email

More in online booking for small businesses (/blog/online-booking-for-small-business/).

## A clear service menu

Clients want to know what you offer and what it costs.

- Group by category: cuts, colour, treatments, nails, massage, facials
- Show prices or "from" prices
- Add durations
- Describe treatments in a sentence, especially spa services
- Link each to booking

Hiding prices leads to phone calls and lost bookings.

## Show the work

- **A gallery** of real results: colour transformations, styles, nails, before and afters
- **Your space:** people choose a salon partly on atmosphere
- **Instagram feed,** used sparingly so it doesn't slow the page

Compress images properly; see image SEO (/blog/image-seo/).

## Introduce the team

A photo, name, specialities and a booking link for each stylist or therapist. Clients often choose a person, not just a salon.

## Homepage essentials

1. A striking image or short video of the salon or your work
2. A headline that captures your vibe: "Sharp cuts. Sharper confidence."
3. Book button
4. Services overview
5. Reviews
6. Location, hours and a map
7. Gift cards or offers

## Extra pages worth having

- **Bridal and events**
- **Gift cards** with online purchase
- **Products** you retail
- **Policies:** cancellation, lateness, patch tests
- **Careers** if you're hiring
- **New client offer**

## Local SEO for salons

Most new clients search "hair salon near me" or "[treatment] [town]".

- Complete your Google Business Profile and add your booking link (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Ask every happy client for a review
- Put your suburb or town in page titles
- Create pages for your key services: "Balayage in [Town]", "Bridal hair [Town]"

Full strategy in our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Design notes

- **Mood matters.** Luxury spa, edgy barbershop and friendly family salon need different palettes and type.
- **Mobile first.** Most bookings happen on phones.
- **Fast.** Heavy sliders and auto-playing video slow sites down.
- **Accessible.** Good contrast and readable text sizes.

## Bilingual and multi-location salons

If you serve more than one language community, offer both. If you have several branches, give each its own page with address, hours, team and booking.

## Buying a ready-made salon site

If you'd like to launch quickly, a professionally designed site you can rebrand is an option. We sell a small number, including salon, barbershop and beauty designs, on our templates page (/templates/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Which booking system should I use?
Choose one that suits your size and budget and integrates cleanly with your website. Fresha, Booksy, Square and Vagaro are common choices.

### Should I list prices?
Yes. "From" prices are fine where services vary.

### Do I need a website if I have Instagram and a booking app?
A website gives you a home that you control, ranks on Google, and brings everything (services, team, booking, reviews) together.

# Dental Practice Website Design: What New Patients Look For
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/dental-website-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What makes a dental website win new patients: reassuring design, clear treatments and fees, online booking, team profiles, reviews and local SEO.

Key takeaways:
- Many patients are nervous, so the site should feel calm, friendly and human
- Make booking or requesting an appointment possible from every page
- Treatment pages with clear explanations and fees rank well and build trust
- Real team photos and patient reviews matter more than stock smiles

Choosing a dentist is personal, and for many people a bit daunting. A new patient visiting your website is asking: will I be looked after, can I afford it, and how do I book? Answer those three questions clearly and you'll convert far more visitors than a site full of clinical jargon.

## Reassurance comes first

- **Warm, real photography** of your team and practice
- **Friendly language:** "nervous patients welcome", "we'll go at your pace"
- **A clean, bright design** that feels modern and hygienic
- **Clear information** about what happens at a first visit

## Make booking easy

- A "Book appointment" button in the header and repeated down the page
- Online booking if your practice system supports it; otherwise a short request form
- A tappable phone number
- Emergency appointment information clearly visible
- Opening hours, including evenings and weekends

## Treatment pages

Give each main treatment its own page. Patients search by treatment: "teeth whitening [town]", "dental implants cost", "Invisalign near me".

On each page:

- What the treatment is, in plain English
- Who it's for
- What to expect, step by step
- How long it takes
- Fees or a guide price
- Before-and-after photos (with consent)
- FAQs
- A booking button

Typical pages: check-ups, hygiene, whitening, orthodontics and aligners, implants, veneers, crowns, emergency care, children's dentistry.

## Fees and payment

Publish a fee guide. Explain insurance, plans and finance options. Transparency removes one of the biggest barriers to booking.

## Meet the team

A photo, qualifications, registration number, special interests and a line of personality for each clinician. Patients like knowing who'll be treating them.

## Reviews

Display your Google rating and a selection of reviews. Stories from nervous patients who had a good experience are especially persuasive.

## New patient section

A dedicated page covering:

- How to register
- What happens at the first appointment
- Forms to complete in advance
- Offers for new patients
- Parking, access and directions

## Local SEO for dentists

- A complete Google Business Profile with the right categories (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Reviews, requested consistently
- Location in page titles
- Treatment pages targeting "[treatment] [town]"
- Dentist and LocalBusiness schema (guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))

See the full local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Compliance

Dental marketing is regulated. Check your regulator's rules on:

- Displaying registration numbers
- Advertising claims and before-and-after images
- Patient testimonials
- Privacy and consent for forms

When in doubt, ask your indemnity provider.

## Accessibility

Many patients are older or have accessibility needs. Use readable text sizes, good colour contrast and clear navigation. See web accessibility basics (/blog/website-accessibility-basics/).

## A ready-made option

Our Dentava dental design is a bright, reassuring practice site with a smile gallery and new-patient booking, available on the templates page (/templates/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Should a dental website show prices?
Yes. A fee guide builds trust and reduces enquiries from people outside your price range.

### Do we need online booking?
It's increasingly expected. If your system doesn't support it, a simple appointment request form is the next best thing.

### How do dental practices get more new patients online?
A fast, reassuring website, strong treatment pages, an active Google Business Profile and a steady flow of reviews.

# Medical Clinic Website Guide: Trust, Access and Appointments
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/medical-clinic-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build a medical clinic website patients trust: clear services, provider profiles, appointment booking, accessibility and privacy considerations.

Key takeaways:
- Patients need three things quickly: what you treat, who they'll see and how to book
- Provider profiles with photos build trust before the first visit
- Accessibility and privacy are essential, not optional
- Keep health information accurate, reviewed and clearly dated

A clinic website is often visited by someone who's worried, in pain or looking after a family member. They need clear answers quickly. The best healthcare sites are calm, well organised and easy to use for people of all ages and abilities.

## The first screen

- A reassuring headline: "Healthcare that feels personal again"
- A real photo of your team or clinic
- "Book an appointment" and a phone number
- Opening hours and location
- An emergency notice telling people what to do in an urgent situation

## Services

List what you offer, grouped sensibly: general practice, women's health, children's health, chronic disease management, vaccinations, minor procedures, mental health, allied health.

Give key services their own pages with:

- What's involved
- Who it's for
- How to prepare
- Fees or coverage
- How to book

## Provider profiles

For each clinician:

- Professional photo
- Qualifications and registration
- Special interests
- Languages spoken
- Days available
- A short personal note

Patients often choose a doctor from these pages.

## Appointments

- Online booking integrated with your practice system
- Telehealth options, if available
- Clear instructions for repeat prescriptions and results
- New patient registration forms
- Cancellation policy

More in online booking for small businesses (/blog/online-booking-for-small-business/).

## Practical information

- Address, parking, public transport and accessibility
- Hours, including after-hours arrangements
- Fees, insurance and billing
- What to bring to a first appointment

## Accessibility

Healthcare sites serve people who may be elderly, unwell or using assistive technology.

- Large, readable type and strong contrast
- Clear headings and simple navigation
- Keyboard-friendly forms
- Alt text on images
- Plain language

See web accessibility basics (/blog/website-accessibility-basics/).

## Privacy and security

- HTTPS across the site
- Don't collect sensitive health details through basic contact forms
- Use secure, compliant systems for bookings and patient information
- A clear privacy policy
- Follow the rules that apply in your country (HIPAA, GDPR, local health privacy law)

## Health content

Articles and FAQs help patients and bring search traffic. Because health is a "your money or your life" topic, Google holds it to a high standard.

- Have content written or reviewed by a clinician
- Show the author and review date
- Cite reputable sources
- Avoid promising outcomes

## Local SEO

- Google Business Profile with categories, services and booking link
- Reviews, within the bounds of your regulator's rules
- Location in titles
- MedicalClinic and Physician schema

See our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Design

Calm colours, plenty of white space, genuine photography. Avoid clutter and pop-ups. Speed matters: many patients are on phones.

## A ready-made option

Our Meridian Care Clinic design is a trust-building practice site with provider bios, services and appointment requests, available on the templates page (/templates/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can patients book online through the website?
Yes, by integrating your practice management or booking system.

### What should a clinic never put on its site?
Unverified health claims, patient information without consent, or forms that collect sensitive data insecurely.

### How often should the site be updated?
Whenever providers, hours, fees or services change, with a full review at least twice a year.

# Mortgage Broker Website: Turning Rate Shoppers into Clients
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/mortgage-broker-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What a mortgage broker website needs to generate enquiries: trust signals, calculators, service pages for each borrower type, reviews and compliant content.

Key takeaways:
- Trust is everything in financial services, so lead with reviews, credentials and real people
- Calculators draw visitors in and start the conversation
- Create a page for each borrower type: first-time buyers, remortgage, self-employed and more
- Offer a free initial consultation with multiple ways to get in touch

People looking for a mortgage are anxious about the biggest financial commitment of their lives. They compare several brokers and choose the one who seems most trustworthy and easiest to deal with. Your website's job is to be that broker before they've spoken to you.

## Lead with trust

- **Review rating and count** near the top: "5.0 on Google from 186 reviews"
- **Awards and accreditations**
- **Real photos** of the advisers
- **Regulatory details** clearly displayed
- **A friendly, human headline**

MDJ Mortgages does this well: "The mortgage advice Basingstoke trusts, from people who pick up the phone."

## Calculators

Calculators are the most engaging feature on a mortgage site.

- **How much could I borrow?**
- **Monthly repayment**
- **Stamp duty or closing costs**
- **Remortgage savings**

Show an instant indicative result, then offer a personalised figure from an adviser. It's value first, lead capture second.

## A page for each client type

Borrowers search for their own situation.

- First-time buyers
- Home movers
- Remortgage / refinance
- Self-employed and contractors
- Buy-to-let / investment
- Later-life lending
- Poor credit
- Protection and insurance

Each page should explain the process, common worries, what documents are needed and include a relevant client story.

## Explain the process

Three or four steps from first chat to keys in hand. Reassure visitors that the first conversation is free and without obligation.

## Make contact easy

- Book a call (embedded calendar)
- Request a callback
- WhatsApp
- Phone
- A short enquiry form

Different people prefer different routes. Offer several. See adding WhatsApp to your website (/blog/whatsapp-for-business-website/).

## Fees

Be upfront about how you're paid: fee-free, a fixed fee or a percentage. Transparency is both a regulatory requirement in many places and a trust builder.

## Content that brings in borrowers

- First-time buyer guides
- "How much deposit do I need?"
- "Can I get a mortgage if I'm self-employed?"
- "Fixed vs variable rates"
- Local property market updates

Helpful guides rank on Google and position you as the expert. See how to write a blog post that ranks (/blog/how-to-write-a-blog-post-that-ranks/).

## Compliance

Financial promotions are regulated.

- Include required risk warnings ("Your home may be repossessed...")
- Display your regulatory status and firm reference number
- Avoid guarantees
- Keep rate examples current and representative
- Have content approved through your compliance process

## Local SEO

- "Mortgage broker [town]" in titles and headings
- Google Business Profile with reviews (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Local landing pages for nearby towns (how (/blog/local-landing-pages/))
- FinancialService schema

## Design

Financial sites don't need to be dull. A warm, premium design with clear typography stands out against competitors' generic templates and signals competence.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do calculators need to be exact?
They should be indicative and clearly labelled as such, with an invitation to get a personalised figure.

### Should brokers show rates on their site?
Only if you can keep them current and compliant. Many prefer to explain that rates depend on circumstances.

### What converts best on a broker website?
Strong reviews, a useful calculator and an easy way to book a free call.

# Restaurant Website Must-Haves: Menus, Bookings and Local Search
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/restaurant-website-guide/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What every restaurant website needs: a readable menu, online reservations and ordering, great photos, hours, location and the local SEO to be found.

Key takeaways:
- Diners want four things fast: menu, hours, location and a way to book or order
- Publish the menu as text, not only a PDF
- Take direct bookings and orders to avoid high platform commissions
- Keep your Google Business Profile and hours accurate at all times

Someone's hungry. They open your website on their phone. They want to know what you serve, whether you're open, where you are and how to book. If they can't find all four within seconds, they'll pick another restaurant.

## The essentials, above everything

1. **Menu**
2. **Hours**
3. **Address** with a tap-to-navigate map link
4. **Phone**, tappable
5. **Book a table / Order online**

Put these on the homepage and in the header or footer of every page.

## The menu

- **Use real text,** not just a PDF or image. Text loads fast, is readable on phones, works with screen readers and can be indexed by Google.
- **Keep prices current.**
- **Mark dietary options:** vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, allergens.
- **Organise clearly** by course or category.
- **Offer a PDF as a download** if you like, alongside the text version.

## Reservations

- Embed your booking system (OpenTable, Resy, SevenRooms, ResDiary or a simple form)
- Show a "Book a table" button everywhere
- Allow notes for allergies and occasions
- Send confirmation and reminder messages

## Online ordering

Third-party delivery apps bring reach and take a large commission. Direct ordering through your own site keeps the margin and the customer relationship.

- Offer pickup and delivery through your own system where practical
- Link clearly to it: "Order direct"
- Still list delivery apps if you use them

## Photography

Food sells through pictures.

- Invest in a short professional shoot
- Show dishes, the room and the people
- Compress images so the site stays fast (image SEO (/blog/image-seo/))
- Avoid stock food photos

## Tell your story

A short about section: who you are, what you cook, where ingredients come from. People love to know.

## Extras worth adding

- Private dining and events enquiries
- Gift vouchers
- Catering menu
- Upcoming events
- Newsletter sign-up
- Press and awards

## Local search

Most diners find restaurants through Google Maps.

- Keep your Google Business Profile complete: menu link, booking link, photos, attributes (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Update hours for holidays
- Reply to reviews
- Add Restaurant and Menu schema (guide (/blog/schema-markup-guide/))

See the full local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Mobile and speed

Nearly all restaurant browsing is on phones. Design for a thumb, test on mobile data and skip auto-playing music or heavy intro animations.

## Common mistakes

- Menu only as a huge PDF
- Out-of-date hours
- No prices
- Music that plays automatically
- A site that only works on desktop
- Hidden address

## Catering and food manufacturing

If you supply equipment or cater commercially, a catalog-style site works well. IB Refrigeration, for example, presents display counters, food carts and commercial kitchen equipment as a browsable product range.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do restaurants still need a website with Instagram and delivery apps?
Yes. A website is the one place you fully control, and it's what Google links to from your profile.

### How often should the menu be updated?
Whenever dishes or prices change. An out-of-date menu causes disappointment and bad reviews.

### Can I take orders without paying commission?
Yes, with a direct ordering system on your own site, paying only payment processing fees.

# Websites for Trades and Home Services: Get More Calls and Quotes
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/tradesperson-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

What plumbers, electricians, roofers, builders and other trades need from a website to win more local jobs: trust, proof, service pages and easy contact.

Key takeaways:
- Customers want to know you're local, reliable and available
- Click-to-call and a short quote form should be on every page
- Photos of real jobs and reviews do the selling
- A page per service and per area brings in Google traffic

When a boiler breaks or a roof leaks, people search on their phone and call one of the first few businesses that look trustworthy. A trade website doesn't need to be fancy. It needs to be fast, clear and convincing in about ten seconds.

## What customers are looking for

1. Do you do the job I need?
2. Do you cover my area?
3. Can I trust you?
4. How do I get hold of you right now?

Design every page around those four questions.

## Homepage must-haves

- **A plain headline:** "Plumbing and heating in Leeds. Same-day callouts."
- **A tappable phone number** at the top
- **"Get a free quote" button**
- **Trust strip:** years trading, review rating, accreditations, insurance
- **Services** with icons or photos
- **Areas covered**
- **Recent work** photos
- **Reviews**
- **A short form** at the bottom

## Service pages

One page per main service, because customers search specifically: "boiler repair", "consumer unit replacement", "flat roof repair", "kitchen fitter".

Each page: what's included, typical problems you solve, rough pricing or how you quote, photos, FAQs, and a call to action.

## Area pages

A page for each key town or district you cover, with local jobs and reviews. See how to create local landing pages (/blog/local-landing-pages/).

## Proof

- **Before-and-after photos** of real jobs
- **Google reviews,** shown with stars and count
- **Accreditations:** trade bodies, licences, Gas Safe, NICEIC, manufacturer approvals
- **Insurance** and guarantees
- **Photos of you and your van.** People like seeing who'll turn up.

## Make contact effortless

- Phone number in the header, sticky on mobile
- WhatsApp button for photos of the problem (how to add it (/blog/whatsapp-for-business-website/))
- A quote form with three or four fields plus photo upload
- Emergency callout information
- Opening hours

## Pricing

You don't need a full price list. Even a guide ("boiler service from £80", "callout fee £60") builds trust and filters time-wasters.

## Local SEO

For trades, Google Maps is the shop window.

- Google Business Profile with service areas, photos of jobs and weekly updates (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Ask for a review after every job
- Consistent name, address and phone everywhere
- LocalBusiness schema

Full plan in our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Keep it fast and simple

- Loads in under two seconds on mobile
- Large text and buttons
- No pop-ups blocking the phone number
- Works well in poor signal

## Extras that help

- A short video introducing yourself
- Finance options for bigger jobs
- A maintenance plan or service contract page
- A blog answering common questions: "why is my boiler losing pressure?"

## Commercial work

If you also do commercial contracts, add a separate page with relevant accreditations, insurance levels and case studies. Business buyers look for different proof.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a website if I get work from Facebook and word of mouth?
A website makes you findable on Google, gives new customers confidence and works when referrals slow down.

### How much should a trades website cost?
A solid lead-generating site typically costs $1,500 to $5,000. See how much a website costs (/blog/how-much-does-a-website-cost-small-business/).

### What's the most important feature?
A phone number people can tap, followed closely by reviews.

---

# Online Booking for Small Businesses: How to Add It to Your Website
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/online-booking-for-small-business/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to add online booking to a small business website: choosing a tool, embedding it well, taking deposits, reducing no-shows and avoiding common mistakes.

Key takeaways:
- Online booking captures customers outside business hours
- Choose a tool that fits your industry and syncs with your calendar
- Embed booking on your own site and keep the path to two or three taps
- Deposits and automated reminders cut no-shows significantly

A large share of appointments are booked outside working hours, when nobody's answering the phone. Online booking means those customers can commit there and then, while you're with a client, at dinner or asleep.

## Who benefits

- Salons, barbers and spas
- Clinics, dentists and therapists
- Coaches and consultants
- Fitness studios and personal trainers
- Photographers
- Trades offering fixed-price services or assessments
- Restaurants and venues

If customers book time with you, it applies.

## Choosing a booking tool

| Need | Popular options |
| --- | --- |
| One-to-one calls and consultations | Calendly, TidyCal, Cal.com, Google Calendar booking |
| Salons and spas | Fresha, Booksy, Vagaro, Timely |
| Classes and studios | Mindbody, Momence, Acuity |
| Clinics | Cliniko, Jane, practice-specific systems |
| Restaurants | OpenTable, Resy, ResDiary |
| General services | Square Appointments, Acuity, SimplyBook |

### What to look for

- Calendar sync, so you're never double-booked
- Embeds cleanly in your website
- Email and SMS reminders
- Deposits or card capture
- Staff and service management
- Fair pricing and no punitive commission
- You keep ownership of your customer data

## Embedding it properly

- **Keep customers on your site** with an embedded widget where possible
- **A "Book now" button** in the header on every page
- **Link each service** directly to its booking flow
- **Match the look:** colours and fonts close to your brand
- **Test on mobile.** Most bookings happen there.

## Keep the flow short

Ideal path: choose service, choose time, enter details, confirm. Every extra step loses people. Ask only for what you need at booking; collect the rest later.

## Reduce no-shows

- **Deposits or card on file** for longer appointments
- **Automated reminders** 24 to 48 hours before, and again on the day
- **Easy rescheduling** via a link
- **A clear cancellation policy** shown before they confirm

## Custom booking flows

Off-the-shelf tools suit most businesses. A custom flow makes sense when you need something specific: multi-step quotes, packages, group bookings, or a booking experience that's part of your brand. We've built custom booking for an escape-room venue and enrol-and-pay flows for school dance programmes.

## After the booking

- Instant confirmation with a calendar invite
- Preparation instructions
- Directions or video link
- A follow-up afterwards asking for a review

## Common mistakes

- Sending customers to a separate site that looks nothing like yours
- Too many required fields
- No mobile testing
- Hidden booking link
- No reminders
- Not showing prices or durations

## Measure it

Track how many visitors start a booking and how many complete it. If many abandon, shorten the flow or reconsider the deposit amount.

## Frequently asked questions

### Will customers still phone to book?
Some will. Offer both. Over time, most businesses see a majority of bookings move online.

### Is online booking expensive?
Many tools have free or low-cost plans for solo businesses. Costs rise with staff numbers and features.

### Can booking connect to payments?
Yes. Most tools integrate with Stripe, Square or PayPal for deposits and full payments. See accepting payments on your website (/blog/stripe-payments-website/).

---

# Adding WhatsApp to Your Website: A Practical Guide for Small Businesses
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/whatsapp-for-business-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How and why to add a WhatsApp chat button to your business website, with setup steps, message templates, etiquette and tips for turning chats into customers.

Key takeaways:
- Many customers would rather message than call or fill in a form
- A click-to-chat link takes minutes to set up and costs nothing
- Pre-filled messages make starting a conversation effortless
- Set expectations for reply times and keep conversations professional

For a lot of customers, sending a quick WhatsApp is easier than making a phone call or completing a form. In many countries it's the default way people talk to businesses. Adding it to your website is one of the simplest changes you can make to get more enquiries.

## Why it works

- **Low effort.** One tap opens a chat.
- **Familiar.** People already use it daily.
- **Asynchronous.** They can ask now and you can reply between jobs.
- **Rich.** Customers can send photos, voice notes and locations.
- **Personal.** A conversation builds trust quickly.

We use it ourselves. One of our favourite pieces of client feedback arrived as a WhatsApp from a wedding photographer: "I got a lot of compliments on it."

## Step 1: set up WhatsApp Business

Download the free WhatsApp Business app and register your business number. Then:

- Add your business name, logo, description, address and hours
- Set a **greeting message** for new chats
- Set an **away message** for out-of-hours
- Create **quick replies** for common questions
- Add a **catalogue** if you sell products or packages

## Step 2: create a click-to-chat link

The format is:

`https://wa.me/<number>?text=<message>`

Use your full number with country code and no plus sign, spaces or dashes. The optional `text` adds a pre-filled message, for example: "Hi, I found you online and would like a quote."

Pre-filling the first message removes the awkward blank box and tells you where the enquiry came from.

## Step 3: add it to your website

- **A floating button** in the corner of every page
- **In the header or contact section** next to your phone number
- **On service pages** with a tailored pre-filled message: "Hi, I'm interested in boiler servicing"
- **On the thank-you page** after a form submission

Keep the button visible without covering content or other buttons on mobile.

## Step 4: reply well

- **Respond quickly** in business hours. Speed is the whole advantage.
- **Use their name** and answer the actual question.
- **Keep messages short.**
- **Move to a call or booking** when it makes sense: "Would a quick call be easier? Here's my calendar."
- **Stay professional.** It's still business communication.

## Etiquette and compliance

- Only message people who contacted you or opted in
- Don't add customers to groups or broadcast lists without consent
- Respect privacy laws in your country
- Avoid sharing sensitive information over chat
- Mention WhatsApp in your privacy policy

## When to upgrade

The free app suits most small businesses. If several staff need to answer from one number, or you want automation and CRM integration, look at the WhatsApp Business Platform through an approved provider.

## Combine with other channels

WhatsApp works best alongside, not instead of, a phone number and a form. Different customers prefer different routes. See contact forms that convert (/blog/contact-form-best-practices/).

## Track it

Add tracking to your WhatsApp link clicks in analytics so you know how many enquiries it generates and from which pages.

## Add automation

A chatbot can answer common questions, collect details and hand over to you when needed. See AI chatbots for small business (/blog/ai-chatbot-for-small-business/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a separate phone number?
It's wise to use a business number so personal and work chats stay separate.

### Is WhatsApp suitable for every business?
It suits most service businesses. For regulated sectors such as healthcare and finance, check what you're allowed to discuss over chat.

### Will it slow my website down?
A simple link button adds no weight. Avoid heavy third-party chat widgets if a plain link does the job.

---

# Barbershop Website Guide: Fill Your Chairs with Online Bookings
URL: https://www.codebunny.net/blog/barbershop-website/
Author: Bhavansh Arora · Updated 2026-11-16

How to build a barbershop website with the right attitude: online booking, a clear price list, barber profiles, a gallery of cuts and local search visibility.

Key takeaways:
- Booking, prices and location are what clients need most
- A strong visual identity sets a barbershop apart
- Barber profiles with their own booking links help clients find their person
- Google Business Profile reviews bring in walk-ins and new regulars

A barbershop is a brand as much as a service. The best shops have a look, a sound and a feel, and their website should carry it. It also has to do the practical job: let someone book a fade at 11pm on a Sunday for Tuesday afternoon.

## What every barbershop site needs

### Online booking

- "Book now" in the header and hero
- Choose barber, service and time
- Reminders by text
- Walk-in information if you take them

Booksy, Fresha, Squire and Square are common choices. More in online booking for small businesses (/blog/online-booking-for-small-business/).

### A price list

Cuts, fades, beard trims, hot towel shaves, kids' cuts, packages. Clear prices and durations.

### Location and hours

Address, map, parking and opening times, visible on every page.

### The barbers

Photo, name, specialities, Instagram handle and a personal booking link for each. Regulars follow barbers.

### A gallery

Real cuts from your chairs. Fresh fades, beard work, the shop itself. Update it often.

## Give it attitude

Barbershops have some of the best branding of any local business. Use it.

- **Typography:** bold serifs, vintage scripts or sharp modern sans
- **Colour:** dark and moody, classic red-white-blue or clean monochrome
- **Photography:** atmospheric shots of the shop and the craft
- **Voice:** confident and short. "Sharp cuts. Sharper confidence."

Our Crown & Blade design shows how far a classic barbershop identity can go:

## Extras that pay off

- **Products** for sale: pomades, oils, tools
- **Gift cards**
- **Memberships** or loyalty schemes
- **Groom and wedding party packages**
- **Hiring page** for new barbers
- **Events and collaborations**

## Local SEO

- Google Business Profile with category "Barber shop", booking link and weekly photos (checklist (/blog/google-business-profile-optimization/))
- Reviews from regulars; ask at the chair with a QR code by the till
- "Barber in [neighbourhood]" in page titles
- Consistent details across Instagram, Facebook and directories

See our local SEO guide (/blog/local-seo-guide/).

## Mobile first

Nearly every visitor is on a phone, often coming from Instagram. Big buttons, fast loading, booking in two taps.

## Instagram and your website

Instagram shows the work. The website turns interest into bookings and shows up on Google. Link them: booking link in your bio, feed highlights on your site.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do barbershops need a website if they use a booking app?
Yes. Your own site ranks on Google, shows your brand properly and isn't dependent on one platform.

### Should I list every barber?
Yes, with photos. Clients choose people.

### Can I buy a ready-made barbershop website?
Yes. Our Crown & Blade design is available on the templates page (/templates/) and sells to one owner only.
